I thought all that later, in the car, as a reason. I went because somebody had made me laugh and I hadn't been for a month.

They offered on the Thursday. More money than I'd have asked for, which was the second thing that should have bothered me. I told Ana at dinner. She said, "A bank? You hate banks," and I said it wasn't a bank, it was older than a bank, and she said that was worse, and then she said, "You've been nicer this week," and I said had I, and she said, "Yeah. Since Wednesday. Did something happen on Wednesday?"
"I played golf with a man who chipped in from the fringe."
"That's it?"
"He said he'd never be able to explain it to anyone."
She looked at me for a bit. "Okay," she said. "I'll take it. I'll take Wednesday golf man. Bring him round."

I drove home from the course the next Wednesday with the window down and the flask coffee in me and Buddy asleep in the back, and I noticed that I was in a good mood, which I hadn't been for a year, and I noticed myself noticing.
And I didn't ask why. That's the honest report. For once in my life there was a thing that had changed and I didn't go looking for the cause. I just drove.
He'd asked about the dog first. I keep coming back to that. Everybody asks about the dog eventually. He'd asked first.

chapters.title: Utrecht, 1993
chapters.what: Third person. Invented people, invented paper, real city. Answers the question the sentence just asked: *who says yes?*
blocks: Wim Koster waited until the corridor was empty before he closed his office door, which was a thing he had never done in eleven years as head of department, and he noticed himself doing it, and he did it anyway.

The paper was on his desk. Thirty-one pages, double-spaced, with the figures stapled at the back the way Verhoef always did it, because Verhoef believed the argument should stand without the pictures. Two rooms, shielded, forty metres apart. Two people who had sat together for twenty minutes beforehand and were then separated. A light flashed in one room. Something moved, a little, in the other. Not much. Verhoef had the decency to say not much in the abstract, which was more than most people managed. The effect was small and it was there, and it was there on four runs out of five, and the fifth run was the one Verhoef had written about at the greatest length, because he was that kind of scientist, and because he was a friend.
The telephone had a long cord. Koster carried it to the window.
"It's Wim," he said. "From the department. You said to call if."

"Yes." The voice on the other end was pleasant and belonged to a man he had met twice, at the foundation, over lunch, and whose surname he could never afterwards remember, which he had come to understand was deliberate. "Go ahead."

"There's a paper. A colleague. He's submitted it, I'm the internal reader." Koster looked at the bicycles in the rack below, the chained wheels, the one with no saddle that had been there since September. "It's good. That's the problem. It's careful."
"What's it about?"
Koster told him. The rooms. The light. The movement. He heard himself make it sound smaller than it was, and he heard the other man hear that, and neither of them remarked on it.
"Recall," the man said, after a moment. It was not a question. It was the sound of a word being placed in a column.
"He doesn't call it that."
"No. He wouldn't." A pause with paper in it. "Is he the sort who corrects himself in public, your colleague?"

Koster thought about Verhoef at the Christmas drinks, telling a room full of people that his own best-known result from 1987 was probably an artefact of the cabling, laughing at himself, buying the next round. "Yes."

"That's worse," the man said, mildly. "Alright. Here's what we'd like. Not the paper; the paper's nothing, the paper's four runs in a cupboard. The category. Does your department have a line for instrumentation?"
"Of course."
"Then it's instrumentation. Cable artefacts, shielding, that family. File it there. Review it there. Let it be read by people who read that line. It'll find its level."
"It isn't instrumentation."

"No," the man agreed. "But it will be. That's all we ever do, Wim. We don't change what a thing is. We change where it's kept." He sounded, briefly, as though he were quoting somebody. "You're not being asked to lie about anything. You're being asked to shelve."

Koster had been going to say something about Verhoef, about the fifth run and the length of the discussion of it, about what it was like to watch a careful man be careful. He found that he was looking at the bicycle with no saddle instead.
"And the other matter," he said.
"Yes. That's confirmed. Yourself, Marianne, the two children." The voice did something small and warm. "You asked about your mother."
"I did."
"It's a budgeting thing, Wim. I'm sorry. The allocation is the allocation. I did ask."
"I understand."
"I know you do. That's why we talk to you." A chair creaked, four hundred kilometres away, in a room Koster would never see. "You'll let me know when it's filed."
"Good man."

Koster put the telephone back on the desk and stood for a while with his hand on it, as though it might ring again and take it back. It didn't. He opened the door. The corridor was still empty. He walked down it, past the noticeboard with the Christmas drinks and the seminar on superconductivity, and he knocked on Verhoef's door, and when Verhoef looked up with that face, that hopeful ruined face of a man who has handed over the best thing he has ever done, Koster said, "It's very good, Anton. Really. I've got some thoughts on the shielding section," and Verhoef said, "I knew you would," and smiled, and pulled out the chair.

They talked for two hours. Koster was kind the whole time. It cost him nothing. That was the part he would think about, years later, in a chair of his own, when he'd stopped being able to remember the foundation man's name and had never once stopped being able to remember the bicycle.
The paper was reclassified in March. It was not published. Verhoef kept his copy. His grandson kept it after him.

chapters.title: Leave it
chapters.what: Follows the sentence. The name arrives on paper. The first lie told to his face.
blocks: I'm going to tell you about a Tuesday at work, and I need you to stay with me through it, because it's the most boring thing in this story and it turned out to be the whole story.

My job, in one sentence, is to look at screens that look at other things. Ten thousand systems, every night, breathing, and my programs count the breaths and put the counts on a wall. Green is fine. Amber is a meeting. Red is my phone at four in the morning. Most of my working life happens in the green, which sounds restful and is actually a kind of low-grade dread, because green doesn't mean nothing's wrong. Green means nothing's wrong that we decided to look for.

Which is why I have the habit. I don't look at the colours. I look at the list under the colours. All the little jobs, the things that run on timers, the housekeeping. Every one has a name, an owner, and a reason, or it's supposed to. In a company our size the list is a few thousand lines long, and nobody reads it, the way nobody reads the ingredients, and I read it the way I read the ingredients, which is to say completely and with a growing sense that I'm the only person who ever has.

The sentence had been in my kitchen for a week by then. Page 118 was in my bag, both copies, in a folder, because I'd stopped trusting the house to keep them. And I'd been sleeping badly, and I don't know whether that's why I saw it or whether I'd have seen it anyway. I've thought about that more than I should. I'd like to think I'd have seen it anyway.
It was called rcl-agg.

That's it. That's the name. Seven characters, which is the kind of name you give something when you're in a hurry or when you don't want it to be read. No owner. The owner field, which is mandatory, which you literally cannot save the form without, was blank. No ticket. No description. And it ran, every night, at fourteen minutes past two, for about nine seconds, and sent roughly forty kilobytes of something to an address that, when I looked it up, resolved nowhere. Not to one of ours. Not to a cloud. Nowhere. The name of the address had the shape of a real one, like a sentence has the shape of a real sentence, and when you asked the internet where it was, the internet said it had never heard of it.

I did the obvious things. I checked the history: who created it, when. There was no history. The first entry in the history of rcl-agg was rcl-agg, already running, like it had been there before the list was. I checked the other offices. Same thing, same minute, same forty kilobytes, in all of them. I checked the backups going back as far as the backups go, which is a long way, because the man who set up the backups was paranoid in the useful way, and it was in all of them too. Every night. Fourteen minutes past two. Nine seconds. Nowhere.
I sat with that for a while. Then I wrote it down and put it in the stand-up.
<hr />

Stand-up is fifteen minutes in a glass box, standing, so that nobody gets comfortable enough to talk. Pieter runs it. Pieter is my manager and a decent man in the specific way that managers are decent, which is that he will defend you to the end of the earth about anything that doesn't cost him anything.
I went last. I always go last; the persona likes to see the room first.
"One thing," I said. "There's a job on the list with no owner. Runs nightly. Sends data to an address that doesn't exist. I want to find out what it is."
"Which job?"
I told him.

Something happened in Pieter's face. I don't want to make it bigger than it was. It was the size of a man remembering an appointment. "That one's old," he said. "It's a diagnostic artefact. From the migration."
"Which migration?"
"The big one. Before your time." He looked at his screen. "Leave it."
"It sends data somewhere."

"It sends diagnostics somewhere. It's fine. It's been fine for years. Leave it, James, honestly, we've got the payments thing and the Antwerp thing and I'd rather have you on either of those than on a cron job from the Stone Age." He smiled, and it was a real smile, and he meant it, and the meeting moved on, and Frank caught my eye across the box and did a little skull with his hand, which is our thing now, apparently, which I've decided to find charming.
Here's the problem. I was there for the big migration. I did the big migration, a lot of it, two years before Pieter joined. There wasn't a rcl-agg in it. I'd have known. I read the ingredients.

I didn't say that. I want to be clear that the reason I didn't say it was not courage or cunning. I didn't say it because Pieter had said leave it in the tone you use for something that's already been decided, and I'd spent thirty years learning that when my memory and the paperwork disagree, I'm the error. So I nodded. And I walked back to my desk, and I sat down, and I felt the thing I'd felt in the kitchen with the two books, the old feeling lifting its head, and I understood, for the first time in my life, that I was feeling it about a person.

Because Pieter hadn't been wrong. People are wrong all the time; it's the main thing people are. Pieter had been ready. He'd had the sentence before I'd finished the question. A diagnostic artefact from the migration. Said the way you say your postcode.
Why lie here?

I'd like to say that's where I started. It isn't. Where I started was: why would anyone bother? And that question kept me at my desk until seven, doing nothing, with the list open, reading the ingredients.
<hr />
Ana was in the kitchen with the dogs when I got home, and the dogs were in the kitchen with Ana's dinner, strategically.
"You're late."
"Payments thing."

"Mm." She was reading something on her phone, and she lifted it without looking at me, the way she lifts it when she wants me to see that she's not looking. "You've got a letter. Actual paper. It's on the side."

It was a good envelope, the kind with a lining, and my name was on it in a hand I didn't know, and that was the first time in this whole business that I saw my own name written down by somebody who was part of it. I'd written, two weeks before, to a dealer in the north, an antiquarian, a man with a website from 2004 and a reputation, asking a dull question: whether he'd ever seen a Leiden-printed second impression of a 1926 English survey of flood legends, and whether he happened to know who'd done the printing.
Dear Mr Klippe, it began, and I stood in my kitchen and felt oddly caught, as if I'd been spotted in a shop I'd told everyone I didn't go to.

He had seen one. He'd sold one, in 2011, to a university man in Deventer, who'd been very particular about the impression. He didn't know the printer; the Leiden houses of that period were "mostly gone and mostly undocumented, as I expect you know." He wished me luck with "what I assume is a bibliographical question," and then, as a postscript, in a slightly different ink, as though he'd come back to the letter after a cup of tea: I would gently say that this title attracts a certain kind of enquiry, and that I have found, over forty years, that it is wisest to be plain about one's reasons.
I read that twice. Then I read it to Buddy, who was under the table in case of a chicken event.
"'Plain about one's reasons,'" I said. "What does that mean?"
"It means he thinks you're a nutter," said Ana, not looking up. "What's the book?"
"The one with the two copies."
"The one you measured."
"The one I measured."
She put the phone down then. "And a man in a shop in — where?"
"Groningen."
"A man in a shop in Groningen has written you a letter on nice paper to tell you to be careful."
"To be plain."
"That's what careful sounds like in a shop." She picked the phone back up. "Did you know Mora ate half a sponge today? Just so we're all plain about our reasons."

I laughed. It was a good line. She has better lines than I do and always has; mine are built and hers just arrive. And I sat down and ate with them, and told her a did-you-know about the Ethiopian calendar being seven years behind everybody else's because they'd counted the start of things differently and never seen a reason to stop, and she said that was a good one, and asked if that meant she was thirty-one in Ethiopia, and I said it did, and she said she'd think about moving.
It was a good evening. I'd like that known. There were a lot of good evenings and I was there for all of them, and I'm not going to pretend I wasn't, to make what came later look cleaner than it was.
<hr />
At one in the morning I was at the kitchen table with the laptop, because of course I was.

I'd like to tell you I was thinking about Tresidder. I wasn't. I was thinking about Pieter's face. About how the sentence had been ready. And about a thing I'd read years ago and filed under interesting-wrong and never thought about again: that the easiest way to hide something isn't to hide it. It's to give it a boring name, and a boring reason, and put it on a list that nobody reads, in the one place where the people who do read lists have already been told to stop.
Two options, I told the dog, who was asleep and did not care.

One: it's exactly what Pieter said. An old diagnostic job that somebody forgot to document, sending its little report to a server that was decommissioned years ago, into the void, every night, like a dog waiting at a door for a man who's not coming home. Sad. Boring. Common as dirt. I've seen fifty of them.
Two: somebody knows exactly what it is. And has told Pieter what to say.
I'm a reasonable man. I gave option one eighty-five per cent, out of habit, and then I sat there and looked at that number and thought about where I'd last used it.
Then I did a small thing. Not a brave thing. A small thing, the kind you can walk back from.

I opened a ticket. Low priority. Plain language. Unowned scheduled job rcl-agg — request owner and purpose for the inventory. I assigned it to nobody, which is how you assign a thing to the system itself, and I put it in the queue where the dull tickets go to be ignored for a year, and I went to bed.
I'd like to be able to tell you I slept.
Forty kilobytes. Every night. For years. To nowhere.
Nothing waits that long at a door unless it's been told the door will open.

chapters.title: The payload
chapters.what: Follows Leave it. He captures the forty kilobytes. A list of people who wrote something down. His own line appears the night after he asked.
blocks: There's a thing engineers do when someone tells them to leave something alone, and it isn't disobedience. I want to be precise about this, because Pieter would call it disobedience and he'd be wrong, and the difference is the only defence I've got.

If a job runs on your systems and you don't know what it does, you don't open it. Opening it is a decision. You don't stop it, you don't change it, you don't touch it. You stand next to it while it runs and you watch what comes out. That's not interfering. That's the job description. I've done it a thousand times to things I was allowed to look at and nobody ever called it anything but Tuesday.

So on the Thursday night I set an alarm for ten past two, and I went downstairs in my socks, and I opened my laptop on the kitchen table where the two copies of page 118 still lived in their folder, and I waited for fourteen minutes past.
Buddy came and lay across my feet. He does that when I'm up at the wrong time. He doesn't ask why. He just makes sure that if I get up to do something stupid, I'll have to move a dog first.
<hr />

I'm going to describe what I did in a way that will satisfy nobody. The technical people will find it too vague and everyone else will find it too much. Fine. The honest version is: I watched the door the job sends things through, and when it sent something, I kept a copy. That's it. I didn't break anything. I didn't log in as anyone I'm not. The data went where it always goes. It also went into a file on my laptop called, I'm embarrassed to say, nothing.txt, because if Ana came down for water I wanted the screen to tell the truth.

02:14:00. Nine seconds. Forty-one kilobytes, which is nothing. A photo of the dogs is a hundred times that. Forty-one kilobytes is a shopping list. It's an email without an attachment. It's the amount of text a person could read in the time it takes to make coffee.

I opened it expecting noise. Diagnostics look like noise. Timestamps, hexadecimal, the digestive sounds of a system talking to itself. Pieter had said diagnostic artefact and some part of me, the part that has spent thirty years losing arguments with paperwork, expected to open the file and find exactly that and go back to bed feeling like the fool, which is a feeling I've made my peace with.
It wasn't noise.
It was a list.
One line per entry, one hundred and twelve lines. Each line was an employee ID, the eight-digit number we all have on the back of our badges, and then a tab, and then two words.
Not a sentence. Two words. Lowercase. Like a note someone writes to themselves.
40217733 posted (forum) 40193058 wrote (dealer) 40221904 asked (hr) 40188120 searched (archive) 40209417 posted (forum)
I sat there with Buddy on my feet and read all hundred and twelve, and then I read them again, and the second time I wasn't reading the IDs. I was reading the verbs.
Posted. Wrote. Asked. Searched. Requested. Enquired. Raised.

Every one of them was a thing a person does with words, to someone else, on purpose. Nobody on the list had thought anything. You can't put a thought in a file. Every line was a moment when somebody in my company had stopped, and typed, or picked up a pen, or opened their mouth in a meeting, and put a question somewhere it could be read.
And the thing in brackets was where.
<hr />

I'd like to tell you I understood it then. I didn't. I want that on the record, because the version of this story where I'm clever is the version where you shouldn't trust me. What I did was the thing I do, which is stupider and slower and the only reason I'm alive: I checked whether I was on it.
My number is 40176502. I know it the way you know your own phone number, because I've typed it into a hundred forms. I searched the file.
Nothing.

I felt two things at once, and I've thought about which came first and I can't tell you. One was relief, the ordinary animal kind. The other was something that took me a day to name, and the name is disappointment. A hundred and twelve people in my building had done something that got them put on a list that went somewhere nobody could find at fourteen minutes past two in the morning, and I'd been reading old books on a kitchen floor for a month and asking questions in my own head, and I hadn't made the cut. Whatever this was, it wasn't about me.
That was Thursday.
<hr />
I need to tell you what else I'd done that week, because the order matters and I almost missed it.

Tuesday was the stand-up. Tuesday I'd said, out loud, in a glass box, in front of Pieter and Frank and six other people, there's a job on the list with no owner, I want to find out what it is. And Pieter had said leave it, and I'd left it, out loud, and gone back to my desk.
Thursday night I captured the file. A hundred and twelve lines.

Friday night I captured it again. I wasn't going to. I'd told myself Thursday was enough, that I had the shape of it and the shape was somebody else's problem. But I woke at two anyway, because the body learns a time faster than it learns a lesson, and Buddy was already at the bottom of the stairs looking up at me like I was late.
02:14:00. Nine seconds. Forty-one kilobytes.
A hundred and thirteen lines.

I didn't search for my number. I didn't have to. New entries go at the bottom; it's a list, and whoever wrote the thing that writes it was tidy. I scrolled down past the hundred and twelve I'd read twice the night before, and the last line was:
40176502 asked (job)
<hr />
I'm going to try to describe the next few minutes accurately, which means boringly.

I didn't panic. I didn't feel watched, not yet; that came later and in a different room. What I felt, sitting at my kitchen table at two in the morning with my own badge number on a list I wasn't supposed to have, was the specific, cold, almost pleasant feeling I get at work when a system finally tells me what it is.
Because it had. In two words. Asked (job).

The list wasn't a list of people who'd done something wrong. Nobody on it had broken a rule. It was a list of people who had asked. Posted a question on a forum. Written to a dealer. Enquired at HR. Searched an archive. Raised a thing in a meeting. The job didn't count what you did or what you knew or what you thought at four in the morning on a kitchen floor. It counted whether you'd turned it into words and handed the words to someone.

I'd been on this for a month and I hadn't been on the list, because for a month I'd kept it in my head and in my kitchen and in a folder in a bag. And then on Tuesday I'd said eleven words in a meeting, and on Friday I was on the list, with a reason beside my name that was exactly, precisely true.
You don't need to read minds. People write.
I looked at the bracket. (job). Not (forum), not (dealer). Someone, or something, had a category for people who asked about the thing itself. I was the only one in it.
<hr />
Buddy had gone back to sleep across my feet. Mora was upstairs on the bed, in my place, which she takes the moment I leave it and defends on my return like a tenant with rights.
I sat there and I did what I do, which is think about the plumbing, because the plumbing is the only part of any mystery I've ever been qualified to look at.

Whatever made the list ran inside our systems. It had to; it was reading our forums and our HR tickets and our stand-up notes, or someone's notes of the stand-up, which was a thought I put down carefully and did not pick up again that night. It ran at the same time in every office. It had been in the backups for as long as there had been backups. And it sent its hundred-odd lines, every night, through a door that opened for nine seconds to somewhere that didn't exist, and closed.

Someone had put it there. Someone paid for it to stay. And someone, somewhere, at fourteen minutes past two, received a list of names every night and knew, by the next morning, who in a four-hundred-year-old bank had asked a question.

There's a story I'd read years ago and filed under things that happen to other people. A technician in San Francisco, an ordinary one, the kind of man who reads the wiring diagrams because somebody has to, found a locked room on the sixth floor of his own building where the internet was being copied through a splitter to a government agency. He found it because he read the documents nobody read. I'd always liked that story. I'd liked it the way you like stories about people who are a bit like you, from a safe distance. I didn't like it that night. That night I thought about what happened to him after, which was lawyers and a long time of being called a crank, and then being right, which as far as I can tell didn't help.
I closed the laptop. I didn't delete nothing.txt. I renamed it, which is the kind of brave I am.
<hr />
Here is what I understood by the time I went back upstairs, and here is what I didn't, because I want both on the record.

I understood that asking had a cost, and that the cost was being counted, and that I'd paid it on Tuesday without knowing the price. I understood that the hundred and twelve other people on that list had each paid it too, for a forum post or a letter or a question to HR, and that most of them had no idea they were on anything. I understood that Pieter had looked at me across a glass box with a face the size of a man remembering an appointment and said leave it, and that whatever he knew, he knew at least that much: that there was something to leave.

What I didn't understand was what the list was for. A list of people who ask is a strange thing to want. It's not a list of thieves or leakers or people who'd fail a background check. It's a list of the curious. And a hundred and twelve curious people in one bank, counted nightly, sent nowhere, is either the most pointless piece of software ever written or it's a piece of something much bigger, the way one gear is a piece of a clock.

I got into bed. Mora moved over by one dog's width, which is her maximum concession. Ana was asleep on her side with her hand under her cheek, and I lay there in the dark next to her and didn't tell her, and I knew already that not telling her was going to be a bigger problem than the list.
The alarm was still set for ten past two. I didn't turn it off.
I'd stopped asking out loud. I want to be clear that I hadn't stopped asking.

chapters.title: The control case
chapters.what: The method, shown. The thin book opened. The professor got there first.
blocks: One hit is a story. Two hits is a coincidence. You don't have anything until you've tried to make it go away and it won't.

That's not wisdom. That's the job. Somebody calls at four in the morning and says the system is dying, and the first thing you do, before you look at the system, is find out whether it's the system or the thing that's watching the system. Half the time the patient is fine and the monitor is broken. People hate that answer. It's the correct answer about half the time.
So before I let myself believe a word of what the kitchen floor had told me, I had to try to kill it. Properly. In writing.
<hr />
The first thing I did was buy another copy.

Second impression, 1931, the Leiden printing. It's not rare; that's the point of it, it turns out, it was printed for the continent and the continent didn't want it, and you can have one for the price of a pizza from any of six Dutch dealers who'd love to see the back of it. Mine came from Zwolle in a padded envelope, smelling of somebody's attic, and I took it into the kitchen and laid it next to the other two and opened all three to page 118.
Blemish, top margin: present. Two typos: present. Arisen among the first.

So it wasn't my copy. It was the run. Every second impression ever sold said the new sentence. Whoever did it had done it once and let the presses do the rest, and that's a very particular kind of patience, and I wrote that down.
The second thing I did was the thing I didn't want to do, which is why I did it second. I needed a control.

The professor's crate had eleven other books in it, and nine of those I either owned or could get. If somebody had been quietly reaching into the plates of dead men's books, then a man who'd kept a first impression of Tresidder on purpose might have kept others on purpose too, and if I checked them and found more edits, I'd have a pattern, and if I checked them and found nothing, I'd have one strange book and a bad week. Either answer was fine. That's what a control is: the test where you're happy to lose.

It took three weekends. Ana called it the Summer of the Ruler. I did it the only way it can be done, which is page against page with a finger on each line, and I will say this for it: there's a kind of peace in it. Four hours with two copies of a 1931 survey of calendar systems is four hours in which nobody is dying.

Nothing. Nine books, nothing. Typos corrected between printings, the honest kind, with the little line on the copyright page to say so. One binding variant. A map re-engraved because the first one was ugly. The ordinary, decent drift of printed things.
And I was relieved, which surprised me. I'd wanted it to be nothing. Nothing is the result I know how to live with.

Then I put the nine back on the shelf and looked at the two I hadn't checked, because I couldn't. The thin one with no title. And the paperback of Blindsight read half to death, which I'd picked up and put down a dozen times by then because of four words in pencil beside a paragraph near the end. Not nobody. Not you. The professor's hand, underlined twice. I didn't know what it meant. I knew what it was like: it was like a man arguing with a book he'd lost the argument to.
<hr />
I should say something here about the window, because it comes back later and I don't want it to arrive like a stranger.

Years ago, before Ana, a friend's garden, a summer, the kind of evening where somebody produces a bag and says it's natural. I was twenty-six and I'd read everything and I thought I knew what I was in for. I'm not going to describe it, partly because I can't and partly because every description I've ever read makes it sound like a film and it was nothing like a film. I'll say this much. For about an hour, the question I've been asking my whole life, the one under the other ones, stopped being a question. It wasn't answered. It was irrelevant, the way the colour of a door is irrelevant once the door's open. And then it came back, around midnight, the way a question does, and sat down in its usual chair, and I lay on my friend's lawn and understood that I'd been shown a window and not a way in, and that I'd spend the rest of my life being very careful never to confuse the two.
I filed it. Fourteen years, filed. I'm mentioning it now because when I finally opened the thin book, the first thing I felt was that lawn.
<hr />

It was a Sunday. Ana was at her mother's. Mora was doing the thing where she lies in the doorway so that nobody can enter or leave without a negotiation, and Buddy was on the blanket, and I took the thin book down for what must have been the fifteenth time, and this time I opened it.

Not a book. A notebook, bound to look like one; the professor had had it done, or his grandfather had, because there were two hands in it. The first hand was older, the ink gone brown, careful, upright, the hand of a man who'd learned to write before biros. The second was the professor's, the one from the margins, the no, just no hand. The old hand had filled the first eleven pages. The professor had filled the next thirty. The last page was in a third version of the professor's hand, shakier, the hand of a man writing from a chair he didn't get out of much.
No title. No introduction. No thesis. Just entries, numbered, in a format that somebody had decided on in the nineteen-fifties and that nobody had changed since:
Source. Page. Printing A → Printing B. Before. After.
That's it. That's the whole discipline. Forty-one times.

I'm not going to go through them. I will later, and they'll earn it. I'll tell you what I did that Sunday, which is that I read the first ten entries with my heart going harder than it had any business going, and they were all books I'd never heard of, printed before the war, in English and German and once in Dutch, and in every one a sentence had gone in one printing and come out another with its middle changed, and in every one the typos were untouched, and in every one the author was dead or gone or had publicly, carefully, taken it back.
Then I got to eleven.
Tresidder, H. M. Waters Before Memory. 1926. p. 118. 1st imp. → 2nd imp. (Leiden, 1931). "transmitted to the early" → "arisen among the first."
In the old hand. The brown ink. The grandfather's.
I put the book down on the table and sat back and looked at it from a distance, the way you look at a thing you've just understood is older than you.

My sentence. Mine. The one I'd found on a kitchen floor with a wet rope on my chest at four in the morning, sure I was the only man alive who'd ever read page 118 twice. Found, and written down, in a notebook, by a man who'd been dead for fifty years, and then kept, and added to, by his grandson, who'd bought a second impression in 2011 from a dealer in Groningen specifically so that he'd have one that did say the new sentence, to hold against the one his grandfather had kept that didn't.

I hadn't found anything. I'd been handed it. Twelve books, "because twelve sounds better," and the thin one at the bottom, and the first impression two spines above it. I was the thirtieth man to walk past that sentence and the third to stop.
Two options, I told Buddy, because he was there.

One: the crate was an accident. A man died, his daughter kept the furniture, a dealer with a beard bought the books by the metre and a man with a hobby happened to be the one kneeling on the cobblestones that Sunday. It happens. It's the ordinary way that old things find new idiots.
Two: it wasn't.

I didn't like two. I liked it less than I'd liked anything in the whole business so far, because two meant I wasn't hunting. Two meant I was being fed. And I sat there and gave it fifteen per cent, and I'd like to tell you I was being generous.
Then I turned to the last page.

Coordinates. Two numbers, lat and long, in the shaky hand, and I knew without looking them up what part of the world they were in, because I'd read about a man walking east out of a Turkish town in 1929 and not coming back. A date, circled three times. And under it, one word, the only word in the whole book that wasn't a citation:
Ask.

The date was that April. I checked it against the dealer's letter, against what Beard Man had said about the estate, against the little I'd found online about a retired reader in comparative religion from Deventer who'd died at home. The circled date was three weeks after the professor's funeral.
He'd written down a day he wasn't going to see. And a word. And then, I suppose, he'd sat in his chair.
<hr />
Ana came home at six with her mother's leftovers and found me at the table with the thin book closed in front of me and my hands flat on either side of it like a man keeping a lid on something.
"You've got the face."
"I know."
"Is this the measuring thing?"
"It's the measuring thing."
She put the leftovers in the fridge. She let Mora out. She came back and stood behind me and put her chin on top of my head, which she does, and looked down at the closed book.
"Are you going to tell me?"
"Yes," I said. "Not all of it. Not yet. I don't have it in a shape yet. But yes."
I felt her nod. "Okay, Mulder."
She went up to change. I sat there a while longer.

Here's what I didn't tell her, and it was the first thing that wasn't a small honest-marriage lie, so I'm going to say it plainly. The professor hadn't just found what I'd found. He'd found forty more. He'd been doing it for thirty years, with his grandfather's notebook, quietly, and nobody had laughed at him, because he'd never told anyone. And then one spring he'd written down a date and a word and died in a chair.
I'd spent three weekends trying to kill the thing. I'd failed. That was the control case.
And somewhere, on a server I couldn't find, at fourteen minutes past two, something was still sending forty kilobytes to nowhere.

chapters.title: Groningen
chapters.what: The dealer who wrote to him. The first helper, told what the phone call does. Ana on the phone from the car. Part One ends here.
blocks: The letter had been on the fridge for three weeks under a magnet shaped like a lemon, which is where things go in our house to be dealt with by someone else.

It was from a dealer. Antiquarian books, a shop in Groningen I'd never been to, a name I'd seen on the inside cover of two of the professor's books in pencil, the way dealers sign their work. It was a nice letter. It said that the writer understood I had acquired the late professor's library, that he had supplied the professor for many years, that he would be glad to be of service should I wish to add to the collection or to part with any of it, and that in his experience it was always best, in these matters, to be plain about one's reasons.

Ana had read it over my shoulder when it came. "That's what careful sounds like in a shop," she said, and went back to her programme, and I'd stood there with the letter thinking that it was the first time I'd seen my own name written down by someone connected to the book, and that I didn't like it, and that I couldn't have told you why.

Three weeks is how long it took me to understand why. Three weeks, and a list with my badge number on it, and the job gone from every backup, and Frank honestly not remembering the stand-up. By then I knew exactly what be plain about one's reasons meant. It meant that somebody had already been plain about mine.

So on the Saturday I told Ana I was going to look at a bookshop, which was true, and she said take Buddy, he likes the car, which was also true, and I drove two hours north with an old dog asleep on the back seat and the letter on the passenger seat under my phone, like a ticket.
<hr />

Groningen is a nice town and the shop was in the nice part of it, down a street with bicycles leaning on everything, and it was exactly what you want a shop like that to be: narrow, deep, smelling of paper and radiator, a bell on the door that had clearly been chosen for its sound. I left Buddy in the car with the window down. He gave me the look he gives me when I leave him anywhere, which is not reproach, exactly. It's more that he's noting it.

The dealer was in the back. He was older than I'd expected and smaller, with reading glasses pushed up into white hair and a cardigan that had been expensive once, and he looked up when the bell went and saw me and his face did something I've only seen once before, on Pieter, in a glass box.
He knew who I was. That was the first thing. I'd never sent a photograph; I'd never replied to the letter. He knew.
The second thing was worse. He wasn't surprised to see me. He was relieved. The way you're relieved when the dentist finally calls your name.
"Mr Klippe," he said. He said it properly, with the right vowel, which almost nobody does. "I wondered when."
"You wrote to me."
"I did." He took the glasses down and folded them and put them in his cardigan pocket, and he looked past me at the door, and then at me. "May I ask," he said, "who sent you?"
<hr />
I need to slow down here, because this is where I got it wrong, and the way I got it wrong is the only reason the rest of the afternoon happened.
I thought he was asking who'd referred me. A dealer's question. Who gave you my name. So I said, "Nobody. You wrote to me. I came."

And he nodded slowly, the way you nod when someone's answered a different question from the one you asked, and he said, "Of course," and he went and turned the sign on the door to closed and came back, and he said, "You'd better sit down, then. I'll tell you what I told them. It's the same."
Them.

I sat down. There was a chair by the desk, a customer's chair, and I sat in it, and he sat in his, and between us on the desk was a ledger, an actual ledger, the kind with a cloth spine, and he put his hand flat on it while he talked, the way you'd steady a boat.

He'd sold the professor the 1931 printing. Years ago. Eleven, twelve. A dry book nobody wanted, from a lot he'd bought at a house clearance; he remembered it because the professor had been so pleased, and the professor was not a man who showed pleasure. A few weeks after, two people had come to the shop. Polite people. A man and a woman, well dressed, with a card from a foundation that did something with archives. They'd been interested in the professor's purchase. They'd asked, very reasonably, whether the shop might let them know if anyone else ever asked for that title. Not the book, you understand; they had the book. The title. They'd left a number. They had not threatened him. He wanted me to understand that. They had said it was a matter of provenance, and that the foundation took an interest in certain editions for conservation reasons, and he had thought, at the time, that it was slightly odd and entirely harmless, and he had written the number inside the back cover of the ledger, and he had forgotten about it for eleven years.
"And then you wrote to me," he said.
"No," I said. "I didn't. I never replied."

"Not to me." He turned the ledger around. There was a line in it, in a neat old hand, three and a half weeks back. My name, the professor's name, and the title of the book. "You wrote to the auction house that handled his effects. You asked whether the professor's library had been catalogued. The auction house asked me, because I'd supplied him. And I," he said, and he took his hand off the ledger, "telephoned the number."
<hr />

I'd done that. I'd forgotten I'd done that. A two-line email to an auction house in week two, before the list, before any of it, asking a question any buyer would ask. It had never occurred to me to count it.

Three and a half weeks ago. Before the ticket. Before the stand-up. Before my badge number appeared on a list at two in the morning with asked (job) beside it, somebody in a foundation had already received a phone call from a bookshop in Groningen saying that a man called Klippe was asking about the professor's books.
I'd thought the list was the beginning. The list was the second thing.
"What did they say," I said. "When you rang."

"Thank you." He looked at his hands. "A woman. She thanked me. She said it was very helpful, and that the foundation appreciated it, and that someone might be in touch with you about the collection. I took that to mean they'd make you an offer. That's what I'd have meant." He paused. "I wrote to you afterwards because I thought, if they do make an offer, he should know to be careful what he says about why he wants the books. Dealers get strange about provenance. That's all I thought it was. Strange about provenance."
"Be plain about one's reasons."
"And when I walked in just now," I said, "you asked who sent me."

He didn't answer that. He didn't need to. He'd thought I was from the foundation. He'd thought they'd come to ask him what else he knew, and he'd turned the sign on the door and sat down to tell them, because that's what you do when the polite people come back.
<hr />

I want to tell you I was angry. I wasn't. I sat in a customer's chair in a bookshop in Groningen looking at a small old man in a good cardigan who had made one phone call in eleven years, and what I felt was something I've only felt at work, in the worst outages, when you find the line of config that did it and it was written by someone decent who was just doing what the ticket said.
So I did what I do at work. I told him what the thing he'd touched actually does.

I didn't tell him about the list. I'm not an idiot, and he was a stranger, and he had a number in the back of a ledger. I told him the shape of it. I said that there was a book, and the book had been changed between printings, and that the professor had noticed, and had died, in a chair, with an appointment in his diary that he didn't keep. I said that I had noticed too, and that I'd asked a question about it, once, at work, and that within a week the question had been erased and I'd been moved somewhere I could be watched. I said that the number in his ledger wasn't a conservation department. I said I didn't know what it was. I said that the woman who'd thanked him had, as far as I could tell, been thanking him for giving her my name before I'd even found anything, so that when I did find it, they'd be ready.

I said: "You didn't do anything wrong. I need you to hear that. You answered a question, because somebody asked it nicely and gave you a reason. That's all anybody on their side ever does. That's the whole trick."
He was quiet for a long time. The radiator ticked. Somewhere out on the street a bicycle bell went, twice.

Then he said, "He asked me once. The professor. Years after. Whether anyone had been in asking about him." He looked at the ledger. "I said no. Which was true, by then. They'd only come the once." He put his glasses back on, and took them off again. "I've thought about that answer more than I'd like, since March."
<hr />

He gave me something before I left. I didn't ask for it. He went into the back and came out with a folder and took one sheet out of it and handed it to me: his copy of the receipt, from eleven years ago, for the 1931 printing. The professor's name. The date. The price, which was nothing. And in the corner, in the same neat hand, the two words he'd written on everything he sold that man, because the professor had asked him to, and he'd never asked why.
First impression.
"He always wanted to know which one," the dealer said. "Even when there was only one. I thought it was an affectation." He almost smiled. "I'm a bookseller. I thought it was a nice affectation."

I folded the receipt into the folder with page 118 and I thanked him, and I meant it, and I asked him not to ring the number again, and he said, "No. No, I don't suppose I will," in the voice of a man who has just understood what a sign on a door is for.
<hr />
Buddy was asleep in the back with his chin on the armrest. I sat in the car for a while before I started it.
Ana rang when I was on the ring road. I put her on the speaker.
"Did you buy anything?"
"You went to a bookshop two hours away and bought nothing."
"He didn't have what I was looking for."
"What were you looking for?"

And I had it right there, the thing I do, the charming deflection, a first impression of something boring, you'd hate it, and the persona had it loaded, and I didn't say it. I don't know why. I think it was the receipt. I think it was a dead man asking a bookseller to write two words on everything, for years, because he wanted to know which one, and never once telling him why.
"Something I should have asked about sooner," I said. "I'll tell you tonight."
There was a pause on the line, and it wasn't a bad pause. It was the pause of a person who has heard a new sentence from someone she's known for fifteen years and is deciding what to do with it.
"Okay," she said. "Drive safe. Give Buddy a biscuit from me."
I gave Buddy a biscuit. He took it without waking up fully, which is a skill.

I drove home south in the dark with the folder on the seat beside me, thicker by one sheet of paper, and somewhere past Zwolle I passed a long straight stretch of canal road with the water black beside it, and I didn't know yet what had happened there, and I didn't slow down.

chapters.title: A pension visit, Zwolle
chapters.what: Third person. Under 900 words. No name, no lore. A kind afternoon. Each ending plausible.
blocks: The man from the pension fund arrived at two, which was when he had said he would arrive, and he had a folder, and he wiped his feet.

Henk Boersma had been expecting a letter and had got a person instead, which he took as a courtesy. He was seventy-three and had worked thirty-one years for the same engineering firm in Zwolle, and he had started, lately, to say things at the bowling club that made the other men look at their shoes. Things about his father. His father had been a draughtsman, and had kept notebooks, and had once said something to Henk about a bridge that Henk had been turning over for sixty years and had recently started to turn over out loud.

The man from the pension fund did not know any of that, as far as Henk could tell. He knew about the indexation. He explained it twice, patiently, with a pen, and the second time Henk understood it, and the man did not make him feel stupid for needing the second time. He had a way of leaving a silence open that made you want to put something in it.

The man had brought his own coffee, in a steel flask, and apologised for it: an old habit from years of sitting in other people's kitchens, he said, he never liked to put anyone to trouble. Henk made coffee anyway, because Marijke would have, and Marijke was at her sister's in Meppel until Monday, which the man was sorry to hear, he'd have liked to meet her. He admired the house, which was a decent house and had not been admired in some years, and he asked about the photographs on the dresser, and Henk told him about the children, and about his father, more than he had meant to, and the man listened in the way that very few people listen, which is without waiting.
At some point, and Henk could not afterwards have said at what point, they were talking about cars.
<hr />

The car was a 1994 Volvo estate in a dark green that Volvo no longer made, and Henk had bought it new, and it had done three hundred and ten thousand kilometres, and he could tell you what each of them had cost. He drove it twice a week. On Tuesdays to the shops, and on Sundays, while Marijke was at church, out along the canal road toward Hasselt and back, for no reason except that the Volvo liked a straight run and so did he.

The man from the pension fund liked cars. Not in the tiresome way; in the way of someone who had grown up with a father who kept one running past its time. He asked the right questions. He knew what the overdrive did. He laughed in the right place at the story about the mechanic in Kampen. And when Henk said, as he had said to a dozen people who had not heard it, that the car would outlast him, the man said, "I believe you," in a voice that made it a compliment to the car and not a remark about Henk.

Then he looked at his watch and apologised and said he had a problem that was not Henk's problem, and Henk said what is it, and the man said that he had a box to move, that afternoon, across town, a box of files from a colleague who had retired, and that the fund's car was a small thing with no boot to speak of, and he had been going to make two trips.
Henk said take the Volvo.
The man said no, he couldn't possibly.
Henk said he was seventy-three and the car was sitting in the drive doing nothing and he would be glad of the excuse to have someone else put petrol in it.

The man said, if you're sure. And he was back in forty minutes, which was less time than it would have taken, and he had put petrol in it, and he had also, Henk saw when he went out to look, run it through the wash on the way back, so that it sat in the drive in the late light the colour it had been in 1994.
"You didn't have to do that."
"It's a beautiful car," the man said. "It deserved it."

He left the flask. Henk noticed it on the table after the car had gone and thought, he'll be back for that, and put it by the door. The man had shaken his hand there. He said the indexation would come through in the new year and that Henk would get a letter, and that if he had any questions he should ring the number on the folder, and Henk said he would, and did not notice until a week later that the number on the folder was the general number, the one with the music.
He did not notice, because by then it did not matter.
<hr />

On the Sunday Henk Boersma drove out along the canal road toward Hasselt, as he did, with the window down, as he did, and somewhere on the long straight after the pumping station the Volvo went off the road and into the water, at no great speed, in daylight, with nobody else on the road.

The police report said the driver was elderly and had been widowed that year and had, according to acquaintances, seemed distracted of late. It noted that the car was old and well maintained. It noted the absence of skid marks, which in a man of seventy-three, on a familiar road, in good light, it did not find remarkable.
The car was recovered. There was nothing wrong with it.

The folder from the pension fund was on the passenger seat, and the water had got into it, and the woman from the fund who came to the house afterwards to help Marijke with the paperwork looked at it, puzzled, and said that it wasn't theirs, and that nobody from the office had been out to Zwolle that month, and that it must have been one of those firms that go round the retired. Marijke said a man had come, a nice man, Henk had said so on the phone, he'd brought his own coffee. The flask was still by the door. Nobody came back for it, and she couldn't bring herself to throw it out, and it is there now, on the shelf above the coats, and she will tell you about it if you ask.

chapters.title: The week it vanished
chapters.what: The turn of Movement I. Somebody reaches into the plate while he's watching.
blocks: Beard Man knew how the professor died, because Beard Man knows everything in the way a river knows everything: it's all gone through him and none of it's stayed in order.

"Chair," he said. He was pricing a box of Reader's Digest condensed novels that nobody on earth would buy, and he priced them anyway, lovingly, at fifty cents each. "Blue one. Daughter found him. Monday. Bin hadn't been put out, that's how she knew, he always put the bin out. Nice man. Didn't haggle."
"You met him?"

"Sold him things. Years. Particular." He held a condensed Hemingway up to the light as if checking it for the parts they'd left out. "Wanted first printings. Not first editions, mind. Printings. Most people don't know the difference. I told him the difference once and he said he knew, thank you, and I liked him for it."
"And the daughter sold you the books."

"Curtains," said Beard Man. "She does curtains. Four streets from the station. Didn't want the books, wanted the shelves. Said he'd stopped sleeping at the end. Said he'd be up all night with them." He put the Hemingway down. "Said the last few months he kept asking her the same thing."
I waited. He let me wait. It's the only power he has and he enjoys it.
"What thing?"

"Whether she'd be alright." Fifty cents. Fifty cents. "Which is a normal thing for a dying man to ask, and I told her so, and she said no, not like that. She said he asked it like a man checking a list."

Mid-sentence, as always. The comet. The prophet. I stood in the cold with my hands in my pockets and let it run over me and didn't hear a word, because I was thinking about a dying man and a list and the word Ask, in a hand that shook.
"Who bought his furniture?" I said, when there was a gap.
"Man in a van." Beard Man shrugged. "Fifties. Good coat. Polite. Didn't haggle either. Everyone's very polite about that house."
<hr />
I need to tell you about the week, and I need to do it in order, because the order is the evidence.

Monday, I checked the ticket. I'd put it in the queue where tickets go to die and I expected it to be where I'd left it, dying. It had been closed. Not by a person. By the system, the way the system closes things when somebody tells it to, with the reason filled in: Resolved — duplicate of #41822.

I looked up 41822. It didn't exist. Not deleted; deleted tickets leave a stone. It had never been raised. My ticket had been closed as a duplicate of a ticket that had never been born, and the person who'd done that had either not cared whether I'd check, or had known that in a queue that size nobody ever checks, and I couldn't decide which was worse.
Tuesday, I checked the list. I'd got into the habit, the way you get into the habit of touching your pocket for your keys. Fourteen minutes past two. Nine seconds. Forty kilobytes.
It wasn't there.

Not a failure, nothing in red. The line was gone. rcl-agg had been in the list on Monday, and it wasn't on Tuesday, and there was nothing between the two states, no entry that said removed by, nothing in the history, which was correct, because there had never been a history. Something that had never been born had stopped existing. I checked the other offices. Gone in all of them. I checked the backups.
That's the part. I want to go slowly here.

The backups are snapshots. That's what they're for. They're paper. You can't reach into last Thursday's backup and change what it says; if you could, there'd be no point having it. The whole reason I've been able to sleep for eleven years is that somewhere there's a copy of last Thursday that nobody can touch.
Last Thursday's backup didn't have rcl-agg in it.

Neither did the one before. Neither did any of them, going back as far as they went. I sat at my desk at ten in the morning with my coffee going cold and paged backwards through two years of snapshots, each one a sealed room, and in every room the thing I'd seen with my own eyes four weeks ago had never been there.

I know what that is. I'd been looking at it for a month on my kitchen table. Somebody had reopened the plates, changed one line, and left everything else untouched so it'd look, to anyone who checked the way people check, like it had always been that way.

Only this time I'd watched them do it. I had my own notes. I had a screenshot, from the first night, because I screenshot things, because the Record. I looked at the screenshot and then at the list and they disagreed, and for the first time in my life I was in the one position I'd never been allowed: the paper said one thing and I said the other, and I was right.
It felt like nothing. That's the honest report. It didn't feel like vindication. It felt like a floor going.
Wednesday, I asked Frank.
I did it casually, by the coffee machine, because I have a persona for a reason. "That job I brought up in stand-up. The orphan one. Did Pieter ever say what it was?"
Frank looked at me with the perfect, open, blank, friendly face of a young man who has no idea what you're talking about and likes you anyway.
"Which stand-up?"
"Couple of weeks back. No owner. Sent stuff to nowhere. You did the skull."
"I do the skull a lot, mate." He laughed. "Sorry. Genuinely. I don't remember. Was it the Antwerp thing?"
"No. Never mind. It was nothing."
"Based on what?" he said, grinning, because it had become a bit, and I laughed, and it was a good bit, and I went back to my desk and sat down and felt my hands go cold.

I believe Frank. I want that understood before anything else that happens. Frank wasn't lying. Frank just didn't remember a fifteen-second item at the end of a fifteen-minute meeting from two weeks before, which is the most normal thing in the world, and which meant that the only witness to the fact that I had raised rcl-agg in a room with six people in it was me.
Thursday, I went to Pieter.
Not in stand-up. His office, door open, the way you ask about holiday. "Quick one. That orphan job. It's gone from the list. Did someone clean it up?"
He looked at me for exactly as long as it takes a decent man to decide to be kind.
"James. Which job?"
"The diagnostic one. From the migration. You said leave it."

"I say leave it about a lot of things." He smiled. He wasn't being cruel. Nothing in his face was ready this time; nothing had been rehearsed. That's what undid me. He'd had the sentence ready the first time and he didn't have anything ready now, because now there was nothing to have a sentence about. "If it's gone, it's gone. That's a good thing, isn't it? One fewer thing on the list."
"Yeah," I said. "One fewer thing."
Friday, I didn't go in.
<hr />

I told Ana I had a cold. I did have a cold, in the way that you can have a cold if you need one. I sat in the kitchen all day with the dogs and the thin book and my screenshot and I did the thing I'm paid to do, which is to work out what a system is from the outside by what it does, without ever being allowed to see in.

Here's what I had. Something ran every night at the same minute and sent a small report to nowhere. I'd asked what it was. Within a week the thing had been removed, the asking had been removed, the record of the asking had been removed, the paper trail had been removed back to the beginning of time, and the two people I'd asked had been left with nothing in their heads but the natural blankness of men who have better things to remember.
Nobody had threatened me. Nobody had so much as frowned. It was the gentlest thing that had ever happened to me and I sat in my kitchen with a cold I didn't have and shook.

Because here's the thing. I'd asked about a book, and nobody cared. I'd written to a dealer, and got a kind postscript. I'd measured and ruled and read nine books page against page and the world had let me, the way it lets a man do a jigsaw. It was only when I'd asked about the job that something had moved. Not the books. Not the dead man. The forty kilobytes.
Why lie here?
Two options, I told the dog, because by then it was a liturgy.

One. It really was a diagnostic artefact, and some conscientious soul in another office had seen my ticket, cleaned up the job, closed the ticket with a typo in the duplicate number, and purged the backups to save space, and Pieter had simply forgotten, and Frank had simply forgotten, and I was a man with a cold reading a conspiracy into housekeeping. It happens. It's always the most likely thing.

Two. Somebody reads the queue where tickets go to die. Somebody has the keys to the backups, which is a list of about four people, and I'm one of them, and I didn't do it. Somebody wanted it to be as though I'd never asked. And whoever it was had done it the same way somebody in Leiden in 1931 had done it: one line, nothing else touched, and the honest certainty that nobody would ever check the way I check.
I gave option one sixty per cent. It was the lowest I'd ever gone. Buddy watched me do it from the blanket and offered nothing, which is a form of support.

Mora brought me the toy at some point, wet, and put it in my hand, and I threw it down the hall without thinking, and she brought it back, and I thought: nothing gets transmitted without someone to catch it. Something had been catching those forty kilobytes every night for years. And the night I'd noticed, it had stopped. Not because of the books. Because of me.
That's when I understood that the thing I'd been hunting could hunt.

I'd like to say that's when I stopped. I'd like to say a lot of things. What I actually did, at eleven that night, with my wife asleep upstairs and a cold I didn't have, was open the thin book to the last page, and look at two numbers and a date and a word, and type the coordinates into a map.
A hill. East of Urfa. Nothing on it. A road that stopped a kilometre short.

And I sat there and looked at a hill in Turkey on a laptop in a Dutch kitchen and felt, for the first time since the funeral, not curious, not afraid, but something I didn't have a word for yet and would, eventually, have to say out loud to a dog.
Ask, the professor had written.
Fine. But ask who?

chapters.title: Deventer, March
chapters.what: Small additions only: the professor's letter now argues, names the shelfmark and asks to consult it, and he is given the December sitting; the visitor photographs every page; the neighbor is given a card and the kind version; Beard Man sold the whole lot so that he would not have to telephone. Source: v6/09.
blocks: The old man had written to them on paper, with a stamp, to an address that was a foundation's registered office and nothing else. Two pages, in a hand that was not what it had been. Most of it was argument. The last four lines gave a shelfmark, asked to consult the item, and asked whether, before that, somebody might come and talk to him about his notebook.
So somebody came.

He parked two streets away, because he always did, and walked, because the walk told him things: the bin at the gate, not yet out; the curtains, good ones, chosen by a woman; the bicycle with a child's seat on it that belonged to a neighbor. He rang. He waited longer than a younger man would have waited. The door opened on a face that had been expecting him for a long time and had not expected him to look like this.
"You're not what I thought," the professor said.
"People say that." He wiped his feet. "May I?"

The chair was blue and the professor lowered himself into it the way you lower something you're afraid of dropping. The notebook was on the side table, closed, under the man's hand, and the man did not look at it and did not look away from it, and the professor noticed both, and smiled.
"Let me," the man said. "You sit."

He made tea in a kitchen that had a woman's handwriting on the calendar and a man's on the shopping list. He brought it through. He sat where he was told to sit, which was the chair opposite, the one with the better light on it, and he understood that he had been placed, and he let it happen, because there was no harm in it.
"I'll say what I've got," the professor said, "and you'll say nothing, and then you'll go. That's how it works, isn't it?"
"More or less."

"Forty-one," the professor said. "My grandfather found the first eleven. I found the rest. I've never published. I've never told anyone but my daughter that the book exists, and I told her it was a bibliography, which it is." His hand on the cover. "I'm not asking you to confirm anything. I'm old and I'm not sleeping and I'd like, before I stop, to have asked somebody. That's all."
The man drank his tea.

"They're all the same edit," the professor said. "Did you know that? I expect you know that. Forty-one books and it's always the same correction, in different clothes. A hand comes out. A giver goes. Early becomes first. Nobody ever adds anything. You only ever take one thing away." He was looking at the window now. "It's very disciplined. I've admired it, God help me. Thirty years I've admired it."
"You wrote us two pages of that," the man said. "Nobody answers that part. You also asked to consult an item, and you gave the shelfmark."
"A student of mine saw it on a crate. I've had it nine years."
"The answer to that part is yes. The room sits once a year. The second of December. You'd come in person and ask at the desk."
"December." The professor looked at his own hand for a while. "You people have a sense of humor."
"It's the date there is."

The professor opened the notebook at the last page, where the reference already was, and wrote the date under it, slowly, and one word under the date, and closed it and put his hand back on the cover.
"There," he said. "I wanted to have done it."
"You should rest," the man said, gently.
"Is that what you came to say?"
"I came because you asked." He put his cup down. "Nobody comes if you don't. That's the only rule I know for certain."

The professor laughed, which turned into something else, and he waited it out with his hand over his mouth, and then he said, "My daughter's going to be alright. Tell me that, at least. You can say that."
"Your daughter's going to be alright."
"You say it like you mean it."

"I do mean it." He stood. He took the two cups to the kitchen and rinsed them and left them on the rack, the way a guest does. When he came back the professor's eyes were closed and his hand was still on the notebook.

He lifted the hand, which weighed very little, and took the notebook to the window, and photographed every page, flat and square and without shadow, the way he had been taught. Then he put it back and put the hand back on it. The hand closed. He stood for a moment in the good light looking at an old man asleep in a blue chair, and then he let himself out, and pulled the door until it clicked, and walked the two streets to the car.

He made one call. "He's asked. Yes. In person. He's been given December; he won't be there. I have the pages, all of them. The original's on the side table. I'd say weeks." A pause. "I'd rather wait. A body's a fingerprint, you've said so yourself." Another pause, longer. "Understood."
Eleven days later the bin was not put out on a Monday and the daughter let herself in with her key.

He came back for the furniture in June, with a van and a man he paid in cash, because the daughter had put a card in the window and the card had been reported to him and it was cleaner to be the buyer than to be anything else. He bought the shelves and the blue chair and he did not haggle, and when he asked about the dresser she said no, that one was her mother's, she was keeping that, and he said of course, and the daughter, who had her father's hands, said she was glad the shelves were going to somebody who wanted them.
"And the books?" he said, lightly, as he had planned to say it.
"Oh, those went," she said. "Weeks ago. Man from the market. He takes anything, by the crate. I couldn't look at them."
He stood in the emptied room and let his face do nothing at all.
"Of course," he said. "That's the best thing for them."

Before he left the street he rang the bell of the neighbor with the bicycle and gave her a card with a foundation's name on it and a telephone number. The professor's papers were of some interest, he said, and the foundation was concerned for their conservation; if anybody came asking after them she would be doing the old man a kindness to ring. She asked how Hendrik had seemed to them, at the end. He said the professor had written some rather confused letters, and had not been sleeping, and that everybody had been very fond of him. She said that was just what she had thought herself.

He drove the chair and the shelves to a lock-up near Zwolle, and he went through the chair, the lining and the cushions and the frame, properly, and found nothing, and the following Sunday he went to the market in a good coat and stood in the cold at a stall where a man with a beard was talking about a comet, and he looked at the ground, where the crates were, and there were two, and they were full of Reader's Digest.
"Professor's books," he said. "Were there any left?"

"Sold the lot," Beard Man said, not unkindly, mid-sentence. "One chap. A fellow left me a number, said to ring if anyone asked after one title in particular. Nobody asked after one. He wanted all of them. I don't ring for a lot."

He thanked him. He bought a condensed Hemingway for fifty cents, because a man who buys nothing is remembered. And he went and sat in the car, and he did not call anybody for eleven minutes, and then he did.

He was not blamed. It had been a question of weeks, and he had been right to wait. His standing was confirmed at the review. He had the photographs. The only thing that changed was that the original was now in a stranger's kitchen, and he would have to find the chap who'd taken the lot, and he had always, in his way, enjoyed that part.

chapters.title: Croton, 530 BC
chapters.what: 🟡 v9 — Claude, 16 Nov 2026. [Interlude, real]. EDITED. Now told as what the source is: a contemporary rival's verse mocking Pythagoras, quoted centuries later, with no place or year in it. Three factual slips corrected (who wrote it down and when, Croton still exists, other lines of Xenophanes survive). Source: v7/16.
blocks: The date and the town are a guess. Pythagoras is thought to have moved to Croton, in the south of Italy, around 530 BC, and to have acquired a following there. The story itself gives no place and no year.

Xenophanes told it. He was a poet from Colophon, about the same age as Pythagoras, and he was not a friend. He made fun of most things people believed, and he told this one the way you tell a story about a man you think is a showman: to make the room laugh.
Once, he says, Pythagoras was passing by when a puppy was being beaten. He took pity on it and said: Stop. Don't beat it. It is the soul of a friend of mine. I knew it when I heard it cry out.

That's the whole thing. Four lines of verse. The poem they came from is lost, and the four lines survive only because Diogenes Laertius copied them into his life of Pythagoras some seven hundred years later, as an example of what people said about the man.
Nobody knows if it happened. Nobody knows who the friend was. The puppy is not described. We aren't told whether the beating stopped.

What we know is that about two and a half thousand years ago somebody was already saying that a dog could carry a person he had loved, and that you could know it by the voice. And that the oldest mention of the idea we have was written by a man who thought it was ridiculous, and wrote it down so that everybody could see how ridiculous it was.
So the first time it appears, it is already a joke.

chapters.title: Frank's kitchen
chapters.what: Movement II opens. Three Noise scenes folded into one evening; one Thread with a page number. Frank's list. Disclosure on the TV, nobody looks up.
blocks: Frank asked me round on a Saturday, which should have told me something, because Frank is twenty-nine and single and lives in a flat where the kitchen is also the living room and the bedroom is a mezzanine, and men like that don't ask colleagues round. They ask friends round. I'd apparently crossed a line without noticing, the way I cross most lines.
"Beer," he said, at the door. "And I need you to look at something. Properly. With the face."
"I don't have a face."
"You absolutely have a face. Pieter calls it the audit face."

There was a television on with the sound down. A hearing, somewhere, men in suits behind a long table, a chyron with the word phenomena in it. Frank had it on the way you have the weather on. Neither of us looked at it all evening, and I'm telling you that now because I didn't notice it then, and I should have, and that's the whole point of everything that follows.
<hr />
The first thing was a video.

Somebody had sent it to him, somebody who sends him things, and he wanted it killed and he wanted to watch me do it, and I'll admit that the persona enjoyed that. It was a montage. Dates of earthquakes against phases of the moon, with a voice over it that had learned to sound like a documentary and a graph that went up and to the right with the confidence of a man who has never had to show his working.
"Right," I said. "Pause it. Go back. The graph."
He went back.

"It's not a graph. There's no axis. It's a line somebody drew on a picture of a graph. Second thing: what's the baseline? How many earthquakes happen on days that aren't full moons? He's never going to tell you, because the answer is the same number, and if you've got no baseline you've got no correlation, you've got a list of nights that something happened, and every night something happens." I drank. "Third thing, and this is the one that matters. Look at the dates he picked. He's got fourteen. There were two hundred quakes above magnitude six in that period. He picked the fourteen that fit. That's not a pattern. That's a man with a drawer full of socks telling you every sock is blue, having thrown the red ones away first."
Frank was grinning. "Go on."
"That's it. That's all it is. It's noise. It's beautiful noise, somebody spent a week on the voice, but it's noise, and you don't need me for it, you need a sock drawer."
"I needed to hear you say it." He killed the video. "Okay. Round two. This one's not a video. This one's got a book."
<hr />
Round two was the one about the missing three hundred years.

You might know it. There's a theory, and it has a book, and the book has footnotes, and the footnotes are what get you, because they look like the real thing. The claim is that a stretch of the early Middle Ages never happened: that a few hundred years were inserted into the calendar by people with reasons, and that's why there's so little from that period, and that's why the dates of a few old buildings don't add up, and that's why a certain emperor seems to have done too much in one lifetime.
"I don't believe it," Frank said. "Obviously. But I can't kill it. Every time I go to kill it the footnotes come up."
"Tree rings," I said.
"What?"

"You don't need the footnotes. Trees. There's a continuous record of tree rings going back twelve thousand years, overlapping, logs out of bogs matched to logs out of roofs matched to living oaks. Year by year. No gaps. If somebody'd inserted three hundred years into the calendar, there'd be three hundred years of rings that didn't exist, and there aren't. The trees don't know what year the pope said it was." I drank. "Also the Chinese kept their own calendar and their own eclipses and never got the memo. Also the Mayans. Also, the eclipses. Astronomers can run the sky backwards; you can't fake where the moon was. It dies on tree rings in four minutes. You don't need a book."
Frank looked at me for a while.
"Then why is there a documentary?"

And that's the thing about Frank. He's a skeptic the way I'm a skeptic, which is that the fastest route to the wrong answer bores him, and he doesn't want to be told a thing is stupid. He wants to be told why someone made a film about it.

"I don't know," I said. And then, because it was Frank's kitchen and the beer was good and I'd had a bad fortnight: "Here's what I notice about it, for what it's worth. A theory refuted by tree rings doesn't need a documentary. It needs a footnote. Somebody made a documentary anyway. Somebody put the money and the voice and the drone shots into a thing that dies on oak. And when I see an explanation working harder than the mystery, I notice. When I see the ridicule working harder than the mystery, I notice that too."
"You think it's a plant."

"I think it's a sock drawer. I think people are shown the blue ones so that when a red one turns up they say oh, that's one of those." I shrugged. "Or I think a man with a book needed a second mortgage. It's usually that."
<hr />
Round three was Frank's. He'd been waiting for it.

He has a list. I should have guessed; he's that kind of mind. On his laptop, a document, years old, headed Things people believe and under it two columns: Still standing and Dead. He's kept it since university. When he hears a claim he puts it in the left column, and when it dies he moves it to the right, with the date and the reason, and he's never once moved anything back.

"This is how I sleep," he said. "Everything goes in. Everything gets a trial. Crashed saucers, dead: the metal was pots and pans, there's a magazine article from 1952. The leaked government documents from the eighties, dead: wrong typewriter, the signature was traced off a letter from 1947, the FBI said so. The man who said he'd worked on the alien craft, dead: he lied about his degrees and had a felony. The water memory thing, dead: a magician was in the room when they ran it blind." He scrolled.
