It was a long document. "And here's what I've got for your lot. The believers. You know what the single most damaging thing is, in the whole history of it?"
"Tell me."
He turned the laptop round. A scanned page, a declassified thing, 1953, a panel of scientists convened by people who had reasons.

"They recommended it," Frank said, with real pleasure. "The debunking. It's policy. They sat down in a room and wrote, I'm quoting, that the subject should be stripped of its special status and its aura of mystery, through a programme of, hang on, training and debunking, using mass media, psychologists, and, I love this, Disney. Walt Disney. It's not a conspiracy, James. It's a memo. Every time one of your forum people says they're being laughed at, they're right, and it's boring, it's a 1953 memo, it's the most bureaucratic thing I've ever read. That's my trump card. That's the whole thing in one page. It's not sinister, it's a committee."
I read the page. I took my time, because I take my time, and because I'd seen something, and I wanted to make sure it was there before I said anything, and it was.
"Read the next line," I said.
"What?"
"The line under the bit you read. Out loud."
He turned the laptop back round. He read it. He stopped halfway and read it again, and I watched his face do the thing mine does when I put a finger on the right line of page 118.
"'The burden of proof is on the sighter,'" Frank said, slowly, "'not the explainer.'"
"Yeah."
"That's — " He sat back. "That's the opposite of science."

"It's a rule. Written down. By scientists. In a government document. It says that whoever sees the thing has to prove it, and whoever explains it away doesn't. That's not a committee being boring, Frank. That's a committee writing a standard of proof. And you've been using it. You've been using it for ten years, in that list, and so have I, and so has everyone we've ever met, and I'm not saying the saucers are real, I think the saucers are mostly pots and pans. I'm saying somebody wrote down the rule for how we'd be allowed to check, and then taught it to us, and then we forgot it was taught."
The television was still on. A man in a suit was saying something to another man in a suit. Neither of us looked.
Frank didn't say anything for a while. Then he said, "Huh," and moved his cursor to the left column, and I watched him not move the 1953 memo to the right.
"It's still dead," he said. "The saucers."
"I know."
"I'm not moving it."
"I'm not asking you to."
"But the memo's — " He looked at it. "The memo's not in either column, is it. The memo's the table."
I didn't say anything. He'd got there on his own, which is the only way anyone ever gets anywhere, and I've learned to shut up when it happens.
<hr />
He walked me down. On the stairs he said, "You've gone quiet lately. At work. Pieter says you've gone quiet."
"Bad month."
"Was it the orphan job?"
I stopped on the stair. He was behind me and couldn't see my face, which is the only reason I let it do what it did.
"What orphan job?"

"I don't know, mate. You said something once, I can't — " He laughed. "Forget it. I'm pissed. Did you know they had to move the definition of hunter-gatherer? Göbekli Tepe. The site's older than farming, so they couldn't have farmers building it, so instead of moving the date they moved the definition. Hunter-gatherers can build temples now. That's a did-you-know. That's one of yours. I'm stealing it."
"It's a good one," I said. "Keep it."

I walked home. It wasn't far. The whole way I was thinking about a sock drawer, and a rule somebody had written down, and a man who'd remembered an orphan job for exactly one second on a staircase before the beer took it back.
Not noise, then. Not all of it.
Some of it was a table.

chapters.title: The math
chapters.what: The style guide arrives as an object. The arithmetic. He stops calling people. The recruiter's email.
blocks: Els Maasen sold curtains four streets from the station, and she had her father's hands, and I knew that because I'd never met her father and still knew it the second she put them on the counter.

I'd gone in on a Saturday with a story. The story was that I'd bought some of her father's books at the market and found a letter in one and wanted to return it. The letter was real, a dull one, a note from a librarian about a renewal, and I'd put it in an envelope and carried it across town and I'm not proud of any of that. The persona handles the small stuff. This wasn't small, and it handled it anyway, which is the first time I noticed that the persona didn't have a line it wouldn't cross, only lines it hadn't been asked to.
She looked at the letter. She looked at me.
"You're the one who took twelve."
"The man at the market told you."
"He tells everyone everything." She almost smiled. "He said you were the only one who went through them spine by spine. Like Dad." She put the letter down. "You didn't come about a letter."
"Then what?"

I've thought a lot about why I told her the truth. It wasn't a decision. I think it was her hands. "He kept a notebook," I said. "It was in the crate. I don't think he meant it to be. I've been reading it and I don't understand it and I thought you might know what he was doing."
She was quiet for long enough that a woman came in, looked at some fabric, and went out again.
"He was doing that for thirty years," Els said. "I thought it was a bibliography. He said it was a bibliography." She came round the counter. "Wait here."
She was gone ten minutes. When she came back she had a folder, cardboard, the kind with an elastic band, and she held it the way you hold something you've decided to be rid of.

"The furniture went to a man with a van. I kept the dresser. I don't know why. Mum's." She put the folder on the counter. "This was in the bottom drawer, under the lining paper. Dad must have put it there. I found it in May. I've looked at it maybe four times. I don't know what it is and I don't want it in the house and I don't want to throw it away, because he hid it, and he never hid anything." She pushed it an inch towards me. "You seem like someone who checks things."
"Then check it. And don't tell me."
<hr />

Three pages. Photocopies of photocopies; you could see the grey ghost of a staple in the corner, copied along with the text, three generations deep. The top of the first page said, in a plain typeface that had never been chosen by anyone who cared about typefaces:
PREFERRED FORMULATIONS. Fourth revision. For internal circulation to readers at level 2 and above.
Below that, two columns. Deprecated on the left. Preferred on the right.
I read it standing at my own kitchen table with my coat still on and the dogs waiting to be let out.

I'll give you a few. I won't give you all of it; I don't think the whole thing should be in a book, and I've thought about that more than I've thought about most things. But you need a few, or you won't believe me.

Deprecated: was given to. Preferred: arose among. Deprecated: taught by. Preferred: developed by. Deprecated: the earlier peoples. Preferred: the first peoples. Deprecated: brought. Preferred: discovered. Deprecated: a visitor. Preferred: a tradition. Deprecated: remembered. Preferred: imagined.

That was the first page. It went on. Thirty-odd pairs, and every pair did the same thing, the thing I'd found on a kitchen floor with a wet rope on my chest: it took the hand out. Nothing was ever added. Nothing was ever denied. If you read the right-hand column on its own, it was perfectly respectable; it was how every careful scholar I'd ever read already wrote. That was the horror of it. It wasn't a lie. It was a style. It was the house style of the people who decided what careful sounded like.

The second page was about dates. Where a date is contested, prefer the later. Where a layer is contested, prefer the shallower. Where a sequence is contested, prefer the one in which the simpler precedes the more complex. Each with a line or two of justification that sounded exactly like every methods section I'd ever skimmed, because, I understood, standing there with my coat on, it was every methods section I'd ever skimmed. Somebody had written the rules for looking, and then the rules had been taught, and then the people who'd learned them had taught them, and three generations later the rules were just what looking was.
The third page had a heading I've never been able to forget.
WHEN A READER NOTICES.

Four paragraphs. The first said that a reader who notices a change between printings is to be treated as a bibliographical enquiry and answered as such: courteously, fully, with reference to the ordinary practice of the trade. The second said that a reader who persists is to be offered the opportunity to publish, and that publication should be facilitated, in an appropriate venue, with an appropriate framing. The third said that a reader who persists after publication is to be reviewed.
The fourth paragraph was two lines long.
In no case is a reader to be contradicted. Contradiction confirms. The preferred response to a correct reader is agreement, followed by reclassification.

I read that one four times. Then I let the dogs out, because they'd been very patient, and I stood in the garden in my coat and watched Mora try to eat a leaf and thought: Dear Mr Klippe. I would gently say that it is wisest to be plain about one's reasons.
Courteously. Fully. With reference to the ordinary practice of the trade.
<hr />
I'd like to say the math came to me in a flash. It came the way everything comes to me, which is slowly, at a kitchen table, while I'm trying to do something else.

Page one said level 2 and above. That means there's a level one. That means there are levels. And a document doesn't get a fourth revision unless it's been used, by enough people over enough years that the first three wore out, and I know what a fourth revision looks like, I've written them, they're what happens when the thing is boring and necessary and has been for a decade.
So: how many people?
I'm not a statistician. I'm a man who counts breaths. But here's how I did it, and you can do it too, and I'd rather you did.

Say the thing is real. Say there's a group of people who maintain what careful sounds like, and a job that runs at two in the morning, and a man in a van who doesn't haggle, and a manager who says leave it, and a dealer who says be plain. Say none of them know each other. How many would you need?

Not a cabal. A cabal couldn't do it; a cabal can't keep a secret in a town, let alone a century. You'd need something duller. You'd need, in a company of five thousand people, somebody who could close a ticket and somebody who could touch the backups and somebody who could tell a manager what to say about a job. That's three. Call it ten, to be safe, for every five thousand. One in five hundred.
One in five hundred. I sat with that.

That's the man who delivers our post. Not is. Could be. One in five hundred means that in a town this size there are a hundred and sixty of them, and they don't know each other, and most of them have been asked to do one small thing once and never asked again, and they did it, because it was small, and because the man who asked was pleasant, and because they'd been told a reason that was true enough.
One in five hundred means that at the funeral, in that slow line of people saying she's in a better place, statistically, somebody was in.
I stopped there. I got up and I put the kettle on and I didn't make anything with it.

Because here's what one in five hundred does to you, if you let it, and I let it. You stop calling people. Not dramatically. You just notice, on a Tuesday, that you haven't rung your mother in three weeks, and that the reason you haven't is that you'd have to tell her about your week, and you can't, and so you'd have to tell her about Ana's week, and you'd hear yourself doing it, performing the normal, and you'd rather not. You stop going for the beer after work. You stop answering Beard Man's questions about what you're reading. You develop, over about a month, the social life of a man in a submarine, and the submarine is your own kitchen, and the people on the surface are all lovely and any one of them could be the man in the van.
I knew that was the wrong lesson. I knew it while I was learning it. It didn't help.
<hr />
The thing with Ana happened over breakfast and it was my fault and I'm going to tell it straight.
"You were up at four," she said. Not a question.
"The payments thing."
She buttered toast. She's a careful butterer, corner to corner, and she did the whole slice before she said anything else.
"The payments thing finished in June. You told me. You said good catch in a voice and did the thing with your hands."
I didn't say anything. There wasn't anything.

"I don't mind that you're up at four," Ana said. "I mind that you've started having a thing you tell me and a thing you don't. I can see the join. I've always been able to see the join, that's the entire reason you married me, you said so, on the third date, you said you're the only person who's ever caught me." She put the knife down. "So catch you. What's the four o'clock thing?"

And I had the shape by then. I had it. I could have put the three pages on the table and the thin book next to them and said: I think somebody's maintaining the world, and I think they've noticed me. And she'd have said okay, Mulder and asked a hundred questions and we'd have had the day, and whatever came after would've come after with two of us in it.
"Reading," I said.

She looked at me for a long moment. Then she picked up her toast and ate it, corner to corner, and went to work, and didn't kiss the top of my head, and that was the whole thing. That was the cost. She was quiet for a day. One day. She was perfectly nice the entire time, and I'd have paid anything by the evening to be shouted at instead.
One in five hundred. And the only person I was certain wasn't in, I'd just put on the outside.
<hr />
The email came that Friday and I laughed out loud at my desk, which I don't do.

A recruiter. I get them; everyone gets them; they're weather. This one was good, though, that was the thing. Somebody had done their homework. It was from a consultancy I'd never heard of, on behalf of a finance house I had, a big one, old money, the kind of place that has a building with a name. They wanted somebody to look at their systems from the outside, it said, somebody with "a reputation for noticing what others have been told to leave." And then, in the last line, the thing that made me laugh: We're told you play off the seventh. We have a member there who'd be delighted to show you the back nine.

Play off the seventh. That's not a golf term. It's a joke about me, the trees on the seventh, and I'd made it exactly once, out loud, on the course, to the four retirees, who'd laughed, and it had turned up on the club's website in a members' photo caption six months ago, under a picture of me and an old dog in a cart, because the secretary thinks she's funny.

So they'd looked at the club's website. Fine. Recruiters do. And they'd found the one line that would make me laugh, and they'd put it at the end where the laugh would land, and I laughed, and then I stopped, because I'd just spent a month learning that the preferred response to a correct reader is agreement.
I looked up the consultancy. Registered two years ago. One director. A name I didn't know and wrote down anyway, because I write everything down.
Kalder.

And under the photo of me and Buddy, in the members' gallery, the caption, the joke, and below it the course's own line, which I'd never read before, because who reads those: Pictured: J. Klippe and companion, every Wednesday at seven.
Every Wednesday at seven. Anyone who wanted to know what I loved had only to look.

chapters.title: The corporate day
chapters.what: The bank's golf day. Kalder with a vendor's lanyard, and James honestly glad. He sells the bank its continuity. Ana at the end, on the phone, about the dogs.
blocks: The bank has a golf day, which it has never once had.

I need to explain that, because it's the kind of sentence that gets you a look. Every spring an email goes round about the golf day. Every spring there's a form, and a date, and a course an hour away with a name like a retirement home, and every spring, two weeks before, a second email goes round saying that in light of the current environment the golf day has been postponed, and nobody is surprised, because the current environment is always in light of something. I've worked there eleven years. I've filled in the form eleven times. I don't know why. I think it's the same reason people buy lottery tickets, which is that filling in the form is the enjoyable part and you'd rather not have it taken from you by realism.
This year, nobody postponed it.

I found out on the Thursday, when a calendar invitation arrived with a tee time on it, an actual tee time, 09:40, and a note from the organiser saying I was in a three-ball and to please confirm my handicap. I sat at my desk and read it twice. Then I did something I'm not proud of, which is that I got up and went to the window and looked out at the car park for a while, the way you do when something good has happened and you don't want anyone to see your face.

It had been a month since the list. Three weeks since Groningen. I'd told Ana, that night, as much as I could put into sentences, which turned out to be about forty per cent of it, and she'd listened, and asked two questions, both of which were better than any I'd asked myself, and then she'd said, "Okay. So what do we do," and I'd said I didn't know, and she'd said, "Then we go to bed," and we had. It was the single most useful conversation of my adult life and it had lasted eleven minutes. Since then I'd been living in the forty per cent and watching the other sixty from a distance, like weather.
And here was a day of golf. A whole day. Outdoors. With a scorecard, which is a document that makes no claims about anything except how badly you played.
I confirmed my handicap. I rounded it down, which is a lie, but a traditional one.
<hr />

The course was an hour north, flat and windy, the kind of Dutch course that's a polder with ambitions. Buddy wasn't allowed, which I'd known and had still, on the morning, half thought about arguing. Ana walked me to the car with Mora at her heel and said, "Try to speak to a human," and I said I'd try, and she said, "A human, James, not a man who wants to tell you about his new wedges," and I said that was a very narrow definition of human, and she kissed me and said go.

I was in a three-ball with two men from Treasury. I'd never met them. I knew within forty seconds that I wasn't going to meet them now either, because the first thing one of them said, as the cart girl went past with the drinks, was something about her that I'm not going to write down, and the second one laughed, and they both looked at me to see if I'd laugh too, and I did the thing I do, which is smile in a way that could be read either way and look at my glove.

Fine. I've played with worse. You play your own ball. That's the whole beauty of golf and the reason I never did team sports: nobody else's behaviour changes your score. I teed off, badly, and walked after it, and the Treasury men talked to each other about a boat, and the wind came across the flat land with nothing to stop it, and for about six holes I was as close to happy as I'd been since a Tuesday on a kitchen floor.
Then I saw him on the practice green.
<hr />
I'm going to be careful here, because I've since gone back over this moment more times than is healthy, and I want to tell you what I saw and not what I know now.

What I saw was a man from the spring. The stranger the starter had paired me with on a Wednesday in April, the one with the swing I'd have paid for, who'd asked about Buddy before he asked my name. I'd driven home that day giddy. I'd told Ana about him, which I never do; she'd said, "You've made a friend," in the voice she uses for the dogs when they've done something clever, and I'd pretended to be offended and wasn't.

He was on the practice green in a company polo, putting, with a vendor's lanyard round his neck, the blue ones they give the sponsors. He looked up as my three-ball came past on the way to the seventh. He saw me. And his face did the thing that I would like, more than almost anything, to have been real, which is that it lit up.
"James!"
He came over. He shook my hand with both of his. He asked after the dogs, by name, both of them, and I felt the Treasury men behind me recalibrating something.
"What are you doing here?"
"Working, I'm afraid." He lifted the lanyard like it was a joke. "I sell you people things."
"What things?"

"Continuity. Dull stuff. If your building burns down on a Tuesday, who does your payroll on Wednesday. Where do you all sit. Who's got the keys." He grinned. "I'm the man who sells the bank its seats. Disaster recovery. Lobbying, mostly, if I'm honest; I talk to people like your head of risk about things that will never happen until they do. It's a living. The golf's the only good part."

I said I'd never known that about him. He said I'd never asked, and that most people didn't, and that he'd found that the less you said about continuity the more people trusted you to provide it. He said it lightly. Everyone laughed. I laughed.

He knew the organiser, it turned out. Of course he did. And when I came off the ninth the three-ball had been rearranged, the Treasury men paired off with each other and a sponsor, and I was walking to the tenth tee with the man from the spring, whose name, I should say, was Julian, and whose surname I didn't catch that day because he said it the way people say surnames they expect you to forget.
<hr />
The back nine was the best golf I've ever played. I'd like to say that was the company and it probably was.

He was good, properly good, and generous with it the way good players sometimes are and usually aren't. He didn't give me tips. He watched me hit a seven iron thin into a bunker and said, "I'd have done exactly the same," which was a lie and a kindness in the same breath. He talked about nothing. The wind. The course. A client in Antwerp who'd insisted on a recovery site with a view. He asked about work, and I said it was fine, and he let it go, and I noticed him letting it go, and I liked him for it.
At the fourteenth he asked about Ana.

Not how's the wife. He asked how she was doing, since the spring, since her grandmother. He remembered. I'd mentioned it once, in April, on a tee box, in the half-sentence you give a stranger, and he'd kept it, and here it was, in October, offered back to me carefully like something I'd lent him.

I told him more than I'd told anyone. Not about the book; I had enough sense left for that. About Ana. About how the grief had changed shape, from a thing that lived with us to a thing that visited, and about the knitting she hadn't finished, and about how I'd been bad at it, at the funeral, at saying the thing people say. He listened. He didn't fill the silences. And when I was done he said, "You're hard on yourself, James. Most people never notice they're lying at a funeral. You noticed and it's still bothering you in October. That's not a defect. That's the thing most people are missing."
I three-putted the fourteenth. I didn't care.
<hr />

There was a dinner afterward, in the clubhouse, the kind with a raffle. He had to leave before it; he had a thing, he said, another client, the glamorous life. We stood in the car park in the last of the light with the wind dropping and he said we should play again, properly, not at a corporate thing, and I said yes before he'd finished the sentence.
"Bring the old boy," he said. "Buddy. He can ride in the cart."
I said he'd like that.

"And James." He had his car keys in his hand and he turned them over once. "If work's ever not fine. You've got my number now." He nodded at my phone, where he'd put it, on the thirteenth, while I was looking for a ball. "Continuity's a small world. Sometimes I hear things before they happen."
I said I'd remember that. He drove off in something German and quiet, and I stood in the car park a while longer than I needed to.
<hr />
Ana rang while I was still there.
"Did you speak to a human?"
"I did."
"A real one?"

"Julian. The golf man. From the spring. He was there. He works for a vendor, he sells us our—" and I stopped, because I was about to say continuity and the word had arrived in my mouth with a weight it hadn't had an hour before, and I couldn't have told you why. "Disaster planning. Boring. He asked after you. He remembered about your grandmother."
"He remembered?"
"He asked how you were doing. By name. Six months later."
There was a pause.
"That's nice," Ana said, and it was, and it was also the voice she uses when she's filing something. "Was he nice?"
"He was great. I played the best back nine of my life."
"Then I'm glad." Mora barked in the background at something only Mora could see. "Come home. Buddy's been at the window since four. He does that now. Did you know he does that?"
I said I didn't.
"He stands at the window and watches the street like he's expecting someone. I don't know who."

I drove home in the dark with the clubs in the back and the wind pushing the car around on the dyke road, and I thought about a man who remembered everything you told him and asked about your dog before he asked your name, and I thought, that's what a friend is, that's what they're like, I'd just forgotten, and I believed it, and it was the last time for a long while that I was simply happy.
I want that on the record too. It was a good day. I'm not going to let what came after take it off me.

chapters.title: A car park
chapters.what: Third person. Reporting upward. The understatement that moves the date. Forty words of his own speech.
blocks: He took the call in the car, in the long-stay car park behind the station, because the car park had no cameras on the third level and because he had always preferred to be told things while looking at concrete.
"He's accepted," the voice said.
"And the Wednesday?"

"Twice now. He's easy. He wants a friend and doesn't know it, which is the best kind. I asked about the dog." He watched a woman two rows over fail to reverse into a space, and then succeed. "He's filed the job. The one at his old place. He's stopped asking about it."
"He's stopped asking at work."
"He's stopped asking."

A silence with paper in it. He knew the silence. It was the sound of a sentence being weighed, and he had chosen the sentence carefully, and he had chosen it to be light, and he waited to see whether the lightness would hold.

"You said stopped asking," the voice said. "I've got a ticket closed in July, a screenshot we can't account for, a letter to a dealer, a visit to the daughter, and a man who now has the pages. I've got a reading on the index that moved the week he found the notebook and hasn't come back down. That's not a man who's stopped asking, Julian. That's a man who's stopped asking out loud."
"He's not a publisher. He deleted the one post he ever wrote."
"That's worse. You know that's worse." A pen, somewhere, on a desk he'd never seen. "I'm going to put the review at the end of the quarter."
"It was the end of the year."

"It was. And now I've got a reader at level two who's been handed a style guide by a woman who sells curtains, and a handler who tells me the reader's gone quiet. You brought it forward, not me. Every time you make him smaller than he is, I have to make the date nearer than it was. That's the arithmetic. You've always known the arithmetic."
He didn't say anything. The woman two rows over got out of her car and looked at how she'd parked it and got back in.
"How near are you?" the voice said.
"Near enough to know what he loves."
"Which is?"
"The old dog. The wife. Being right about a thing nobody else checked." He considered. "In that order, I think. He'd say the wife. It's the dog."
"Good. Then stay there. And Julian. Don't tell me he's stopped. Tell me what he's doing. I'd rather hear it from you than read it off the index."
"Understood."

The line went. He sat for a while with the phone in his lap and the concrete in front of him and did the arithmetic the voice had said he'd always known, which was that a date had just moved three months because of a verb, and that the verb had been his, and that this was the second time.

He had, in his coat pocket, a flask. He'd bought it on the Tuesday, because he'd said he was a flask man, and he had never in his life owned a flask, and he'd found that he wanted the sentence to have been true when he said it.

He put the phone in the glovebox. He drove to the lock-up near Zwolle and sat in the blue chair for twenty minutes without turning the light on. Then he drove home, and fed a cat that was not his, that belonged to the flat, that came with the flat, the way the flat came with the name on the bell.
The review was moved to the end of the quarter. The index was read on Monday. It was up.

chapters.title: Leiden
chapters.what: The second head. Not alone. The generals' manual on a kitchen table. Entry #26. The second column.
blocks: The message came through the forum, which I'd stopped reading, under the handle I'd had for twelve years and never once used for anything that mattered.

I should explain the handle. For twelve years, under a name that was a joke only I understood, I'd posted did-you-knows. The light kind. The steam engine. The calendar. A door ten metres up a wall. Never a theory. Never a question. A man standing at the edge of the strange and dark corner with his hands in his pockets, saying huh, look at that, and leaving. A few hundred people had followed it. Ana knew about it and thought it was sweet. It was the one place on the internet where I'd been, for twelve years, exactly as much of myself as I could afford.

And in July, after the week it vanished, I'd done the thing I'd deleted in the spring. I'd posted. Under that name. Not a question about the dead. A question about a sentence: has anyone compared the two impressions of this 1926 survey, p. 118? With the photographs. Dry as toast. Dull, correct, no theory, the Record's own format.

Three people had replied. Two said interesting and went away. The third was polite, long, and knowledgeable, and explained, courteously and fully, with reference to the ordinary practice of the trade, that variants of this kind were common, that the author had very likely revised the sentence himself before his departure, and that the Leiden houses of the period had been notoriously casual about recording such things. It was a lovely reply. I'd thanked him. And I'd gone to bed with a line from the third page of a style guide going round in my head like a song.
Six weeks later, a private message. No greeting.
Whoever corrected you used a phrase my supervisor showed me on a photocopy in 2009. He said if I ever saw it in the wild I should assume the person who wrote it was not a scholar. Who are you?
<hr />
Her name was Noor Haverkamp and she lived in Leiden, which, if you've been paying attention, is where the plates were.

She had been Hendrik Maasen's last doctoral student. She'd left the university in 2017 when the library's special collections were "restructured" under a digitisation grant, which is a sentence that sounds like nothing and that she said in a tone I recognised, the tone I use for the word migration. Now she repaired paper for a living. Freelance. Which meant she could get into rooms I couldn't and knew what a page looked like under a light held at the wrong angle on purpose.
Her kitchen was small and the table was covered in a sheet of glass and under the glass, I understood after a while, was a page from something four hundred years old that she was keeping flat.
"Don't put your coffee on it."
"Wouldn't dream of it."
"Everyone dreams of it. It's a table." She sat. She was fifty, maybe, grey at the front, with the hands of a person who does one thing extremely carefully all day. "You want to know if you're mad."
"I want to know if I'm alone."

"That's a better question. The answer's no. Which doesn't help as much as you'd think." She pulled a folder across the glass, not opening it. "Hendrik had the list from his grandfather and he had me for four years, and he showed me the Preferred Formulations once, one page, a photocopy, in 2009, in his office with the door shut, and he said, Noor, if you ever see this phrasing in the wild, assume the person is not a scholar. And then he never mentioned it again and I thought he'd gone a bit strange, and then they restructured the collections and I understood what strange was for." She looked at me. "You were corrected on the forum by somebody using the preferred formulation for a bibliographical enquiry. Word for word. It's a template. They don't even change the template."
"Why would they?"
"Exactly. Why would they. Nobody's ever noticed it twice."
<hr />

I'd brought the thin book. She'd known I would. She put on gloves to touch it, which told me more about her than anything she'd said, and she went through it the way I'd have gone through it if I'd been a better man, slowly, and she stopped where I'd stopped, at eleven, and then she stopped at twenty-six.
"This one," she said. "You've looked this one up."
"It's not a book."

"No." Entry twenty-six was a paper. Verhoef, A. Utrecht, 1993. Withdrawn before publication. Reclassified: instrumentation. And then, in the professor's hand, the only entry in the whole list with a note on it: two rooms, 40 m, correlated. Grandson sent copy 2015. Same edit: "shared" → "coincident."

"Anton Verhoef's grandson found Hendrik on a forum in 2015," Noor said. "Your forum. He had his grandfather's paper in a drawer, the original, with the word shared in it, and a copy of the version that went into the department's archive under instrumentation, with the word coincident in it, and he couldn't understand why anybody would have bothered. Hendrik could. Hendrik wrote to him. I scanned it." She closed the book. "It's the only entry on the list that isn't about the past. Everything else is a hand being taken out of a story about the beginning. This one's a hand being taken out of a story about last Tuesday. Two people in two rooms, and something moved."
"Why would the same people care about that?"
"That," said Noor, "is the only question. Hendrik spent his last three years on it. He thought he'd got it. He wrote a word at the end of the book."

"He asked. I've no idea who. And then he died in a chair, and his daughter sold his books to a man with a beard, and here you are in my kitchen." She took the gloves off. "So. Are you alone. No. Is that good. I'll tell you what I tell myself. I've never published a word of this. Not one. Not a forum post, not a footnote, not a conference paper with a careful title. I have the photocopy and I have what Hendrik told me and I have a job repairing paper, and I'm alive, and he's not, and I think those two facts are related, and I think you should think so too."
"The third page," I said. "A reader who persists is to be offered the opportunity to publish."
"And then reviewed."

"Yes." She looked at me across four hundred years of paper under glass. "They don't stop you talking. They stop you being heard. And if they can't, they've got a word for what happens next, and it's a word from a budget meeting."
<hr />
She had a book on the table. Not under the glass; on it. A paperback, French, with a title I could read and a text I couldn't, and a long section near the back that she'd tabbed.
"You know this?"
"I know of it. Generals. The nineties."

"Generals, an admiral, a report commissioned by nobody and published in a magazine, and the whole world laughed, and the last chapter is the one nobody reads, because by then they've got what they came for." She opened it at the tab. "The last chapter's a thought experiment. They put themselves in the shoes of whoever's out there, and they ask: if we had been watching a population for a thousand years, how would we manage contact? And they answer. In phases. They write it down. Covert observation for as long as you like. Then furtive appearances that can't quite be dismissed. Then influence, and I'm translating, by providing sacred texts, by accentuating the intellectual and moral tendencies of selected individuals. And then contact at the highest level of the states, kept secret, after which the contacted leaders run, their words, information, disinformation and counter-information campaigns." She looked up. "They name the instruments. Science-fiction novels. Films. Advertisements. And I quote: why not suitable sects?"
I didn't say anything.

"They were thinking of aliens," Noor said. "That's the defence. They were writing about what they would do. Read the last paragraph." She turned the page and put her finger on it. "They say the only thing that would make contact fail is if the gods couldn't stay out of reach. If the population got close enough to see their faces, they'd stop being gods and start being neighbours, and the whole thing would collapse into, I'm translating, contingency." She took her finger off. "They were writing a manual. For themselves. In 1999. And they put it in a magazine, and everyone laughed, and it's been in print ever since, in plain sight, and the one thing it tells you, James, the one thing, is that the people running it are terrified of being seen up close."
She said my name. I noticed. Nobody says it.

"So that's why I never published," Noor said, quietly. "Not because I'm afraid of them. Because I'm not useful to them unless I'm loud. A loud reader is a story they can manage. A quiet one is a neighbour."
<hr />
I asked her the math on the way out, standing in her hall with my coat half on. I'd been carrying it for a month and she was the only person I'd met who could take it.
"One in five hundred," I said. "That's what I get. If it's real. One in five hundred people has been asked to do one small thing, once."
"That sounds low."

"You're counting the wrong column." She had her hand on the door. "You've worked out how many it takes to run it. Fine. Now do the other number. If this is a thing that gets done to people who notice, how many people have noticed? In a hundred years? Hendrik noticed. His grandfather noticed. Verhoef noticed, from the other end. I noticed. You. That's five I can name without trying, and I'm a woman who repairs paper in Leiden." She opened the door. The street was wet and ordinary. "One in five hundred is the ones who keep it running. The ones who've seen it, James. Do that column. And then ask yourself why there's a list of forty-one books and not a list of forty-one people, and whether that's because nobody made one, or because somebody did."
I stood on her step.
"You're asking the wrong column," she said again, kindly, and shut the door.
I walked to the station. It had stopped raining. I did the other column on the train, on the back of the ticket, badly, with a pen that kept giving up.

It wasn't low. It was the same number. The same ratio, from the other end: for every person who's been asked to do one small thing, there's one who's noticed something small and said nothing, and they don't know each other either, and the machine, if there was a machine, had been counting only one of those columns, and I had a feeling it was the wrong one.
Not alone, she'd said. Which doesn't help as much as you'd think.
She was wrong about that, as it turned out. It helped exactly as much as I'd thought. It just took a year.

chapters.title: The drill
chapters.what: First week on the continuity programme. The recovery site. Desk forty. A glass door upstairs he isn't badged for. He notes a reference-number format and doesn't connect it.
blocks: My first week on the continuity programme was a bus.

I'd been moved on a Monday. Pieter had said it in his nice voice, three weeks after the stand-up, the way you'd tell someone they'd been upgraded: they asked for the person who reads things. A woman called Saskia had walked me through a lobby telling me to notice everything, and I'd noticed that she said it like a line she'd been given, and I'd noticed that my badge, when I touched it to the reader on the new floor, made a different sound. Higher. One note up. I don't know who tunes those things, but somebody does, and somebody had decided I was a semitone more important than I'd been on Friday.

Continuity is the department that plans for the building not being there. Floods, fire, the thing nobody says out loud. If the bank can't open its doors on a Tuesday, continuity knows where everyone sits on Wednesday. It's a department made entirely of lists, which is why they'd want a man who reads lists, and I'd have believed that, actually, if I hadn't been on one.

On the Thursday there was a test. There's one every year. Forty named staff, chosen in advance, get on a bus at seven in the morning and are driven to the recovery site, and they sit at desks that have their names on them, and they log in, and they pretend the building has burned down, and at four o'clock they get back on the bus. It's called a drill. The word made me think of dentists, and of the thing you do to a wall, and I was on the list.
Number forty. Last name on the sheet. Pieter was twelve.
<hr />

The bus went east, out past the ring road and into the flat country where the business parks are, the kind of landscape that's nothing but sheds with company names on them, each one the size of a village and containing, as far as anyone can tell, three cars. The recovery site was one of these. Low, long, grey, behind a car park with a sign at the entrance that said the name of a foundation I'd never heard of and, underneath, smaller, the name of a company I had, because it was on the lanyard of a man I'd played eighteen holes with in October.
I looked at that for a while, through the bus window, while the driver found the gate.

It didn't mean anything. I want to be clear about what I thought at the time, which was: of course. He sells the bank its recovery seats. This is the recovery site. His company's name is on the sign. That's not a coincidence; that's a supply chain. I'd have been more surprised if it hadn't been there. I noted it the way you note the make of a car, and I got off the bus with the other thirty-nine and collected a lanyard of my own, a temporary one, white, with my name printed on it and a number.
Forty.
They gave us a sandwich. At eight in the morning. I've never understood that about these things, the sandwich at eight; I think it's less about hunger than about giving people something to hold.
<hr />
Inside, it was an office. That's the thing nobody tells you about the end of the world: it has carpet tiles.

A big open floor, a hundred desks maybe, in rows, each with a screen and a phone and a laminated card with a name on it. Half the names were ours. The other half were other banks, other companies, other people's Tuesdays. Everyone shares the site; that's how the economics work. You don't buy a building for a fire that might never come. You buy a seat in a building somebody else owns, and you hope that when your fire comes, theirs hasn't.

My desk was at the back by the window. Desk forty. My name was on the card, spelt right, with the vowel, which almost nobody manages. I sat down and logged in and the screen came up exactly as it would at work, same wallpaper, same six things I'd left open on Friday, and for a disorienting second I was at work, and then I looked up and saw forty people I half knew sitting in rows under strip lights eating sandwiches, and I was somewhere else.
Pieter came past. He was twelve, which put him in the second row, and he'd walked the length of the floor to find me, which he didn't need to do.
"Settling in?"
"It's a desk."

"It is a desk." He looked at the window. "Good spot, actually. You can see the car park." He said it as if the car park were a view, and then he said, in exactly the same voice, "How's the programme treating you?"
"Lots of lists."
"You like lists."

He nodded, and stood there a moment longer than the conversation needed, and I had the feeling, which I'd had with him twice before, of a man wanting to say something and finding the sentence isn't in the building. Then someone called him, and he went.

I ate the sandwich. I did the drill. You log in, you open the things you'd open, you ring a number and tell a voice that you're operational, and the voice says thank you and you hear it typing. By eleven I'd done everything the laminated card asked of me and I had five hours left, and a window, and I'm not good with five hours.
So I read the building.
<hr />

I'd like to say I was looking for something. I wasn't. I was doing the thing I do in hotels and other people's offices and, Ana says, other people's bathrooms, which is read every piece of paper in reach, because paper is where people put the things they've stopped noticing.

The fire plan by the door. The evacuation routes. The floor map, laminated, with our floor in blue and a second floor above us in grey, labelled, in a smaller font, ARCHIVE (FOUNDATION) — NO ACCESS. The cleaning rota. A notice about the car park gate. A list of extensions, and at the bottom of the list, one that said Reading Room, with a number that was the same as ours except for the first digit.

The floor map was the thing. Not because of what it said; because of what it was next to. There was a staircase at the far end of our floor, behind the kitchenette, with a glass door at the top, and through the glass door, from where I sat, I could see a landing, and a wall, and on the wall a sign in the same font as everything else that said the same two words, and under them, in the way these places do, a shelfmark. Not a room number. A shelfmark, the kind libraries use, with the letters and the dash and the numbers.

I wrote it down. On the back of the laminated card, with the pen they'd given us. I didn't know why. I know now that I was writing down a format, not a number, the way you'd write down a licence-plate style from a country you've never been to, in case you see it again.
Then I got up and went to look.
<hr />

The glass door didn't open. My badge made no sound at all against the reader, which is a sound in itself, and I stood on the landing like a man who's wandered into the wrong part of a hospital and looked through.

A corridor. Carpet, better than ours. A door at the end with a window in it, and through the window, a room with a long table and a lamp and shelves, and a desk at the near end with a woman at it, with her back to me, doing something with a card index. An actual card index, wooden, with drawers. I hadn't seen one since I was a child.

She didn't turn round. I stood there for maybe ten seconds. There was a smell, even through the glass, or I imagined one: paper and dust and the specific cold of rooms that are kept at a temperature for the sake of what's in them and not who.

A reading room. The foundation's archive. On top of a bank's recovery site, in a shed in a business park, behind a glass door that didn't answer to the badge of a man whose name was on a laminated card forty desks away.
I went back down. I sat at desk forty and looked at the car park, which Pieter had called a view.

And there, in the car park, in a good coat, talking to a man in a high-visibility jacket who I took to be the site manager, with one hand in his pocket and the other making the small open gesture of someone explaining something simple to someone who should already know it, was Julian.

He didn't look up. He had no reason to; he didn't know I was there, and from the car park the window would have been a sheet of grey. I watched him talk for a minute. The site manager nodded a lot. Then Julian clapped him on the arm, lightly, the way you do with someone whose name you've made a point of learning, and got into something German and quiet and drove away.
I thought: he sells the seats. This is where the seats are. Of course he's here.
I thought: he said he'd hear things before they happened.

I thought, and I want to be honest about this, that it would be nice to tell him I'd seen him. That I'd ring him, that evening, and say I was at your shed today, I waved and you didn't see, and he'd laugh, and we'd fix a round.

I didn't ring him. I'd like to tell you it was instinct. It was the shelfmark. I had a format written on the back of a card in my pocket, and I didn't know where I'd seen it before, and some part of me that is slower and better than the rest wanted to find out first.
<hr />

The bus went back at four. Pieter sat near the front. I sat at the back with the laminated card in my pocket and watched the sheds go by, each one the size of a village, each one with a name, and I thought about a floor map with one floor in blue and one in grey, and about the fact that in all the years the bank had been buying seats in that building, nobody on our side had ever asked what was upstairs, because why would you. It's an archive. It says so on the map.
At home, Buddy was at the window.
Ana said he'd been there since three. "He gets up when a car slows down. Any car. Then he lies back down. He's done it four times." She watched me take my coat off. "How was the end of the world?"
"It had a sandwich."
"Of course it did."

Later, in the kitchen, with the dogs asleep and Ana upstairs, I took the laminated card out of my pocket and turned it over and looked at the shelfmark I'd copied off a wall. Letters, a dash, numbers. A format.
I'd seen it. I knew I'd seen it. Not in a library. On a page.

It took me until the Saturday to remember where, and when I did I sat down on the kitchen floor the way I do, and I took the thin book out of the folder, and I turned to the last page, where a dead man had written a library reference, and a date, and the word Ask, and I put the card next to it.
Same letters. Same dash. Same shape.
The appointment the professor hadn't kept was upstairs from desk forty.

chapters.title: The money
chapters.what: The invoices. A line to the foundation, billed per flagged person, stepping up for thirty-one years; the last step the week he opened his ticket. The second contract. The annex: the seat list, no dogs. Ana reads it over his shoulder.
blocks: I'll tell you the rule first, because it's the only thing in this chapter I'm sure of, and it isn't mine.
When the files are gone, look for the receipts.

Everybody knows the famous version. In 1973 the head of an intelligence agency ordered a programme's records destroyed, every page, and they were, and four years later twenty thousand pages turned up anyway, because somebody had filed them in the finance department under invoices. The men who burned the files were thinking about what the files said. The men who kept the receipts were thinking about whether the money added up. Those are different kinds of men, and the second kind always wins in the end, because the second kind is boring, and boring is what survives.
I didn't know I was following the rule. I thought I was doing my job.
<hr />

The continuity programme runs on contracts. That's what it is, under the lists: a set of agreements with other companies that say, if this happens, you will do that, and here is what we pay you per quarter for the promise. Somebody has to read them. Nobody wants to. Saskia gave me the folder on my second Monday with the face of a woman handing over a chore she'd been dreading, and said, "See if anything's expired," and I said I would, and I did, and nothing had, and that's where a normal person stops.
I read the invoices.

I need you to understand that this is not detective work. It's the opposite. Detective work is looking for the thing. What I do is read everything in the order it comes, at the same speed, with the same attention, whether it's the twenty-page master agreement or the line that says parking. I don't skim. I can't. I learned at ten that the error is always in the part you were sure of, and I've been reading the boring part ever since, like a man who's been bitten once and now checks every dog.

The invoices came quarterly from four suppliers. Three of them were exactly what you'd expect: the recovery site, the data people, the company that tests the phones. The amounts went up a little every year with inflation and down a little when someone renegotiated, the way money breathes.
The fourth was a foundation.

I knew the name. It was on the sign at the entrance to the shed in the business park, above the smaller name on Julian's lanyard. The foundation owned the building; the bank rented seats in it through Julian's company; that much was on the master agreement and made sense. But the foundation also invoiced the bank directly, separately, every quarter, for something else.
One line. The same line, every quarter, for as far back as the folder went, which was eleven years.
Continuity reconciliation (recall index). Per flagged person. And a number of persons, and a rate, and a total.

I read it the way I read the sentence on page 118. First time, nothing: a service line, consultancy-shaped, the kind of thing that gets approved because it's been approved before. Second time: per flagged person. Third time, out loud, in the empty office at seven in the evening, like a man being punished: recall index.
I didn't know what a recall index was. I knew what flagged meant. I'd been flagged. There was a file on my laptop with a hundred and thirteen lines in it and a two-word reason beside each one.
<hr />
Here's what I did next, and it took two evenings, and Ana thought I was working late, which was true.

The folder went back eleven years. The finance system went back thirty-one. I pulled every invoice from the foundation since the first one, which was dated the year the bank moved into the recovery site, and I put the numbers in a sheet, quarter by quarter, and I looked at them the way I look at anything that breathes.

They didn't breathe. That was the first thing. Inflation goes up by two or three per cent and wobbles. These numbers didn't wobble. They sat flat for years, perfectly flat, the same number of flagged persons every quarter, and then they stepped. Up. Once. By a clean amount, a round multiple, like a dial being turned one click. And then flat again, for years. And then another step.
Six steps in thirty-one years. Each one a multiple of the one before, give or take nothing. Nobody negotiates a contract like that. Contracts drift. These were set.
I looked at the dates of the steps. I'm not going to give you all of them, because you'd want to know what they mean and I didn't, then. I'll give you the last one.
The last step was dated the Monday of the week I opened my ticket.

Not the week I asked in stand-up. The ticket. The thing I'd typed into a system on a Thursday afternoon a week after Pieter said leave it, a two-line request to investigate an unowned job, which I'd opened anyway, because a dealer in Groningen had told me to be plain about my reasons and I'd taken it as advice. That Monday, the number of flagged persons in a four-hundred-year-old bank had gone up by one click of a dial, and the foundation had sent an invoice for it, and somebody in Finance had approved it, because it had been approved before.
I sat with that. The office was dark except for my screen. Somewhere down the corridor a cleaner was doing the thing with the bins.
They hadn't just counted me. They'd billed for me.
<hr />
The second contract I found the next night, and it was easier, because by then I knew what I was looking for, which is the only kind of looking I distrust.

It ran through Julian's company. Work-area recovery; seats, annual; the straightforward one, the one the bank thought it was paying for. Forty desks in a shed, tested once a year with a sandwich. The master agreement was twenty pages and I'd read them all on the Monday and they were fine.

The annex wasn't in the folder. Annexes never are. They live in the system, attached to the contract record, and you need a role to open them, and on my second Monday on the programme I hadn't had the role. By the second Thursday I did. Saskia had added it with a sigh, because I'd asked, and because she'd learned in two weeks what Ana learned in two months, which is that it's quicker to give me the thing than to explain why not.
Annex C. Seat allocation.

It was a list. Of course it was a list. Everything in this story is a list; I've come to think that's not a coincidence but a fact about how these things are done, that if you want to do something enormous and have nobody notice, you do it as a list, because nobody reads lists.

Names. Our names. The forty from the drill, and then more, a hundred and twenty, with a column headed role, and a column headed dependants per allocation, with a number in it, two or three or four, and a column headed notes.
My name wasn't on it. I checked. I want you to notice that I checked, and that this time I didn't feel disappointed.
Pieter's was. Dependants per allocation: 3. He has two children.

And under the table, in the small type where the terms live, among the clauses about access and badging and the hours of the canteen, one line, which I read three times and then photographed with my phone, because I'd stopped trusting systems to still contain things in the morning:
Companion animals are not accommodated.
<hr />
Ana found me on the kitchen floor at eleven.

I hadn't meant to be there. I'd come home, I'd eaten, I'd said work was fine, and then at some point I'd gone to the kitchen for water and the folder was on the table and I'd sat down on the floor with my back against the cupboard the way I do, and Buddy had come and put his chin on my leg, and I'd been there for a while.
She didn't say anything. She sat down on the floor too, across from me, with her back against the oven, which she hates, and Mora came and lay between us like a border.
"Show me," she said.

So I showed her. Not all of it; the forty per cent, which had grown. I showed her the sheet with the steps. I showed her the invoice line, and I watched her read per flagged person, and watched her get it, faster than I had, because Ana is faster than me about people and this was, in the end, about people. I showed her the annex. She read the names. She found Pieter. She looked at the number beside him and then at me and didn't say anything, and then she read the small type, and I watched her find the line.

She read it twice. Then she looked at Buddy, who had fallen asleep with his chin on my leg, and at Mora, who was upside down between us with her legs in the air, and then she looked at me, and her face did a thing I'd never seen it do, which was go completely still.
"Not accommodated," she said.
"They've got a plan. For something. With desks and a canteen and a number of dependants. And the dogs aren't in it."
"And you're not in it."
"But Pieter is."
"Pieter said leave it."
She was quiet for a long time. Then she said, in the other voice, the one she uses maybe twice a year: "What are they planning for, James."

And I said I didn't know. Which was true. I had a sheet of numbers that stepped like a dial, and a receipt for my own curiosity, and a list of my colleagues with their children counted, and a shed in a business park with a reading room on top of it that a dead man had an appointment in, and I didn't know what any of it was for. I knew what the files said. I'd been reading the files for a month. It was the receipts that had finally told me something, and what they told me was only this: that whatever it was, it was old, and it was paid for, and it had been paid for by us.
Ana got up. She put the kettle on, which is what she does, and while it boiled she stood at the counter with her back to me and said, "The golf man. Julian. He sells them this."
"He sells them the seats. Yes."
"Does he know what's in the annex?"
I said I didn't know that either.
She turned round. "You said he remembered about my grandmother. In October. Six months after you'd mentioned it once."
"Nobody remembers that," Ana said. "I'm good with people and I wouldn't remember that." The kettle clicked. She didn't move. "Men don't remember that unless it's their job."

I didn't have an answer. I had a feeling, and the feeling was the one I get at work when two graphs that shouldn't be related start moving together, and I'd learned long ago that the feeling is usually nothing, and that the times it isn't are the only times that matter.
Buddy woke up and looked at me, and then at Ana, and then he got up, with the grunt, and went and stood at the window. At eleven at night. Watching the street.
"He does that now," Ana said. "I told you."
"You did."

I got up off the floor and went and stood next to the dog, and looked out at nothing, at a quiet street with parked cars on it, and I put my hand on his head, and I thought about a line of small type that said he wasn't accommodated, and for the first time since a Tuesday on this floor I was not curious.
I was frightened. And I want it on the record that it was the dog that did it, not the invoice. The invoice was just the receipt.

chapters.title: Enjoy it while it lasts
chapters.what: Meerwijk. The defaults with the blind spot built in. Access shrinks by exactly the right amount. The White Knight, by email. Dave at the barbecue is next; this is the turn.
blocks: Meerwijk has a building with its name on it and a lobby with a ceiling you could land a plane in, and on my first morning a woman called Saskia walked me through it at the pace of somebody who'd walked a great many people through it and had stopped noticing the ceiling in 2009.

"You'll sit with Infrastructure," she said. "You don't report to them. You report to me, and I report to a committee, and the committee reports to the board, and nobody on the board has ever read anything you'll write. That's the arrangement. That's why you're here. You're the person who reads it."
"Reads what?"

"Everything." She stopped at a glass door and badged it. "The brief is simple. We have four hundred years of records and forty years of systems and nobody who's looked at the second as a whole. We want to know what we've got. Not what it does. What it is. You notice things. We've been told that. Notice."
I'd like to tell you I was suspicious. I was flattered, which I'm told is the same thing from the other end.
<hr />
Here's what you need to know about a place like Meerwijk, and it took me a month to see it.

Nothing is thrown away. A finance house that's been going since people wore wigs does not delete; it accumulates, and the accumulation is the point, it's what they're selling, four centuries of never having lost a thing. Which means that under every system there's an older system, and under that an older one, and at the bottom, in the oldest layers, there are things that were set up by people whose names nobody knows for reasons nobody can find, and that still run, every night, because turning off a thing nobody understands is the one sin the house doesn't commit.

I read the ingredients. All of them. It's a bigger list than my old place by a factor of twenty and I read it the way I read the other, completely, with a growing sense of being the only person who ever had, and three weeks in, at eleven at night, in a building with the lights on timers, I found it.

Not rcl-agg. They don't call it that here. Here it was a line, in a ledger, in a system so old that the ledger was still called a ledger, and the line was a monthly payment, modest, unremarkable, the kind of sum a house like this spends on stationery, going out on the first of every month for thirty-one years to a foundation whose registered office was a post box, under a description that somebody had typed once in 1994 and nobody had touched since:
Continuity reconciliation (recall index). Nightly.

Nightly. Thirty-one years. And on the second screen, when I pulled the thread, the thing itself: a job, no owner, no ticket, that ran at fourteen minutes past two, for nine seconds, and sent forty kilobytes to an address that resolved nowhere.
I sat in a building with a ceiling you could land a plane in and felt my hands go cold for the second time that year.

It wasn't a diagnostic artefact from a migration at my old place. It was here. It had been here before my old place existed. And the one difference, the one thing Meerwijk's four centuries of never throwing anything away had given me that my old place couldn't, was a name. Recall index. Somebody, in 1994, had been asked what the line was for, and had written it down.

I didn't open a ticket this time. I'd learned that much. I wrote it in the Record, in the kitchen, at one in the morning, with Buddy under the table, and I photographed the screen, and I put the photograph in three places, and I told nobody. Not Noor, not Frank, not Ana.
Especially not Ana. And I knew that was wrong while I was doing it, and I did it anyway, and I filed that too.
<hr />

Frank's tools arrived at Meerwijk in October. Not Frank; the tools. The AI-driven monitoring he'd sent the link about with the skull, two years earlier, in another life. Enjoy it while it lasts, boys. The house had bought them, through a consultancy, and the consultancy had done the setup, and I was asked to review the configuration before it went live, because that's what I was for.
I'd like to explain what a default is, because this is where the book turns and I don't want you to miss it because of a word.

When you buy a thing that watches, it comes with opinions. Out of the box, before anyone's touched it, it already knows what's normal and what isn't, what to wake you for and what to let through. Those opinions are called defaults, and nobody reads them, because they're long and they're boring and they've been chosen by experts, and the whole promise of the thing is that you don't have to. You install it. It watches. You sleep.
I read them. I read all of them. Four hundred pages of what the thing had been told was normal.

And on page two hundred and twelve, in a section about scheduled jobs, there was a class of thing the tool had been told not to report. Ever. Not to log, not to flag, not to show. A pattern, described in the dry language of patterns: jobs with no owner, no ticket, and no history, running on a nightly schedule and emitting small payloads to unresolved addresses. Classified, out of the box, by the experts, as noise.
My job. My forty kilobytes. Described in a sentence, in a default, in a product sold to ten thousand companies, as the one kind of thing the watcher should never see.

Nobody had hidden anything. I want to say that as plainly as I can. There was no secret file, no hooded man. Somebody had just been boring in the right place. They'd written one sentence into the defaults of a tool that would be installed everywhere, by people who'd never read it, and from then on every company on earth that bought the thing would have a watcher that had been told, before it opened its eyes, that there was one shape it would never have to look at.
The ruleset had a version number. Rev. 4. And a review date, at the bottom, the way a policy has a review date, and the date was the end of the quarter.
<hr />

I asked for access to the ledger history. Not the line; the history of the line, who'd set it up, what the foundation was, where the post box went. That's the kind of thing a man in my position asks for a dozen times a week, and a dozen times a week somebody says yes within the hour.
On Monday somebody said no.

Not rudely. There was a process. The ledger history was in a category of records that required a role I didn't have, and the role required a form, and the form required a sponsor, and Saskia, who'd walked me through a lobby telling me to notice everything, said she'd look into it in a voice that meant she'd been told not to.

On Tuesday I found that my access to the list of scheduled jobs, the ingredients, the thing I'd been hired to read, had been quietly narrowed. I could see everything except one class of job. I'll let you guess which.

I sat at my desk and did the arithmetic. They'd taken away exactly what I'd need to see it again. Not more. Not my job, not my badge, not my login. Just the one shape. It was the most precise thing that had ever been done to me, and it had been done with a form.
And on Wednesday, at seven, on the sixth green, Dave said, "You look like a man whose bank's being difficult."
"It's not a bank."

"Whatever it is, it's got the face." He crouched for Buddy. "Hello, foreman. Is he being a misery? He's being a misery." And then, standing, easily, the way he said everything: "If it's an access thing, it's always an access thing, the consultancy that did your tools will have someone. They always have someone. That's what you're paying them for. Ask."
"Ask who?"
"Whoever's name's on the invoice, Jim. That's who you always ask. The person who'd be embarrassed."

I did. That afternoon. I wrote to the consultancy whose name was on the invoice for the tools, a dull two-line email, could someone help me with a role request that's stalled, and I got a reply in eleven minutes from a man who signed himself Julian K., who was sorry to hear it, who'd had a word, and who thought it'd be sorted by close of play.

It was. By four. The ledger history was open. The form had never been needed. Saskia came past my desk and said, "Oh, that got through, did it, good," in a voice that meant it hadn't gone through her.

I wrote back to thank him. He wrote back to say it was nothing, that these things were always a form somebody'd forgotten, and that if I ever needed anything else, he was the person who'd be embarrassed, so I should ask.
The person who'd be embarrassed. Dave's phrase. In Julian's mouth. On a Wednesday.

I noticed. I'd like you to know that I noticed, and that I filed it under coincidence, under it's a common phrase, under everyone in continuity talks like that, and that the filing system doesn't ask questions, because that's what it's for.
I check paper. I don't check people. It's the thing I'm worst at and it's the thing that nearly killed me.
<hr />

That night I opened the ledger history and read thirty-one years of a payment to a post box, and I found the thing I'd known I'd find, which was that it had been set up in 1994 by a man whose name appeared nowhere else in four centuries of records, and I found the thing I hadn't, which was that the sum had changed. Four times. Not with inflation. In steps. 1996. 2008. 2019. And this year, in July, the week I'd opened a ticket in another building about a job that didn't exist.
Up each time. By a clean multiple. The kind of number a committee agrees.
Somebody had been told, four times in thirty-one years, that the index was up, and had voted the money to match.
And the fifth time, it had been me.

chapters.file: 26 — A room with a long table.md
chapters.title: A room with a long table
chapters.what: Third person. Kalder and Bram. The reader learns what the count counts, in conversation, not in a memo. Movement II ends here.
blocks: The table was long because the room had been built for twelve and was only ever used by two, and Bram Lievens sat at the end of it with his back to the window because he liked people to have the light, and because he'd been told once that it was kind, and he had taken it to heart.
"Sit anywhere," he said. "No, not there. That's where the chairman sits when there's a chairman. Sit here. How's the dog?"
"Which?"
"His. The old one."
"Slow. Happy. He puts his hand on its head when he's thinking and doesn't know he's doing it." He sat. "I've told you that."

"You have. I like hearing it." Bram had a folder and didn't open it. He never opened the folder in the first ten minutes; he'd explained once that the folder was for after, that the first ten minutes were for the man, and that he'd learned this from someone who'd learned it from someone, and that it was the only part of the job he'd have missed. "The access went through."
"Yes. Eleven minutes. He thanked me."
"He thanked Julian."

"He thanked the name on the invoice. That's all anyone ever thanks." He put his hands on the table, flat. "He's read the ledger history. He's seen the steps. He'll have the dates by now; he's that sort. Ninety-six, oh-eight, nineteen. July."
"July," Bram agreed, mildly. "That was you, I think. The quarter."
"That was the index."

"The index is a number, Julian. Somebody has to read it to somebody, and somebody has to write the sum down, and that's me, and I write what I'm told." He smiled. He had a good smile, apologetic, as though the world had been arranged slightly to his advantage and he'd noticed and was sorry. "Tell me what he's doing. Not what he's stopped. You've been asked that before."
"He's reading. He's quiet. He's stopped calling his mother, which the wife has noticed. He plays on Wednesdays and he's happy on Wednesdays and he doesn't ask why. He's been to Leiden."
"We know about Leiden. Leiden's been quiet for nine years. Leiden's a model." Bram turned the folder a quarter turn on the table without opening it. "And the other thing?"
"Not yet, or no?"

"Not yet." He said it carefully. "He's close to it. He's got a chair in the kitchen he sits in with the dog. He says things to the dog. I've heard some of them. He's got all the parts of it and he's never put them together, because he's a man who checks paper, and it isn't on paper."
Bram was quiet for a moment, and then he did open the folder, and took out one sheet, and turned it round so that the light fell on it, and slid it halfway down the table, where it stopped.
"I'd like you to look at this and tell me what you see. Honestly. I'd like to know whether I'm reading it right."
Two columns. The left one was a code and a number and a date. The right one was the same code, and a different number, and the same date.
"It's the weekly."

"It's the weekly for one subject. His. Over since April." Bram sat back. "Left is reporting. Posts, enquiries, letters to dealers, visits to curtain shops. You can see him go loud in July and go quiet in September. Lovely. Textbook. You've done well. The right column is the index." He let it sit. "Which has gone up every week since April and has not come down once. Not when he went quiet. Not when the access was pulled. Not when you gave it back. Not when his wife stopped kissing his head, which, yes, we know, it's a small house."
"I don't understand the right column."

"No. Nobody at your level does. Nobody at mine did, for years. I'll tell you what I was told, which is more than I should, because I like you, and because I think it'll make you better at this." Bram folded his hands. "It was never belief. We don't count belief. Belief's weather; belief goes up every time somebody puts a light in the sky on television and down every time a magician's in the room. We've never been afraid of what people believe. The index counts the ones who've stopped being afraid. That's all. That's what the forty kilobytes are. A reading, every night, of how many people in a given population have, that week, stopped needing what we sell."
The man at the table didn't move.

"A frightened reader is a reader," Bram said. "He publishes, or he doesn't; he's loud or he's quiet; either way he wants something, and if a man wants something you can seat him. A man who's stopped being frightened doesn't want a seat. He doesn't want to be believed, even. He just looks. And you can't house that, Julian, and you can't buy it, and you can't laugh it off a stage, because he's not on the stage. He's in a kitchen with a dog. And the index goes up by one. And when the index goes up far enough, the people above me bring the review forward, and when the review comes, it comes for the population, not the man, because the man was never the point." He unfolded his hands. "That's the arithmetic. You've always known the arithmetic. You've just never known what it was counting."
"He's not stopped being afraid. He's terrified. He's not sleeping."

"He's terrified of us," said Bram. "That's different. That's new. Fear of us we can work with; fear of us is a man who'll take a seat. I'm talking about the other thing. The thing underneath. The one that was in him at his wife's grandmother's funeral and has been going out of him, a little, every week since, like a bath." He looked at the sheet. "He hasn't crossed. You're right. Not yet. But the index doesn't wait for the crossing. It counts the slope. And his slope is the steepest I've seen since Leiden, and Leiden went quiet nine years ago and we've never had a reading on her since, because she stopped reporting, and we only ever measured one column."
"So what do you want from me?"

"What I've always wanted. Be near. Know what he loves. And when he gets to the kitchen floor, which he will, I'd like to know the week." Bram slid the sheet back to himself. "Because that's when the review moves, Julian. Not when he finds the ledger. Not when he finds the style guide or the generals or whatever the Leiden woman put on her table. When he stops being afraid of dying. That's the only week that's ever mattered. Everything else is just a man reading."
He closed the folder.
"You've got a flask now, I hear."

"Good. I like that. Take him coffee." He stood, which meant it was over. "And Julian. The wife's going to find the schedule. They always do. It'll be an address. Let her. A frightened wife is a seat we don't have to pay for."

The index was read on Monday. It was up. The review stayed at the end of the quarter, which was eleven weeks away, and the man with the flask drove to Zwolle and sat in a blue chair and did not turn the light on for longer than usual.

chapters.title: Leiden, nine years ago
chapters.what: Third person. Kalder's crossing, from his side. Twenty minutes of Noor's silence. He files it, watches the date move, asks for more names. The seat is a promotion he wanted.
blocks: The library was being restructured, which is the word people use when a library is being taken apart, and Julian Kalder had a clipboard.

He was thirty-four and good at this. The foundation sent him wherever a collection was being moved, because collections being moved are where things go missing, and because he had a gift, noted early and used often, for learning the names of everyone in a building in the first two days and using them, correctly, in the third. Porters, cataloguers, the woman who did the tea. He didn't do it as a technique. That was the thing his handlers had understood about him before he had: it wasn't an act. He liked people, briefly and completely, the way some men like weather.

The transfer took three weeks. Forty thousand volumes from a university annexe that was closing to a depot that wasn't, in numbered crates, by van, with a manifest. Kalder's job was the manifest. He stood at the loading door with the clipboard and ticked, and talked, and by the end of the first week the porters were telling him about their divorces.

The conservators worked upstairs. There were two of them. One was a man in his sixties who treated Kalder with the polite contempt of someone who knows what a clipboard means. The other was a woman of about thirty called Noor, who did not treat him with anything, because she did not, as far as he could tell in three weeks, treat people. She worked.
