Whether anybody here knows, actually knows, not guesses, what happens in the room on the last night, because he has a feeling, from the way the nurses have started to look at his mother, that it is going to be tonight, and that nobody is going to say so, and that the not-saying is a kindness that he is expected to accept the way he is expected to accept the coin.
"No," he says. "Thank you."
She squeezes his arm and goes.

Later, in the room, his father's hand is on the sheet, and the boy looks at it, and he knows the hand better than he knows his own, the knuckles, the one nail that never grew right after the door, and he does not take it, because taking it would mean something and he does not know what, and he is afraid of doing the wrong thing in a room where everything is being done right.

A doctor speaks to his mother in the doorway. He is a kind doctor, and tired, and he has a clipboard, and he says a sentence that the boy will not remember and then another that he will. "There's some paperwork. Not now. Leave it for now."

Leave it for now. His mother nods. The boy watches her nod and watches the paperwork go away under a kind man's arm and understands, at sixteen, in a corridor, that there is a category of thing that is not his, that is handled, that goes away under an arm, and that the correct response is to nod.

It's tonight. Nobody says so. At four in the morning the sounds change and then there are no sounds and a nurse he hasn't seen before puts a hand on his mother's shoulder and says, very gently, "He's at peace now. He's in a better place."

The boy hears it. He hears it as a sentence. He turns it over, once, in the corridor, standing by the chocolate machine with a coin in his fist, and he thinks, clearly, in the voice he will have for the rest of his life: based on what? And then he thinks: don't. And he doesn't. He puts it away. He has nowhere to put it, so he puts it where there's nowhere, and he will find out, twenty years later, on a kitchen floor, that it's still there, exactly as he left it, with the coin.
His mother is crying. He holds her coat. He stands half a step behind and to the left. He is good at it. He has no idea what he's doing.

At six they let him go back in for a minute, alone, and the hand is on the sheet, and he does take it now, when it can't mean anything, and it's cool, and the knuckles are the knuckles, and he stands there holding his father's hand for the first time since he was small and thinks nothing at all, which is the only time in his life he will manage it, until the floor.
Afterwards, on the way out, he puts the coin in the machine. It takes the coin and gives him nothing. He looks at it. He doesn't press anything. He doesn't ask anyone. He leaves it.

The paperwork was done in the spring. He never saw it. He went back to school on the Monday and was fine, and was told he was fine by a series of professionals over the next twenty years, and was graduated by every one of them, and never once mentioned the machine.

chapters.file: 38 — The night he stops being afraid.md
chapters.title: The night he stops being afraid
chapters.what: The crossing. Sober, flat, domestic. No light. No how. The list re-reads itself. He says the word once, to a dog, and is embarrassed.
blocks: I'm going to tell you what I did and what happened and I'm not going to tell you how, because I don't know how, and because every book that says it knows how is lying, and I've read them all now.

What I did was sit on the kitchen floor. That's it. Every door in the house shut. Phone in the drawer. Lights off except the one over the cooker, which Buddy likes, because it means food is possible. I sat with my back against the cupboard where the dog's biscuits are and my legs out and my hands on my knees, and I did nothing.

I'd read enough to know you're supposed to do nothing. I'd read enough to know that nobody can tell you what nothing is, and that the moment you try to do it you're doing something, and that this is the whole joke and nobody finds it funny. I didn't find it funny either. I sat there the first night for an hour and did nothing so hard that I got a headache, and Buddy watched me from the blankets with an expression I'd have described, if I were being honest, as concern for a colleague.

The second night, the same. The third night, I nearly didn't. I sat down, and the review date was in nineteen days, and Noor's number was dead, and my wife was at her mother's with a Doberman, and I thought, this is the stupidest thing you have ever done. You're a man on a floor. Nothing is going to happen, because nothing is a thing that happens to other people, the ones on the forums, the ones with the glow. You check paper. Go and check some paper.
And I didn't have any paper left. That was the thing. So I sat.
On the fourth night I stopped trying.

I don't mean I gave up. I mean something smaller and I can't make it bigger. I'd been trying to do nothing for three nights the way you try to fall asleep, which is the one thing that trying prevents, and on the fourth night, around one, with the cooker light on and the dog breathing, I thought: fine. Nothing's coming. Sit here anyway, because the floor's warm and the dog's here and there's nothing on upstairs. And I stopped waiting for something to happen.
That's the trick, if there is one, and nobody can be told it, and I've just told you, and it won't work, because I've told you.
<hr />
The wall went.

Not down. I want to be careful. It didn't fall and there wasn't a light and nobody spoke. It was more like the thing that happens in my job when a system you've been watching for weeks, one that's been reporting itself fine, fine, fine, stops reporting, and in the silence you can hear what it was covering.
What it had been covering was me.

Hands. That's the first thing, and it's the thing I'd been told, by my own notes, since April, and had filed. In the cemetery I'd seen a hand, cracked at the knuckles, reaching for mine out of cold mud, and I'd filed it under lack of sleep, and I'd been right that it wasn't a dream, and wrong about everything else. It wasn't a hand. It was a hand I'd seen before. Many times. All my life. Reaching, in a flash, the length of a camera flash, in waiting rooms and on trains and once in the middle of a presentation to forty people, and every single time I'd done the same thing, the thing I'm good at, the thing the shrinks graduated me for: I'd looked away, and filed it, and been fine.
Not the first time.

Sitting on the floor with my back against the biscuits, I understood that I had been doing this since I was six. Misfiling. Thirty-five years of a very clean Record with every anomaly in it except the only one that was mine.
And then the lives.

I'm not going to give you the lives. Not because they're secret. Because they're boring, and that's the thing nobody tells you, that's the thing that makes it unbearable. I'd expected, if I'd expected anything, something with trumpets. What I got was short, and brutal, and ordinary. Somebody cold. Somebody in a field. Somebody very young, holding on to somebody else's coat. A door. A lot of doors. And love, every time, a different one, cut off mid-sentence, not by anything dramatic, by administration: by a war that was somebody's policy, by a winter that was somebody's harvest, by a cart, by a fever, by a man with a list. Over and over. Somebody's hand. Then nothing. Then somebody's hand.
Dealt back into the deck. I'd said that at a grave, in April, doing the arithmetic for the first time. A machine for making sure no one ever finds anyone again. I'd thought I was describing a belief.
I'd been describing a mechanism.
<hr />
Here's where I have to stop and tell you about the kitchen, because this is a book about checking, and I checked.

After, when it had gone, whenever it went, I sat on the floor and I looked at the kitchen. On purpose. The way you look at a room after you've been told a system's fine, to see if it is. The cooker light was on. The clock on the oven said 02:14, which I'd like to tell you I made up, and didn't. The dog's bowl was where the dog's bowl is. Buddy was on the blankets with his head on his paws, watching me, awake, and had been, I think, the whole time. The fridge was humming the hum it has. My hands were on my knees. I was not glowing. I was a forty-one-year-old man in socks on a kitchen floor at two in the morning and the kitchen was exactly the kitchen, and I knew that if Ana had walked in at that moment she'd have seen a tired man and a dog and said come to bed, and she'd have been right.
Nothing had changed in the room. I want that on the record, and it's the last time I'm going to say that.
What had changed was that I wasn't afraid.

Not brave. I don't mean brave. I mean that a thing that had been running in me since I was six, since a corridor, a thing I'd never once heard because it had always been there, the way you don't hear the fridge, had stopped. And in the quiet I could hear what it had been: it had been fear. Not of the men in vans. Of the thing. The one thing. The one under the other ones. The one I'd asked a nurse about with my mouth shut at sixteen and asked a grave about at forty with my mouth shut and had built a hobby and a job and a persona and a folder called Reading in order never to hear myself ask out loud.

It was gone. Like a bath. I sat there and listened to it not be there and I could not, for the life of me, remember what I'd been so frightened of, and I knew exactly what I'd been frightened of, and both of those were true at once, and that's the closest I can get.
<hr />
"Buddy," I said.
He lifted his head.
"I think I've got a soul."

And I was embarrassed. On the floor, alone, to a dog. My face went hot. I heard the sentence in the kitchen and it sounded like the forums, like the glow, like a man in a tinfoil hat, and I nearly took it back, and then I thought: he's a dog. He's a professional. He's not going to tell anyone.
"Sorry," I said. "I know. Bit much."
Two thumps of the tail. He put his head back down. He's heard worse.
<hr />

Then the list re-read itself. I don't know how else to say it. I didn't get up and get it. I didn't need to. I'd read it thirty times; I had it. And sitting there I understood that I'd been reading it wrong, the way I'd read page 118 wrong the first three times, by its shape.

Forty-one entries. Forty of them about the beginning: a hand taken out of a story about where things came from. And one, twenty-six, about last Tuesday: two rooms, forty metres, something moved. I'd asked Noor why the same people would care about both, and she'd said it was the only question, and now I had it, and it was simple, and it had been on the floor the whole time.

They weren't two kinds of edit. They were one edit. Transmitted to arisen. Shared to coincident. Remembered to imagined. Every one of them took the same thing out: the thing I'd just felt go through me on a kitchen floor. The thing that goes between. Between the givers and the given. Between two rooms. Between a man and a hand in cold mud. Between whoever I'd been and whoever I was now, carried across, like a wet rope, from hand to hand. The one thing that can't be gated, because it isn't information.

They'd never been hiding history. They'd been hiding this. And the only way to hide a thing that isn't information is to edit every sentence in the world that says it's transmitted, so that nobody goes looking for the hand.

Thirty-eight, further down the list, I'd never understood. The observer question. A withdrawn paragraph in a textbook about measurement, 1971, the observer changed to the apparatus. I understood it now. I was the observer. I'd just observed. The apparatus was a job that ran at fourteen minutes past two, and what it counted, every night, in forty kilobytes, was how many of us had.
<hr />

I stayed on the floor till it was light. Not doing anything. Just sitting with it, and with the dog, the way you sit with a system that's finally reporting the truth and you don't want to touch it in case it stops.

Somewhere in there I went back to a corridor. I knew I would; it had been waiting since the hand. Sixteen, a coin, four machines with four sounds. A man saying leave it for now. A nurse saying he's in a better place and a boy turning the sentence over once and putting it somewhere there was nowhere. I went back and I stood in the corridor and I took the hand while it still meant something, which I hadn't, and I said the thing I hadn't, which was nothing, just the sentence, out loud, based on what, to a kind tired doctor who couldn't hear me and wouldn't have known. And then I let it go. Twenty-five years. It had a container now. It was a kitchen floor and a dog, and that was enough, and nobody had told me it would be, and I'd never have believed them.

At seven I got up, slowly, with the noise men my age make, and let the dog out, and made coffee, and stood at the back door watching him drink from the bowl by the gate, and the morning was grey and ordinary and I'd have signed for forty more years of it.
At nine I rang Ana.
"I'm okay," I said.
Silence on the line. Then, in a voice I'd never heard from her, careful, the voice you use near something that might be real: "You sound okay."
"What happened?"
"I sat on the floor."
"James."

"I sat on the floor for four nights and on the fourth one I stopped being afraid of the thing. The big thing. The one from the funeral. I can't tell you how and I'm not going to pretend I can. But I'm not afraid of it any more and I don't think I'm going to be again, and I wanted you to hear it from me before you heard it in my voice." I had my hand on the dog's head. "I'd like to come to your mum's. Not to come back. To tell you. All of it. On a table. Twenty minutes. You can decide after."
A very long quiet.
"Bring the hat," Ana said.
<hr />
I need to tell you one more thing about that night, and then I'll stop, because the rest is the book.

The clock on the oven had said 02:14. I noticed it, the way I notice things, and I filed it, under coincidence, where it belonged, because there are 1,440 minutes in a day and one of them has to be that one.
But I'd like you to hold it. Because somewhere, that night, a job with no owner ran for nine seconds and sent forty kilobytes to nowhere. And whatever it counted, it had just counted me.

chapters.title: Urfa, 1994
chapters.what: 🟡 v7 DRAFT — Claude, 21 Oct 2026. [Interlude, real]. A German archaeologist climbs a hill the farmers call Potbelly. Real events; Tresidder is fifteen kilometres away and the chapter never says he found it. Follows The night he stops being afraid.
blocks: The hill had been looked at before. That is the first thing to say, because it is the thing that matters.

In 1963 a joint survey from Istanbul and Chicago had walked the plateau north-east of Urfa, in the far south-east of Turkey, near the Syrian border, cataloguing anything that looked old. They noted a low mound with broken limestone slabs on top, and flint on the surface, and a stand of mulberry trees that the local farmers treated as holy, and they wrote it down as a likely medieval cemetery, and they moved on. The slabs were taken for gravestones. The hill was given a line in a report. The report was filed.

The farmers called it Göbekli Tepe. Potbelly Hill. They had been ploughing around the stones for generations and moving the ones that got in the way, and nobody had asked them, and they had not thought to say.

Thirty-one years later a German archaeologist called Klaus Schmidt, who was forty and had been working at a site forty kilometres away and was looking for somewhere of his own, read the 1963 report. He read the line about the hill. He read medieval cemetery and limestone slabs and he thought, later, by his own account, that it did not fit: there was no reason for a cemetery on a bare hilltop with no water, and the flint, by the survey's own description, was wrong for the Middle Ages by about ten thousand years.
So in October 1994 he drove out and climbed it.
<hr />

What he saw from the top he described many times afterwards, and the description did not change, which in an archaeologist is a kind of honesty. The slabs were not gravestones. They were the tops of pillars, T-shaped, limestone, set in rings, mostly still buried, and the whole hill, as far as he could tell from standing on it, was not a hill at all. It was a mound of what people had put there. Fifteen metres of it. Deliberately.

He said he knew within a minute. He said, in the version he gave most often, that he had a choice on that hilltop, which was to walk away and tell nobody, or to spend the rest of his life there, and that there was no third option, and that he chose the second, and that he was right about the rest of his life, because he died in 2014, at sixty, swimming, with the site barely a tenth dug.

The first excavation season was 1995. The dates came back from the laboratory and were sent again because nobody believed them. The pillars had been raised around nine and a half thousand years before Christ. Before pottery. Before farming. Before the wheel, before writing, before any of the things that the textbooks said had to come first, because you cannot build on this scale without a surplus and you cannot have a surplus without agriculture and you cannot have agriculture without settling down. That was the order. Everyone knew the order. Schmidt's pillars were seven thousand years older than Stonehenge and six thousand older than the first cities, and they had been carved, with reliefs of foxes and boars and vultures and scorpions and a headless man, by people who were supposed to be living in caves and following herds.

He put it in a sentence that got him into trouble and is now in the guidebooks. First came the temple, then the city. Not the other way round. People had gathered to build this, and the gathering had required feeding, and the feeding had, perhaps, taught them to farm. The thing that the whole story of civilisation said was the effect might have been the cause.

And then, at some point around eight thousand years before Christ, the people who had built it buried it. On purpose. Carefully. They filled the enclosures with rubble and bone and flint and earth, ring by ring, and they walked away, and the hill grew mulberry trees, and farmers ploughed around the stones, and a survey wrote medieval cemetery, and the file was closed for thirty-one years.
<hr />
That is the record, and it is enough. But there is one more thing on the record and it belongs here.

Nobody hid Göbekli Tepe. There was no conspiracy. A survey team in 1963 looked at a hill and saw what they expected to see, because the thing they were looking at was not possible, and when you are standing in front of something that is not possible the human eye is very good at finding the possible thing nearby and settling on that. Gravestones. Medieval. Move on. The report was honest. The men who wrote it were competent. They were simply looking at a thing from the wrong side of a sentence that everyone knew was true, and the sentence did the rest.
It took one man, reading the middle of an old report instead of the summary, to notice that the flint was wrong.
<hr />

Fifteen kilometres from that hill, in the autumn of 1929, an Englishman with one book to his name walked out of Urfa on foot, heading east, with a notebook, and did not come back. He was last seen on the road. He had spent a year in the region. He had, in his one book, said that the traditions of the first settled peoples appeared to have been transmitted to them, and two years after he disappeared somebody changed that to arisen among.

There is nothing in any archive that puts H. M. Tresidder on Potbelly Hill. The farmers who might have remembered an Englishman asking about the stones were dead by 1994. The 1963 survey did not record any earlier visitor. This book will not tell you he found it, because it does not know, and neither did the professor, and neither does James, and he has looked.

What is known is where he walked out of. And what is known is what was fifteen kilometres from the road, under the mulberry trees, in 1929, where it had been for eleven thousand years, waiting for somebody to read the flint.

chapters.title: The long table, again
chapters.what: Third person. The crossing, reported. He uses the first name. The reader learns Kalder has hands. The date moves. Movement III ends.
blocks: "You've got the week," Bram said. It wasn't a question. He had the folder and he hadn't opened it, and he was looking at the man at the table the way he looked at the index on a Monday: fondly, and for a number.
"When?"

"Thursday. Between one and three. The light over the cooker was on till seven, which it never is; he turns it off when he goes up. He rang the wife at nine instead of her ringing him. He let the dog out and stood at the door for eleven minutes with a coffee, and he didn't check the street." He had his hands flat on the table. "He's not afraid."
"Of us?"
"Of anything. He's terrified of us, still, in the way you'd be terrified of a car. But the other thing's gone. You can see it. He stands differently." A pause. "He said soul to the dog."
Bram smiled. "Did he."
"He was embarrassed about it. He apologised. To the dog."
"That's the one I like. That's the one that goes in the file, if we kept that kind of file." Bram turned the folder a quarter turn. "And you watched it."
"I was in the lane. The back. Yes."
"And you'd know."
The man at the table didn't say anything.

"I'm not asking to be cruel, Julian. I'm asking because I've got six handlers who'd have stood in that lane and seen a man on a floor, and one who'd have seen what you saw, and I need to know I'm reading the right one." Bram folded his hands. "You'd know. You're the only one of mine who would."
"How long, for you?"
"Nine years."
"Leiden."

"The month after the transfer. Her kitchen. I'd been in and out with a clipboard for three weeks and on the last day she gave me tea and didn't say anything for twenty minutes and neither did I." He looked at the table. "I didn't go looking for it. It was in the room. It went through me the way it's gone through him, and I drove to Zwolle, and I sat in the car, and I understood what the index was. Before anyone told me."
"And you reported it."
"I reported it."
"Your own."

"I'd been told what the arithmetic was. I knew what a true line did to the date. I filed it, and I watched the review come forward by a quarter, and I understood that I had become the only instrument you had that could see the thing it was measuring, and that there was a seat in that." He lifted his hands off the table and put them back. "So I took the seat."
Bram was quiet for a long moment.
"I've always thought that was the bravest thing anyone's done in this building," he said, eventually, and he meant it, and that was the problem with him too. "And the saddest. You know that."

"And now there's another one. In a kitchen. With a dog. And he's not going to take a seat, is he, because he's past wanting one, and the only thing that stops him being a reading we can't act on is that you're the one who knows how to read him." Bram opened the folder, finally, and took out the sheet, and turned it to the light, and the right-hand column had a line on it that wasn't a number. It was a name. "I need the line, Julian. Hands, yes or no. In your words. It's the only week that's ever mattered. You said so yourself, in a car park, when you still thought it was about books."
The man at the table looked at the sheet for a long time.
"James has hands," he said.
The first name. He heard himself use it and so did Bram, and neither of them remarked on it, and it sat on the table between them like a cup.

"Thank you." Bram wrote. One word, in the right-hand column, next to the name. "The review's in three weeks. I'm going to recommend two. I'd like you to have a conversation with him before then. Not on a course. Somewhere with the wife. I'd like him to be offered what you were offered, properly, with the arithmetic, and I'd like you not to be there, because I think you'd be a problem for him and I think he'd be a problem for you." He closed the folder. "You'll be at the depot. There's a transfer. Your name's on it. That's not a punishment."
"I know what it is."
"Good." Bram stood. "The old dog. Was it you?"

"I'd believe you either way. I want you to know that." He went to the door, and stopped, with his hand on it, and said, not turning round: "Nine years, and you've never once asked me whether I've got them. Hands."
"Why not?"
"Because you'd have told me," the man said. "You tell everyone everything. It's how you seat them."
Bram laughed, once, surprised, and went out.

The review was brought forward to two weeks. The index was read on Monday. It had gone up by one, and the line beside the one had a name on it, and for the first time in nine years the man with the flask did not drive to Zwolle, because the chair was no longer there. It had been transferred.

chapters.title: Twenty minutes
chapters.what: Movement IV opens. He tells Ana everything, with objects, in her mother's kitchen. She gets the plan, not the memoir. The cooling half, understood.
blocks: Ana's mother lives in a house where every surface has a cloth on it, and I put the objects on the cloth, one at a time, in the order I'd decided on in the car, and Ana sat opposite with her arms folded and her mother upstairs with the television up loud on purpose, and Mora under the table with her chin on my foot because it had been nineteen days and in Mora's world that's a resurrection.

"Twenty minutes," I said. "You can stop me. You can throw me out. I'm going to put things on the table and tell you what they are, and I'm not going to tell you what I think until the end, and then you can decide."

The two books. "This is a sentence that was changed in 1931, two years after the man who wrote it walked into some hills. They changed one line and left the typos so nobody'd check. I found it on our kitchen floor. That's the night you came down for water and I said I hadn't found anything weird."
"I remember."
The thin book. "This is a list of forty more. Kept by a dead man and his grandfather. I was handed it in a crate. I don't know whether that was an accident."

The three pages. "This is the style guide the edits were made from. Fourth revision. His daughter found it in a dresser. It's got a section on what to do when someone like me notices, and the answer is: agree with him, and reclassify."

The screenshot, printed. "This is a job that ran every night at my old place and sent forty kilobytes to nowhere. I asked what it was. Within a week it was gone and so was my asking. It's at the new place too. It's been there for thirty-one years. It's called a recall index. The sum they pay for it goes up in steps, and the last step was the week I asked."
The schedule. She looked at it and didn't touch it. "You've seen that."
"Our address."
"Our address. The word in the box is the golf club's word for Buddy. The visit was the night he got sick. Nobody came to the door. I don't know what happened and I'm never going to."

The slip from Noor. "This is a number a woman in Leiden gave me because I asked instead of argued. It's an item in a depot. She's gone quiet since. Not dead. Quiet. There's a difference and I've learned it."

The ruleset, the one page, 212. "This is the tool my old mate Frank sent us a link about with a skull. It's been told, out of the box, never to see the job. Somebody wrote one boring sentence into the defaults and it's installed everywhere. It's got a review date. The date's in two weeks."
And then the last thing, which wasn't an object, so I put my hand flat on the cloth where it would have gone.

"And this is me. On the floor. Four nights. I can't put it on the table. I can tell you that I was afraid of dying from the age of sixteen, in a corridor, and that I'm not any more, and that it happened on a kitchen floor with the dog watching and the oven clock on, and I'm not going to tell you it was anything but that, because it wasn't. I'm not glowing. I'm not going to make you do anything. I just don't have the thing any more, and I think that's the only thing they've ever been counting, and I think they've counted me."
I took my hand off the cloth. "That's it. Nineteen minutes. What I think is on the table. You can throw it out."
<hr />
Ana didn't say anything for a long time. Her mother's television laughed upstairs at something.

Then she reached across and picked up the thin book, and opened it at the back, and looked at the word, and closed it, and put it down exactly where it had been, square to the cloth, the way her grandmother would have.
"I don't believe it," she said.
"Okay."

"I want to say that first, so you've heard it. I don't believe there's a them. I don't believe a bank in a wig has been paying for a machine that counts souls. I don't believe you've got a soul, or I do, but not like that, not like a thing that gets counted, that's insane, James, that's the most insane thing anyone's ever put on my mother's tablecloth." She wasn't crying. She was doing the other thing, the clear thing. "And I've been sitting here for nineteen minutes watching you put it there, and you did it the way you do the toaster. In order. Boring. With the bits you couldn't prove labelled. You said I don't know six times. I counted. You've never said I don't know six times in a year."
"I've stopped pretending."

"I can see that. That's what I can't get past." She unfolded her arms. "You look different. You've looked different since the phone call. You stand like somebody who's put something heavy down, and I've been married to you for eleven years and I've never once seen you without it, and I didn't know it was there until it wasn't."
"So what do you believe?"

"You." She said it like a slap and a kiss at once, the way she says most things that matter. "I believe you. I don't believe it and I believe you and I don't know what to do with that, so I'm going to sit here until I do."
<hr />
What she did, in the end, was ask for the plan. Not the memoir. That's her. Twenty minutes of what, and then: so what are you going to do about it, Mulder.

"I don't have a plan. I've got a problem. Here's the problem." I moved the schedule next to the ruleset. "Everything I've done to find out what it is has made it worse. Not for me. For the date. I asked about the job and the sum went up. I found the notebook and the sum went up. I sat on the floor and I'm fairly sure something happened to the date that night, because that's what it's for. It's a thermostat. The more people stop being afraid, the sooner it does whatever a review is, and I don't know what a review is, and I've got two weeks."
"Then stop."

"I did stop. That's the thing. I stopped in October. I stopped publishing, I stopped telling Frank, I stopped telling you, I went quiet like the woman in Leiden, and I think that's exactly what they want, and I think it's also exactly what they're afraid of, and I can't make both of those be true and I've been trying for a month."
Ana looked at the table. "What did the pub man want?"
"To know what I loved. He said so, I think. Not to me."
"And what do they want?"

I thought about Bram, whom I hadn't met. About a man on a phone in 1993 saying it's a budgeting thing, Wim. About a column headed Visit. "To house me. I think. There's a word for it; I've seen it in the ledger. People who've worked it out and are offered a seat. Somewhere. With their families. On a list."
"A seat where?"
"I don't know. Wherever you go when the review happens."
Ana was quiet. Then she said, "They'd offer you me."
"And the dogs."
"I think so. I think that's what N seats means."
"And you'd say — "

"I'd say no." I heard how it sounded and I said it again, slower, so she could check it. "I'd say no. Not because I'm brave. Because I don't need it. That's the thing that changed on the floor, Ana, that's the only thing. A seat is a rescue. I don't need rescuing. And I don't think they've got a thing to do with a man who doesn't."
"Except visit the dog."
"Except that."

She stood up. She went to the kettle, which is what her family does instead of deciding, and she filled it, and she didn't turn it on, and she stood with her back to me, and Mora's chin stayed on my foot.
"You're staying," she said. "Here. Tonight. With him. Mum's got the back room and he can't do the stairs so he'll have the kitchen, which he'll prefer."
"Ana, if they've got our address they've got — "

"Then they've got this one too, and you've just told me the list has got two weeks on it, and I'm not spending two weeks in my mother's spare room on my own waiting for whoever they send to turn up at our house and offer you a bunk while I'm here. If they want to offer you a bunk they can offer it with me in the room." She turned round. "That's the plan. That's the whole plan. I don't believe it and I believe you and the four of us are going to sit in my mother's kitchen, and if somebody comes to the door, I'll open it. Because I'm not in. Whatever that means. I'm not in, and I'm the only one of us who can say that, and I'd like to see what happens to whoever they send when the person he's threatening answers the door and offers him tea."

I looked at my wife, standing by a cold kettle in her mother's kitchen with her arms folded, and understood that she'd just done the thing I do, the thing I'm supposedly good at, which is to look at a system from outside and work out what it can't handle, and that she'd done it in four minutes, and that it was her.
"Okay," I said.
"Good. Bring the hat in. It's in the car, I saw you not bring it in."

I brought the hat in. I hung it on her mother's hook, by the door, because there wasn't anywhere else, and it looked ridiculous there, and Ana looked at it, and for the first time since a terrace in November, she almost laughed.
Almost. We're not there yet. But I saw it go across her face, and I'd have signed for forty more years of almost.

chapters.title: Frank, loose
chapters.what: James shows Frank the money. For the first time they talk the big ideas straight. Frank's verdict: I still don't believe it; I believe the invoice. Buddy under the table. Ana home.
blocks: Frank came round on a Thursday because I asked him to, which I'd never done, and he knew it, and he brought beer anyway, which is how I knew he was worried.

Ana was home. She'd been home a week, with Mora, who had eaten a cushion at her mother's and shown no remorse, and the house had gone back to being a house: two dogs, a kettle, somebody upstairs. I'd forgotten how much of my thinking I do against the sound of another person in a building. On my own, for those weeks, I'd thought very clearly and very fast and I'd got to some places I wouldn't have got to otherwise, and I'd also sat on a kitchen floor for four nights, and I'd stopped being able to tell which of those was the point.

Frank sat at the kitchen table. Buddy went and lay under it, across his feet, which he does to people he's decided about, and Frank said, "Oh, hello," and went very still the way people do, and I thought, good, that'll keep him here.
"So," Frank said. "You've got the face."
"I don't have a face."
"You've had the face since about March. Pieter's noticed. Pieter thinks you're job-hunting." He opened a beer. "I told him you don't job-hunt. You'd have to talk to people."
"Thank you."
"So what is it. And if it's the Egyptians, I'm going home."
<hr />

I'd thought for a long time about how to do this. I'd thought about doing it the way I'd done it for Ana, at her mother's, with every object on a tablecloth, and I'd decided against it, because Ana loves me and Frank is a sceptic and those need different things. Ana needed to see that I'd labelled what I couldn't prove. Frank needed to see one thing he couldn't argue with, and nothing else, and to be allowed to argue with it.
So I put one sheet of paper on the table.

It was the spreadsheet. Thirty-one years of quarterly invoices from a foundation to a bank, one line per quarter, continuity reconciliation (recall index), per flagged person, with the number of persons and the rate and the total, and the six steps marked in yellow, and the last step, the Monday of the week I'd opened a ticket, marked in red.
"What am I looking at."
"Money."
"I can see it's money. Whose?"

"Ours. The bank pays this. Every quarter. For thirty-one years. To a foundation that owns the recovery site. For a service called reconciliation, billed per person, and the number of persons goes up in steps, and the steps are clean multiples, and the last step was the week I asked about an orphan job in stand-up."

Frank looked at it. He's good with numbers; it's why he's good at his job and why he was hired to replace mine. He looked at the steps and I watched him see what I'd seen, which is that money doesn't move like that unless somebody's turning a dial.
"Per flagged person," he said.
"Flagged how?"

I told him about the list. I'd decided to, in the car back from Zwolle. Not the file; the shape. A nightly job. A hundred and twelve lines. Two words each. My own number on it the night after I'd opened my mouth.
He didn't say anything for a while. Then he said, "The job I don't remember."
"The job you don't remember."

"I've thought about that," Frank said. "The stand-up. I've gone back over it. I remember the stand-up. I remember Pieter being Pieter about something. I don't remember you saying anything about a job, and I've tried, and I can't get it, and that's not—" He stopped. "That's not like me. I remember stand-ups. I remember what people had for lunch."
"I know."

"So either you didn't say it, or I've been—" He made a small gesture at his own head and didn't finish, and Buddy shifted under the table, and Frank looked down at the dog and then back at the sheet of paper, and I saw him decide to stay on the paper, because the paper was a thing he could do something with.
<hr />
What happened next I hadn't planned, and I want to describe it accurately because it's the only time in this whole story that two people who like each other talked about the actual thing.

Frank asked what the foundation did. I told him what I knew: an archive, a reading room, a building on top of a shed. He asked why an archive would want a list of people who'd asked questions. I said I didn't know. He asked what questions. I said, as far as I could tell from the two-word reasons, any question, about anything, as long as it was the kind of question that doesn't have an answer in the building. Old books. Dead people. What happens after. He asked why anyone would count that.
And I said, because I'd been sitting on it for a month and it had to come out somewhere: "Suppose you wanted to know how many people were awake."
"Awake."

"Not asleep. Not—" I didn't have the word. I've still not got the word; I've since learned that everyone who's thought about this has a different one and that the different words are half the problem. "Suppose there's a thing most people don't look at. Death. What it is. Whether there's anything. And suppose most people have agreed not to look at it because looking at it is unbearable, and the agreement is what holds everything together. Work. Mortgages. Showing up on Monday."
"The wall of comfort," Frank said. He'd heard me say it. Everyone's heard me say it.

"And suppose somebody, somewhere, thought it was important to know how many people had stopped agreeing. Not to punish them. Just to know. The way you'd want to know how many people in a building had stopped believing in the fire alarm."
Frank drank some beer. "That's a thermostat."
"What?"

"You're describing a thermostat. A thing that measures a temperature and does something when it crosses a line. You've got the measuring. You've got the invoice for the measuring. What's the something?"
I didn't answer. I had the schedule in a folder in a bag and eleven addresses on it and I wasn't going to put that on the table, not yet, not with Frank, who had children.
He saw me not answer. He let it go. That's the thing about Frank that nobody who's only met him at a barbecue would guess: he knows when to stop pushing, and he does it as a kindness, not a tactic.
"Okay," he said. "Let me do you the favour of taking it seriously for ten minutes. Then I'm going to tell you what's wrong with it."
<hr />
He took it seriously. I'd never seen him do that before with anything of mine, and I'd like it on the record that he was better at it than I was.

He said: suppose the count is real. Suppose there's a nightly job in a bank that lists people who've asked. Fine. You can't read minds. All you can read is what people write down. So the thing you're counting isn't awake; it's awake and talking. The quiet ones never appear. Which means whatever the thermostat does, it does it to the people who said something, and leaves the people who didn't. "Which is a very old idea," Frank said. "You don't need a conspiracy for that. Every institution on earth does it by accident. The people who speak up get managed."

He said: suppose it's not an accident. Then the interesting question isn't who's counting. It's why the count would need to be secret. "If I wanted to know how many people in a building were scared of dying, I'd run a survey. Nobody runs a secret survey unless the number itself is dangerous. Unless the thing they're afraid of is the number getting out." He tapped the sheet. "Which fits your steps. The steps aren't inflation. The steps are the number crossing a line, and somebody paying more because it did."
And then he said the thing I've thought about every day since.

"You know what this reminds me of? Not the books. The other thing. The thing you and I never talk about because it makes us look like the people we take the piss out of." He turned the beer bottle on the table. "There's a version of physics, respectable people say it, Nobel people, where the world only resolves when it's looked at. The electron doesn't have a position until you measure it. Fine. Everyone's heard that. But there's a stupider version that I've never been able to get out of my head, which is: what if it's not the electron. What if it's everything. What if the world is only rendered where there's an observer, like a game only draws the room you're standing in."
"You've been reading."

"I read things. Don't tell Pieter." He almost smiled. "The point is: in a system like that, the system knows who's logged in. It has to. It's rendering for them. It knows which rooms are being looked at. What it can't do—" he held up a finger "—is see what they see. It knows you're in the room. It doesn't know what you're thinking about the furniture."
"A count without a camera."
"A count without a camera." He sat back. "That's your list, James. A hundred and twelve people logged in. The system doesn't know what they found. It just knows they looked."
Buddy sighed under the table, enormously, the way he does when humans have been talking too long.
<hr />
"Now," Frank said. "What's wrong with it."

He told me. He was thorough. He said that every step on my spreadsheet could be a renegotiated contract, that foundations are badly run and bill in round numbers because somebody's nephew does the accounts, that flagged is a word consultants use for anything, that the orphan job could be exactly what Pieter said, that my badge number appearing on a list the night after I'd asked about the list was the single most obvious thing a diagnostic tool would do, because I'd asked about it, and that if I showed this to a psychologist they'd nod a lot and ask about my father.

"And the thing with the book," he said. "The sentence. Transmitted, arisen. I believe you found it. I believe it's real. I think it's a variant reading and a dead scholar's second thoughts, and I think you've built a cathedral on it because you needed somewhere to put what you felt at that funeral, and I say that as your friend, and as someone who's watched you do it with smaller things for three years."
I didn't argue. I'd heard it all before, in my own head, in my own voice, which is better at it than Frank's.
"That's the honest version," he said. "I don't believe it."
"Okay."
"I don't believe any of the story." He put his finger on the sheet, on the red cell. "I believe the invoice."
I looked at him.

"That's the bit I can't do anything with," Frank said. "I've sat here for forty minutes trying to make that number be something boring and I can't. Consultants don't bill in clean multiples for thirty-one years. Nephews don't do accounts that neat. And nobody, nobody, steps a contract up by exactly one unit on the Monday of the week a monitoring engineer opens a ticket about a cron job, unless the unit is the engineer." He took his finger off. "Everything else you've said, I can explain. That, I can't. And I've learned, from watching you, that the thing you can't explain is the thing."
"The memo's the table," I said.
"Don't quote me at me."
<hr />
He left at eleven. At the door he said, "What are you going to do with it."
"Show the people on the list what they're paying for."
"Which list."
"The one with the children on it."
He looked at me for a long moment, and I saw him decide not to ask, and I was grateful.
"Pieter's got kids," he said.
"I know."
"Is Pieter on it?"
He nodded slowly. He looked back into the kitchen, where Buddy had got up from under the table and was standing at the window now, in the dark, watching the street.
"He does that," Frank said.
"He does that."
"Since when?"
"Since a man started walking down it."

Frank looked at the dog for a while. Then he said, "I still don't believe it," and he went out to his car, and sat in it for a minute before he drove away, and I know that because I watched him from the window with my hand on the old dog's head, the two of us standing there like a pair of guards who've never been told what they're guarding.
Ana came down. "Well?"
"He believes the invoice."
"Is that good?"
"It's Frank," I said. "It's the best he's got. It's better than I had."

chapters.title: Leiden, 1931
chapters.what: Third person. The one far back. Invented men, invented book, real city. The reader recognises the machine. The plate.
blocks: The visitor had a good coat and did not take it off, and he stood in the composing room with the smell of ink and hot metal around him as though it were a smell he'd known all his life, which the printer, whose name was Van der Hoeven and whose father's name had been on the door before his, took to be a courtesy and later understood to be a method.
"One line," the visitor said. "Page one hundred and eighteen. I have it written out."
He had. On a card, in a hand that had been taught to be legible, with the old words on the left and the new words on the right, and a vertical rule between them, drawn with a straightedge.

Van der Hoeven read it twice. He was a careful man. His father had been a careful man and had gone bankrupt being one, and the son had learned that care was a thing you did with your hands and not with your opinions, and so he read the card with his hands, holding it to the lamp, and then he said, "It's not a correction."

"The old line is not wrong. I don't read English well. But I read enough. The old line is a scholar's sentence. The new line is also a scholar's sentence. They say different things, and neither of them is a mistake."
"That's right."
"Then I don't understand what you're paying me for."
The visitor looked, for a moment, almost pleased. "You're the fourth printer I've asked," he said. "The first three understood immediately. I'd rather it was you."

He explained. Not why; never why. What. The plate for page 118 was to be opened. The one line was to be re-set, exactly, with the spacing adjusted so that the justification would hold and the line count would not change. Nothing else on the plate was to be touched. There were two misprints on that page, and a flaw in the top margin where the metal had pitted, and they were to stay. The copyright page was to say second impression and nothing more. No corrected. No revised. The book was to go out under the same words on the title page, to the same continental trade, at the same price, and the author, who had walked into some hills in Anatolia two years before and had not walked out, was not to be mentioned, because there was no one to mention him to.
"A reader will see it," Van der Hoeven said. "Someone. Eventually. Somebody will have both."

"Somebody will. In fifty years, or a hundred. And when he does, he'll find two typos left in and a flaw in the margin, and he'll think: they didn't even clean the plate. Who would go to the trouble of changing one line and fix nothing else? And he'll decide that it must have been the author, before he went. Or a lazy compositor. Or nothing." The visitor put the card down on the stone. "The misprints aren't an oversight, Mr Van der Hoeven. They're the reason he'll stop looking. A clean plate is a confession. A dirty one is just a printer."
Van der Hoeven looked at the card on the stone for a long time.
"My father would have refused."
"Your father went bankrupt."

"I'm not threatening you. I want to be clear about that. I don't do that. I'm telling you that there is a foundation, in this city, that is about to take an interest in the Leiden printing trade, and that it will be placing work for forty years, and that the houses it places work with will be the houses that are still here in forty years. That's all. I've told the other three the same thing. I'd rather it was you, because you asked what you were being paid for, and in my experience the man who asks that is the man who'll do it properly and then never think about it again." He buttoned his coat, which had never been unbuttoned. "You have two sons."
"They'll be looked after. Not because of this. Because of the forty years. This is one line." He went to the door. "I'll come back on Thursday for the proof. Leave the flaw."

Van der Hoeven set the line himself. He did it at night, when the apprentices had gone, because he found that he didn't want to be watched doing it, and he noticed himself not wanting that, and did it anyway. He set it with the spacing adjusted so that the justification held. He left the two misprints. He left the pit in the margin, and when he inked the proof and pulled it and held it to the lamp, the page was perfect, and identical, and said something else, and he stood in his father's shop with it in his hands and felt, he would have said, if there had been anyone to say it to, like a man who has been asked to move a chair in a room and has done so and the room is the same room and will never be the same room again.
On the Thursday the visitor came, and read the proof with his hands, and nodded, and paid, in cash, and did not haggle.
"It's very good," he said. "You'll never see me again."

He did not. The foundation placed work with the house for forty-one years. The two sons took it over in 1958 and sold it in 1972 to a firm that became a firm that became a firm, and the plates were melted in a war, and the books went out, every copy, under the same words on the title page, to every library and every dealer and every scan, wearing the first impression's clothes.

Van der Hoeven kept the card. He never knew why. His grandson found it in a drawer in 1994, with a straightedge rule down the middle, and threw it away, because it was in English, and it was one line.

chapters.title: The reading room, continued
chapters.what: The opening, picked up from the cut. James puts the recent, cool stuff on the table. The old man confirms only the general method, and makes the offer: five seats, no dogs. James says no. Part Two ends here.
blocks: The generator stopped.

I don't know how long it ran. Long enough for the tray to stop vibrating, which it had been doing, very slightly, against the table; I'd been watching the ledger shiver. The old man had waited for it to finish the way you wait for a lorry to pass before you go on with a sentence. The woman by the window hadn't moved at all.
"Tests," he said. "They test it on Tuesdays. I've asked them not to and they tell me it has to be Tuesdays. One doesn't argue with engineers." He smiled at me. "Does one."

I had a bag by my chair. I'd brought it up the stairs past Aylin, who had looked at it and said nothing, and I'd put it down beside the chair the way you'd put down a dog you'd been told to leave outside and hadn't. I reached into it now.
"You said everyone who gets this far finds the seats."
"I did."
"I didn't come about the seats."
I put the first sheet on the table, next to the ledger, on the professor's side of the tray.
<hr />

I'd thought about how to do this for three weeks and in the end I did it the way I'd do it at work, which is in the order the evidence arrived, with the newest first, because the newest is what they'd least expect me to have, and because I wanted to see which one made the woman by the window move.

Page 212. A photocopy of one page from a four-hundred-page ruleset shipped with a monitoring product sold to every bank in the country, and on it, in the vendor's own language, a rule telling the tool never to report jobs of exactly one shape, and the shape was the job I'd found, and under the rule a review date, end of quarter. "A blind spot," I said. "Sold as a default. Every company that bought the tool bought it. Nobody who bought it knows it's there."
He glanced at it. He didn't pick it up. "Products are complicated," he said. "I'm told."

The accounts. The foundation's own, published, as charities must. Thirty-one years of grants, and beside each year a number I'd got from somewhere else, and the pattern that fell out when you put them side by side: that every grant to a documentary company, a publisher, a festival, a retreat in the hills with a name like a yoghurt, fell in a year when the other number was low. "You fund nonsense when too few people are asking," I said. "And you stop when enough are. It's a thermostat. You've got a heating half."
He looked at that one a little longer. "We fund a great many things," he said. "Some of them are embarrassing. That's philanthropy."

The hearings. I didn't have paper for this one; I'd watched it on the bar TV at the pub a month earlier, a parliament somewhere releasing files, a general saying that forty per cent of the sightings had no explanation and that the public could draw its own conclusions, and the ticker underneath already saying no evidence of. "Every admission comes bundled with a finding of nothing," I said. "Every time. For seventy years. That's not how disclosure looks. That's how a thermostat looks when the needle's high."
He said nothing to that. He looked, if anything, pleased, the way a teacher looks when a student has got to the bit of the syllabus the teacher likes.

The forum. My own account, twelve years old, with my deleted question restored and a paragraph about bloodlines added that I'd never written, and my correction underneath, seen by eleven people. "You farm them," I said. "The places where people ask. You don't shut them down. You make them stupid, so that anyone who asks a real question is standing next to a man in a tinfoil hat."
The invoice. The thirty-one-year sheet, with the steps in yellow and the last step in red. I put it down and I said the date, and for the first time the woman by the window turned her head.

Not much. A few degrees. Enough that I saw her face properly for the first time, and it was a face I knew from a photograph on an intranet page: Anneke de Wit, head of risk, who had approved that invoice, or whose department had, thirty times, and who was sitting in a reading room on a Tuesday in December watching an engineer from her own bank put it on a table.
"Per flagged person," I said. "The last step was the week I opened a ticket."
She didn't speak. But she looked at the sheet, and she kept looking at it, and the old man noticed that, and something in the room changed temperature.

And then the last one, which I'd saved, and which I put down without a word: the schedule. The quarterly field schedule, with its column headed Visit, and eleven addresses, and what had happened at seven of them, in my handwriting, in the margin. Heart. Sold. Fire. Quiet. Quiet. Quiet. Quiet. And the eighth, with a date nine days from the day I'd got it, and in my handwriting beside it: I was there. Nobody came. Why.
<hr />

He read the schedule. He read all of it. He took longer over my handwriting than over the typed part, and when he was done he put it down square on the tray beside the ledger and he sat back and he did something I hadn't expected, which was laugh.
Not at me. It was a small, delighted sound, the laugh of an old man who's been shown a card trick and seen how it's done and likes it more for that.
"Oh, this is very good," he said. "This is very, very good. Anneke, isn't this good?"
She didn't answer.

"You've done the modern part," he said to me. "That's the part nobody does. They all come in here with the old stuff. The pyramids. The flood. The thing in Turkey. They sit where you're sitting and they tell me about Sumerians, and I listen, because it's polite, and it's never once been interesting, because the old stuff is a result. It's what's left when the thing has been done. You've brought me the thing being done. Page two hundred and twelve." He said it like a vintage. "A rule in a product. I didn't know that one myself, I'll be honest. I'm told things, I don't read manuals."
"Is it yours?"

"Mr Klippe." He folded his hands. "I'm going to do you the courtesy of not insulting you, and I'd ask the same. You've put seven pieces of paper on this table and asked me, in effect, to confirm each one, and I'm not going to, because I don't need to, because you already know, and because each one of them is a thing that could be explained in a court by a bored man in an hour. A vendor's default. A charity's grants. A forum. An invoice for a service you don't understand. A list of addresses and some sad things that happened in the east of the country in an autumn." He tilted his head. "You know what they are. I know what they are. What they are in a room is nothing."
"And the schedule."

"The schedule is a schedule." He said it gently. "We move records for conservation. We visit people. Sometimes the people we visit are old, and sometimes old people die. You went to the eighth address and nobody came. Did it occur to you that nobody came because you'd gone?"
It had. It had occurred to me on the drive home.
"I'll tell you what I will confirm," he said, "because it's old, and because it's true, and because I'm vain and you've earned it. The method. You've got the method right, and almost nobody does."
<hr />
He talked for a while then. I'm going to give you the shape of it and not the words, because the words were his and he enjoyed them too much, and because I don't want them in your head in his voice.

He said: stories were always the tool. Not force. Force is expensive and leaves marks and makes martyrs, and a martyr is a story you can't control. What you want is to own the story, and the way to own a story is to be the one who tells the other version. Every time a thing is seen that shouldn't be, you don't deny it. You tell it back, bigger, sillier, with a man in a mask standing next to it, until the true version can't be said in a room without the room thinking of the mask.

He said: every new way of telling stories had frightened them, for a while. Print. The newspapers. Radio. Film. Television. Each one, for a decade or two, had looked like the end, because each one let people say things to each other faster than the other version could be told. And each one, in the end, had become theirs. Not by taking it over. By using it. By being the best customer. "The cinema," he said, "was the greatest gift we were ever given, and we didn't give it to ourselves. We just bought the most tickets."

He said: the internet had frightened them more than anything since the printing press, for about five years. And then it had turned out to be the best thing that had ever happened to them, because it didn't make people believe the wrong things. It made them doubt everything. And a person who doubts everything is a person who will never, ever, finish a sentence that begins based on what.
"That's the method," he said. "It hasn't changed in four hundred years. We're not clever. We're consistent."
<hr />
"Now," he said, and he unfolded his hands, and I understood that the part he'd enjoyed was over. "You've put your papers on my table. Let me put mine."
He didn't put anything down. He didn't need to.

"There are seats in the building below us. You've sat in one. Forty of them belong to your employer, under a contract you've read, with an annex you've read, and the annex has names on it and a column that bothers you. I'm going to tell you something about that column, and then I'm going to make you an offer, and then you're going to go home, and I'd like you to think before you answer, because I'll only make it once."
"The column."

"The column is real. The building is real. The thing the building is for is real, and it is not what you think, and I'm not going to tell you what it is, because you'd tell your wife, and she'd tell her mother, and it would be in a forum by Thursday next to the bloodlines." He smiled. "What I'll tell you is that it's old, and that it's coming, and that we have never once, in four hundred years, been wrong about the date. The people on that list are not being rewarded. They're being kept. Because somebody will need to do the payroll on the Wednesday, Mr Klippe. That's all continuity ever is."
"And the offer."

"Five seats." He said it flatly, like a price. "You. Your wife. Her mother, if you like, I'm told they're close. Two more, your choice; a friend, a colleague, the man who sells curtains, I don't care. Five names on Annex C, dependants per allocation, in a building you've already got a desk in."
I waited.
"No dogs," he said. "I'm sorry. I'm told it's a question of air."
<hr />

I'd like to tell you I thought about it. I didn't, and that's not courage; it's that I'd already thought about it, for three weeks, on a kitchen floor, with the dog in question asleep across my feet, and I'd found that there was a sentence underneath all the other sentences, and the sentence was Ana's, from a kitchen floor at four in the morning, and it was run where, I've got a Doberman.
"No," I said.
He nodded, as if I'd confirmed a delivery time. The woman by the window had turned back to the window.
"May I ask why? Not to persuade you. I'm curious. Most people, at this table, take a day."

I looked at the tray. At the ledger from 1931, open at the page where one line was struck through and another written beside it. At my seven sheets of paper. At a book I'd never seen before, on the far corner of the tray, thin, with no title, that had been in my kitchen until a night in November when a dog went down at the gate.
"Because you asked about the dog before you asked my name," I said. "All of you. Every time. It's the first thing you do. And I've worked out why."
For the first time, the old man didn't have a face ready.

"You count people who've stopped being afraid," I said. "That's the right column. That's what the handlers are for. And you can't see it directly, so you look for the thing that goes with it. And the thing that goes with it is love. Not the big kind. The stupid kind. The kind that gets up at two in the morning because an old dog's legs have gone. Because a man who loves a dog that much has already done the arithmetic about losing it, and come out the other side, and that's the arithmetic you're afraid of." I stood up. "You can't have the seat without the dog. Not because I'm brave. Because the dog's the only reason I'd be worth a seat."
I picked up my bag. I left the papers on the table. They were copies.

At the door Aylin looked up from the card index and said, "Mr Klippe. Same time Thursday?" in the voice of a woman who books rooms, and I said yes, and I don't know why I said yes, and I went down the stairs past the glass door and through forty desks and out into a car park where it had started, very lightly, to snow.

Buddy was in the car. He'd got up. He was standing on the back seat with his nose against the window, watching the door I'd come out of, and when he saw me his tail went, once, and he lay down again, with the grunt, like a foreman who's seen the shift end.
I sat in the driver's seat for a long time before I started the engine.

I'd said no. I'd said it to a man who had never been wrong about a date. And I had, in my bag, a copy of a schedule with three dates still on it, and one of them was ours, and the word in the notes column was still companion, and now they knew that I knew, and I'd given them, for free, the one thing I'd kept back from everyone, including Ana, including Frank, including myself until I'd heard it come out of my mouth in that room.
I'd told them what I loved.

They already knew. That was the whole point. But I'd confirmed it, out loud, to their faces, and in my work that's the one unforgivable sin. You never tell a system what you're watching for. It'll give you exactly that, and nothing else, forever.
I drove home in the snow. Part of me, the part that counts things, was already counting the days.

chapters.title: The dinner
chapters.what: The cold open, reached. The offer. The reveal that hurts, as an object. Ana present. Cat and mouse: nobody says the word. Ends on him.
blocks: He came at eleven on the Sunday, which is when people come for coffee, and Ana opened the door, and I heard her say, from the kitchen, "You must be the one who talks," and I heard him laugh, surprised, pleased, and I knew before I saw him that she'd already won something.
"I'm Bram," he said. "I am the one who talks. I'm sorry about that. Is that tea?"

He was sixty, maybe. A good jumper, the kind a wife chooses. No coat; he'd left it in the car, I understood later, because a man without a coat isn't going anywhere, and a man who isn't going anywhere is harder to throw out. He had a folder under his arm and he put it on the chair, not the table, and he looked at the table, where I'd laid out the twenty things the way I'd laid them out for Ana, and he looked at them for a long moment with an expression I can only call professional appreciation.
"That's a very good bibliography," he said.
"Sit down."
"May I? Not there, I think. That's yours. Here." He sat where the light was on him, which I noticed, and filed, and then unfiled, and looked at. "And this is the foreman."

Buddy was under the table. He'd come in from the radiator when the door went, slowly, and put himself under the table by my feet, and he looked at Bram from there the way he'd looked at a man by a heater, and Bram looked back, and said, "Hello, old man," gently, and didn't try, and Buddy put his head down.
He'd asked about the dog second. After Ana. I noticed that too.
<hr />

"I'll say what I'm not going to do," Bram said, with his tea, "so we don't waste the morning. I'm not going to confirm anything. Not the book, not the list, not the job at your old place or the line at your new one, not the pages from the dresser, not the gentleman from the golf course. I'm not going to tell you there's a we. If you say there is, I'll listen. I've found that it goes better if I listen." He smiled at Ana. "Your husband's going to think that's a technique. It is. It's also true."
"Then what are you here for?" Ana said.

"To make an offer. And to hear what James thinks he's found, because I've read the summaries and I'd rather hear it from the man." He turned to me. "Go on. You've laid it out. Walk me through it. Pretend I'm your wife."
"He's never once walked me through anything," Ana said. "I had to get it in twenty minutes with objects."
"Then I'm honoured," said Bram, and meant it, and that was the problem with him.

So I walked him through it. The sentence. The list. The pages. The job, and the line, and the steps, and the grants in the cold years. I did it the way I do the toaster, in order, labelled, with I don't know where I didn't, and he listened the way Dave had listened to Ana's grandmother, with his whole body, and when I'd finished he sat back and said nothing for a while, and then he said:
"You've got the band."

"Nobody gets the band. I've been doing this for twenty-two years and I've had four people in that chair who'd got the sentence and two who'd got the job and one who'd got the pages, and nobody's ever once sat there and told me it heats." He shook his head. "Who told you?"
"A thermostat."
He laughed, properly, and Ana looked at me, and I saw her see that I'd made the one who talks laugh, and file it.
<hr />

"I'm going to tell you a story now," Bram said. "I'd like you both to hear it, because it's the only part of this I actually believe, and it's the reason I do it, and I'd rather you heard the reason than the arithmetic. You can throw it out after. People do."
He put his cup down.

"Imagine a world where it's happened before. Not the end. The shift. Imagine that every few thousand years, something goes through a population, I'm not going to say what, you've put a hand on a tablecloth about it, I'm told, and people stop being afraid. Not all of them. Enough. And it's wonderful. It's the best thing that ever happens to anybody. And then, within a generation, every single time, the ones who've stopped being afraid build something faster than the ones who haven't can understand, and they build it together, because they're not afraid of each other any more, and then the ones who are still afraid, which is most people, because it's always most people, look at what's being built and they do the only thing frightened people have ever done with a thing they can't understand."
"They burn it," Ana said.

"They burn it. And the ones who built it. And it ends worse than it would have if nobody had woken up at all, because now there's a giver. There's a hand. There's somebody to blame, and somebody to follow, and a story about where the fire came from, and the next lot build a religion on the story and the one after that builds a war on the religion." He turned his cup. "So, a very long time ago, some people who'd watched this happen more than once sat down and asked a question. Not how do we stop people waking up. You can't. Nobody can; it's weather. The question was: how do we stop the hand. And the answer, after a great deal of trying, was: you take the hand out of the story. Every story. You don't deny the fire. You don't deny the flood. You just make sure that when a child reads about it, it arose. Nobody gave it. Nobody brought it. There's nobody to burn." He looked at the two books. "That's not a lie, James. That's a style. We don't change what a thing is. We change where it's kept. And we keep the number of people who've stopped being afraid inside a range where they can be laughed at instead of followed, because being laughed at is survivable, and being followed, I promise you, I have the records, is not."
"And the seats?"

"The seats are for the ones who've done the arithmetic and would rather not be laughed at. There aren't many. There's a review, periodically, when the range is exceeded, and I'm not going to tell you what a review is, because I don't know, I've never seen one, I've only ever seen the budget for it. And there's a provision, for the people who've helped, and their families, and the provision is called a seat, and I've got a folder with your name in it and a number next to it." He said the next part very quietly. "A population that remembers is not a population you can house. We've tried. It's not cruelty. It's capacity."
Ana said, "That's a beautiful story."
"Thank you."

"I half believe it. That's what's horrible. I'm sitting in my mother's kitchen half believing a man I've never met about the end of the world, because he's told it well and he's kind to the dog." She folded her arms. "What's the number?"
<hr />
"Yourself," Bram said. "Ana. And three. Five seats, in total. The allocation is the allocation; I don't set it, I'm sorry, I did ask."
"And the dogs," I said.
He looked, for the first time, like a man who'd rather be somewhere else.
"Companions aren't seated," he said. "I'm sorry. It's a budgeting thing."

Ana's hand went to Buddy under the table without her looking. I watched it go. I watched her face not change, the way Dave's hadn't changed, and I understood that she'd learned it from him, on a terrace, and that she was using it now against the man who'd sent him, and I loved her so much that for a second I couldn't see.
"So that's the price," she said.

"That's the price. For the seats. I'd be lying if I said otherwise and I don't lie, it's the one thing I've got." He took the folder off the chair, finally, and opened it, and took out a single sheet, and turned it to the light, and slid it halfway across the cloth. "And this is the other thing. I was asked not to show you this. I'm showing you because you check paper, and I'd rather you checked it in front of me than found it later and thought I'd hidden it."

Two columns. A code on the left, a number, a date; the same code on the right, a different number. My week. I knew it before I'd read it, the way I'd known page 118. J-0417. April to now. The left column going loud in July and quiet in September. The right column going up, every week, and never once down.
And at the bottom of the right column, a second line. A different code. H-114. Same class as mine. A date beside it. Nine years ago.
"What's that?" said Ana. "Is that a book thing?"

I didn't answer. I'd stopped being able to. I reached across the table, past the ruler and the mug with the chicken, to the transfer schedule, folded in thirds, and unfolded it, and ran my finger down the lines to the one I'd read forty times and never once looked at: the depot transfer, this week, with a handler reference in the margin in a box I'd taken for a stamp.
I put the two sheets side by side on the cloth and put one finger on each line, the way I should have read everything from the start.
Nobody said anything. Bram watched me do it. He'd known I would. That was why he'd brought it.

James has hands. He'd said it in a room with a long table; I knew that now without having been there, the way I'd known the kitchen was the kitchen. And he'd been able to say it, and Bram had been able to believe him, because nine years ago, in another kitchen, in Leiden, with a clipboard and a flask, it had gone through him too, and he'd filed it. His own. And watched the date come forward. And taken the seat.
The first person I'd ever met who'd seen what I'd seen on a floor was the one who'd been sent to count me.

That's the thing that hurt. Not the lying. I'd known about the lying since a terrace. It was that it hadn't made him good. I'd thought, I understood, sitting there with my fingers on two lines, I'd thought since the floor that the thing was a key; that once it had gone through you, you'd be one of us, whoever us was, the ones in the other column, Noor's column. And here was a man it had gone through nine years ago who'd spent them in a car park moving a date with a verb. It didn't make you good. It made you known. To the machine, and to yourself. What you did after was yours.
"He told me," I said, eventually. "At three in the morning. That he'd moved it. I didn't understand why he'd tell me."
"No," Bram said. "Neither did I, when I read it. I think he wanted somebody to have asked about the dog."
<hr />

Here's what I'd worked out, in the car, on the way to a terrace, on a floor: he needed me to be afraid. Not of him. Of the thing. Because a seat is a rescue, and you can't sell a rescue to a man who isn't drowning, and every word he'd said since he sat down had been a very kind, very patient attempt to find out whether I still was.
"What are you afraid of, James?" he said. Gently. The way you'd ask a child.
"Nothing you've got."
"That's a line."

"It's a line. It's also the answer. I was afraid of one thing for twenty-five years and it went on a kitchen floor and it hasn't come back and I don't think it's going to. I'm afraid of you, a bit. The way you'd be afraid of a car. I'm afraid of a van on Noor's street. I'm afraid for him." The dog. "But the thing you count? The thing your forty kilobytes are for? I haven't got it. And you can't seat what I haven't got, and you can't laugh at a man who's stopped trying to be believed, and you can't vanish me, because a body's a fingerprint and your whole shop is built on never leaving one." I took my fingers off the two lines. "So I think you've driven out here on a Sunday to offer a bunk to a man who doesn't need rescuing, and I think you knew that before you got in the car, and I think you came anyway, because it's your job, and because you're decent, and because you wanted to see one."
Bram was quiet for a long time.
"Yes," he said. "That's about right."

"Then here's what I think you've got, and then you can go. You've offered me a seat. That's the obvious thing. That's the one for people who are frightened, and it's a good one, I'd have taken it in November, I'd have taken it on a terrace and thanked you. And you've told me a story about hands and fires, and that's the beautiful thing, that's the one for people who've seen through the first one, and I half took it, you watched me half take it, Ana said so, it's a very good story." I looked at him. "And there's a third thing, and you can't offer it, because it isn't yours. It's on a floor. You've been paying a post box for thirty-one years to count it and you've never once had it, have you. You've got the budget. You've never seen a review and you've never had the other thing either."
"No," Bram said. "Nobody at my level has. We call the seats decanting, among ourselves. It's an old joke. Older than me. I never understood it until about a minute ago."
<hr />
He turned to Ana then. I'd known he would. It was the last thing he had.

"And you," he said. "There's a seat for you whatever he decides. I can do that. It's within the allocation. You don't have to be — " he searched for the word, the one he wasn't going to say — "involved. You'd just have to be on the list. You've been in the room; that's enough. I can put you on the list and you'll never hear from us again, and if there's ever a review, somebody will come, and you'll be alright."
"I'm not in," Ana said.
"You're in the room."

"I'm in my mother's kitchen. With my husband. And a dog you can't seat." She unfolded her arms and put her hand on mine, on the cloth, on item twenty, and she squeezed it. Once. Hard. The way she squeezes when the plane takes off. "I don't believe it. I want you to write that down, in your folder, in whatever column you've got. I don't believe a word of it. The world isn't a thermostat and there isn't a them and my husband hasn't got a soul that gets counted like a gas meter. I don't believe it." She looked at him. "And I believe him. That's the only thing I've got, and it's mine, and it's not on your list, and you can't put it there."

Bram looked at her for a long moment, and then at her hand on mine, and I watched him understand what I'd understood in the car: that the one person at the table who wasn't in the machine was the one who'd read the room, and that she wasn't afraid either, by proxy, through a hand, and that there was no column for that.
"No," he said. "I can't."
