He put the sheet back in the folder. He closed it. He finished his tea, because he was a man who finished his tea.

"I'll report that you declined," he said. "Both of you. I'll report it accurately. I always have; it's the one thing I've got." He stood. "I don't know what happens now. I want you to hear that, because it's the truest thing I'll say today. I know what happens to a man who takes a seat and I know what happens to a man who shouts. I've never once seen what happens to one who just sits there. Nobody has. It's not in the folder." He looked at the dog. "If I had to guess, I'd say nothing. That's what happens to most things, in the end. You'd be surprised how often the answer that comes back is leave it."
At the door he stopped. The hat was on the hook, where I'd hung it, on a hook it didn't belong on. He looked at it.
"That's very good," he said. "Who made it?"
"I did," said Ana.
"You should be careful with that," Bram said. "It works." And he thanked her for the tea, and went down the path without a coat, and got into a car, and that was the one who talks.
<hr />

I sat at the table for a long time after. Ana didn't move either. Buddy came out from under it eventually and put his chin on my knee and looked at me like a foreman inspecting a site after the contractors have gone.
Twenty things on the table. One of them my wife's hand, and it had squeezed.

I'd thought, the whole time, since I'd first counted the things on that table, that the sheet with two columns said which of us was afraid, and that it was wrong. It wasn't wrong. It had said me, in April, and it had been right, and it had watched me go, week by week, like a bath, and it had been right about that too. It had never once been wrong about me.

It had been wrong about him. Not Bram. The other code. The one in my class, with a date nine years back, who'd known what the index counted before anyone told him, and had filed himself, and taken the seat, and come to a window at three in the morning to tell me so.
The sheet said he had hands. The sheet was right. What the sheet couldn't say, because it only ever measured one column, was what he was going to do with them.
Neither could I. I'd stopped checking people, and then I'd started, and I'd got him wrong twice. I was going to have to let the third one happen without me.
"Well," said Ana. "That got weird."

And she laughed. Not almost. The whole thing, the real one, with her head back, in her mother's kitchen, with a tinfoil hat on the hook behind her, and I laughed too, and the dog thumped twice, and upstairs the television laughed at something else entirely.

chapters.title: What was on the phone
chapters.what: Follows The dinner: Kalder asleep at the table, Ana's mother's pills, the phone unlocked with a sleeping thumb. Forty minutes. The handlers by code. The schedule. The seats for four companies. And the list he didn't expect: what each helper had been told.
blocks: He slept with his mouth slightly open, which made him look younger, and his phone was face down by his plate, where he'd put it when he sat down, the way he always did, the way you put something down when you want everyone to see you're not looking at it.

Ana was standing by the sink with her arms folded and her mother's pill bottle still in her hand. She hadn't moved since he'd gone. Neither had Buddy, who had stopped growling the moment Kalder's head went down and now stood in the doorway watching the sleeping man with an expression I can only describe as professional.
"How long," I said.

"Mum takes one and she's out for seven hours. He's had two." She looked at the bottle. "In the wine. I didn't—" She stopped. "I didn't plan it, James. I want that clear. He asked if Buddy was okay now, and you'd never told him Buddy was ill, and I was standing by the cupboard, and the bottle was there, and I thought: he's going to sit here being lovely until one of us says something we can't take back, and I'd rather he slept."
"You improvised."
"I improvised." She put the bottle down very carefully. "Is that a crime?"
"Probably."

"Good," said Ana, and sat down, and put her face in her hands, and started, very quietly, to shake. Not crying. The other thing. I've seen it in people after outages, when the system's back up and there's nothing left to do with the adrenaline.
I didn't go to her. I'd like to say I did. I looked at the phone.
<hr />
I need to explain something about myself that I've never said plainly, and this is the place.

I'm not a hacker. I can't code; not really, not the way Frank can, not the way the people who built the thing I found can. I've spent eleven years watching other people's systems and I couldn't build one of my own to save my life. Everything I know about getting into things I know from the outside: from watching, for a decade, how people get in, so that I can tell when they have.

And one of the things I know, from a hundred incident reports, is that nobody breaks into a phone. They don't need to. People unlock their phones for you. They leave them face down on tables. They fall asleep with their hand on the cloth beside a glass of wine, thumb up, in a kitchen, in December, at a house they've been visiting for months because they liked the dog.

I picked up his hand. It was warm and heavy and it didn't resist. I turned the phone over and put his thumb on it, and it opened, and I put his hand back exactly where it had been, and I sat down with another man's life in my palm, and I looked at the clock on the oven.
Forty minutes. I gave myself forty, because at forty I'd have to decide whether to stay or go, and I didn't want to decide that with his phone in my hand.
<hr />
I'm going to tell you what was on it in the order I found it, because the order is how I understood it, and because the thing I understood wasn't on any one screen.
No messages. That was the first thing. Not deleted; absent. The messaging app was there and it was empty, the way a show house is empty. Whoever he talked to, he didn't talk to them here.
Then a folder. No name, a grey square, the kind of thing you'd scroll past. Inside it, three things that looked like spreadsheets and one that looked like a map.

The first spreadsheet was people. Not names. Codes: two letters and three digits, a region, and a status, and beside each one a short note in the register I'd come to know from the schedule, the register of a man confirming a delivery. Active. Active. Reassigned. Active. Retired (natural). Forty-odd rows. I didn't know what I was looking at until I found his own: a code with a region that was ours and a status that was active and, in the note column, the only one with anything personal in it, a single word that I understood immediately and have not stopped understanding since.
Hands.

Handlers. The people who do the visiting. By code, by region, for the whole of the east of the country, and I had a dozen of them, and I didn't know a single name, and I understood that this was on purpose and that the purpose was that nobody, not even the man asleep at my table, should ever be able to give the names, because he'd never had them.

The second spreadsheet was the schedule. Next quarter's. The one after the one I'd had in my bag for a month. Addresses, dates, a column headed Visit, a column of notes. I read it with my heart doing something I didn't like. Our address wasn't on it. I read it again. It wasn't. The eighth, ninth and tenth from the old schedule were, carried over, with new dates, and nine new ones, and beside three of them the word pension, and beside one the word companion, and I photographed every row with Ana's phone because mine was in the hall and I wasn't leaving the table.

The third was seats. Not ours. Four companies. Four annexes, like the one I'd found in our system, with names and dependants per allocation and the line about animals, and the companies were a shipping firm, a hospital group, an energy company and a university, and the total across the four, when I added the column in my head, was a number of people that would fill the shed in the business park three times over.
So there were other sheds. Of course there were.
<hr />

And then the fourth thing, the one that looked like a map and wasn't, and I want to tell you about this one slowly, because it was the thing I didn't expect and it was the thing that told me how to win.
It was a list of helpers.

Not handlers. The others. The people who make the phone calls and close the tickets and sign the invoices and catalogue the records and drive the vans. The dealer in Groningen. The site manager in the high-visibility jacket. Pieter. Hundreds of them, in our region alone, and they weren't by code. They were by name, because nobody had ever thought a helper needed protecting. They weren't the ones who knew anything.

And beside each name, in a column with no heading, was a word. One word per person. And when I'd read enough of them I realised that the column had a heading after all, it just wasn't written down, and the heading was: what we told them.

Honeypot. That was Pieter, and about a dozen others in the bank, and it meant they'd been told the orphan job was a security test, a trap for leakers, and that they were helping catch bad people by leaving it alone.

Disaster recovery. That was the site manager, and the bus driver, and the people who stocked the canteen in the shed, and it meant exactly what it said, and it was true, and that was the genius of it.

Conservation. That was the dealer in Groningen, and a woman in Deventer who turned out to be the professor's neighbour, and a records clerk in Apeldoorn, and it meant they'd been told that certain old books and papers were being tracked for their own protection, and that a telephone call now and then was a kindness to the past.

Heritage. A brewer in a small town whose family firm had a cellar. A man who owned a quarry. The site in the business park was listed under heritage too, and so, I saw, was a building I'd never heard of near Nijmegen. It meant: you're looking after something old and important and we'd be grateful if you didn't ask what.
Four words. Four small, believable, flattering reasons, and against every single name in the fifth column, the same word, over and over, down the whole list like a watermark:
Continuity.

That was the promise. That was what they'd all been told they were part of. Not saving the world; nobody believes that. Continuity. The thing that goes on. The payroll on Wednesday. And every one of them, I understood, sitting at my own kitchen table with a sleeping man's phone, had heard that word and had taken it to mean, without ever once examining it, you'll be all right.
I looked for the names on the four annexes. I looked for Pieter's helpers, the honeypot dozen, on the seat lists. I looked for the dealer. I looked for the site manager. I looked for the brewer.

None of them. Not one. Hundreds of people who'd been told continuity and had heard you're kept, and the lists of who was kept had been in the next folder along the whole time, and not one of their names was on it.
<hr />
The oven clock said thirty-one minutes.
I put the phone down. I put it face down, exactly where it had been, at the angle it had been, and I sat back, and Ana lifted her face out of her hands and looked at me.
"Well?"

I didn't know how to say it. I've thought about it since and the only way I can put it is this: for a month I'd thought the thing I'd found was a machine, and machines are strong, and you don't beat a machine, you leave it, you go around it, you take the seat. And in thirty-one minutes on a stranger's phone I'd found out that it wasn't a machine at all. It was a few dozen people who knew, standing on a few hundred who'd been told four different lies, standing on everybody else. And the few hundred had never once been shown the list they weren't on.
"It's not strong," I said. "It's wide. That's different."
"I don't know what that means."

"It means I know what to do." I looked at the man asleep at my table. His breathing hadn't changed. In a few hours he'd wake up with a headache and a blank where the evening should be, and he'd check his phone, and it would be exactly where he'd left it, and he'd never know, because the one thing a man like that never considers is that somebody might do to him what he does to everybody else, which is simply pay attention. "It means I've got the paper, Ana. I've got what every one of them was told, and I've got the list they're not on. And nobody's ever put those two things side by side in front of them. Nobody's ever needed to. They never asked."
Buddy came out of the doorway, finally, and walked, slowly, past the sleeping man's chair without looking at him, and lay down across my feet.
"So what do we do," Ana said.
I'd been waiting fifteen years for someone to ask me that in a voice that meant it.

"We make him comfortable," I said. "We let him sleep. And in the morning we're very surprised he dropped off, and very nice about it, and we send him home with coffee." I looked at the phone. "And then I'm going to need a printer. And three weeks. And you're going to have to drive."

chapters.title: The sheets
chapters.what: Three weeks. One page per person. We watch him deliver them: Pieter after hours; the dealer; the brewer who reports it; Anneke, who reads the invoice thirty times and asks for the rest; Aylin, who shows him the visitor book. The sheets are diffs, not claims.
blocks: A sheet looked like this. I'm going to show you one, because I made three hundred and eleven of them and they were all the same shape, and the shape is the argument.
At the top, a name. Then four short sections, in this order, with a line between each.

What you were told. One sentence, in the words from the phone. The nightly job is a security honeypot; leave it in place. Or: Certain editions are tracked for conservation; please telephone if asked for. Or: Your cellar holds heritage material; access is restricted for its protection.

What you did. Their own records. The ticket they'd closed, with its number and date. The call they'd logged. The invoice line they'd approved, with their initials. The access they'd granted. Taken from systems they had the right to look in and never had, and printed with the reference numbers, so they could check.

What it was part of. One line from the schedule. Their line. The date their ticket was closed, or their call was made, set beside the date on the schedule that it had moved, and the address it had moved, and, in the margin, in my handwriting, one word for what had happened there. Heart. Sold. Fire. Quiet.

Who is kept. The seat list. The real one, from the annexes, for the four companies and ours. Names, dependants per allocation, the line about animals. Printed small, two columns, a page and a half. And at the top of it, in the only sentence on the whole sheet that was mine:
Your name is not on this list. Please check.

That was it. No theory. Nothing about books or sentences or what happens when we die. I'd learned that from Frank, in my own kitchen: don't give them the story, give them the invoice. A sheet made no claim they could argue with. It was a diff. Here is what you were told, here is what you did, here is what it was for, here is who's kept, and the space between the last two was theirs to fall into.
Three hundred and eleven. Three weeks. Ana drove.
<hr />
I'll tell you about five of them. The rest were variations, and some of them I'll never know how they landed, because the whole point of a sheet is that you hand it over and walk away.
Pieter first, because he had to be, and because I owed it to him.

I did it at his desk, after seven, when the floor was empty and the cleaners had gone through. He was still there because he's always still there; Pieter works late the way other men drink, steadily and without enjoyment. I put the sheet on his keyboard and sat down in the chair beside his desk, the one people sit in when they've come to resign, and I didn't say anything.

He read it. I watched him read the first section and recognise the sentence, because it was his, from a meeting I'd never been in, and I watched his ears go red. I watched him read the second section and nod, because the ticket number was right, and the date was right, and the closing note was his. I watched him read the third, and stop, and read it again, and look at the word in the margin, which for his line was fire.

And then he turned the page and found the list, and he found his own name, which was there, which I'd left there on purpose, and I watched his face start to clear, and then I watched him read the number beside it.
Dependants per allocation: 3.
"I've got two," he said. It came out very quietly. "Two kids. Lotte and Bas. And Marieke. That's three." He looked up. "That's three with Marieke."

"So that's—" He stopped. He put his finger on the number as if it might change. "That's us. That's all of us. Why does it say three like it's a—" He couldn't find the word. I had it; I'd had it for a month. Allocation. But I didn't give it to him. He'd get there.
"Read the sentence at the top, Pieter."
He read it. Your name is not on this list. Please check. He read it twice. Then he said, "But it is. I'm on it. I'm right here."
"You are. I know. I put that sentence on every one. Now read the names around yours."

He read them. He knew most of them. Heads of department. Two board members. Anneke. The forty from the drill, and then the others, the hundred and twenty, and the people he reported to and the people they reported to, and no one, not one person, from the floor he managed. Not Frank. Not the six people in the glass box. Not the woman at the next desk who'd been at the bank twenty-two years.
"They're not on it," he said.
"My team's not on it."
"No. You are. Because you said leave it. That's what the seat's for, Pieter. It's not a reward. It's a retainer."

He sat there for a long time with his finger on the number three. Then he said, in a voice I'd never heard him use, "What do I do," and I said the thing I'd decided to say to all of them, because it was true and because it was the only instruction that couldn't be reported upward as a threat.
"Nothing. That's the point. Next time, don't."

I left him there. I don't know how long he stayed. The next morning he said good morning to me in the glass box exactly as he always had, and I thought I'd lost him, and then, four days later, a ticket I'd opened against page 212 as a test came back not closed. Not actioned either. Just open. Sitting there. For the first time in eleven years Pieter had failed to tidy something, and I knew what it had cost him, and I said nothing, and neither did he.
<hr />

The dealer in Groningen I did by post, because he'd earned the courtesy of not having me in his shop again, and because I wanted him to be able to read it alone. I put a note in with it. You asked who sent me. Nobody. This is what the number in your ledger does. Two weeks later a parcel came. It was the ledger. The actual one, cloth spine, eleven years of his handwriting, with the number cut out of the back cover with a scalpel, cleanly, the way a conservator would do it, and a card that said, in the neat old hand, I find I no longer need it.
<hr />
The brewer went to them.
I knew somebody would. I'd told Ana one in ten would, and it was closer to one in twenty, and he was the first, and I want to describe him because he wasn't a bad man and I'd like that on the record.

He had a family firm in a small town, four generations, with a cellar under the brewhouse that went back to the seventeenth century, and twenty years ago a foundation had come to him with a grant and a request: the cellar was heritage, it was dry and cool and stable, would he allow part of it to be used for the storage of archival material, under seal, with access restricted to the foundation's own staff. He'd said yes. He'd have said yes to anyone with a grant and a kind word about his great-grandfather. His sheet said heritage, and his record was a key register with his signature on it four times a year, and his line on the schedule was a date on which a van had come, and I'd watched the van, from a lay-by, with Ana reading the pumping station sign out loud to keep me from doing it.

He read the sheet standing in his own yard with the smell of malt coming off the brewhouse. He read it carefully, all of it, and he looked at the seat list, and he looked for his name, and it wasn't there, and he looked up at me with an expression that I didn't understand until later, which was not anger and not fear. It was embarrassment. The embarrassment of a man who's been told, in front of a stranger, that he's been had.
"Thank you," he said, formally, and went inside.

He rang them that afternoon. I know because of what happened on the Thursday, which I'll get to. But I want to say this about him: he rang them because he'd been told, for twenty years, that the foundation was the kind of institution you rang when something strange happened, and a stranger in his yard with a sheet of paper was something strange. He wasn't betraying me. He was doing what the word heritage had taught him to do. He was being a good helper, one last time, and it was the last time, because the people he rang could not explain the sheet to him, and he was a man who'd run a business for forty years and knew what it sounded like when somebody couldn't explain an invoice.
<hr />
Anneke de Wit I'd left till the end of the second week, because she was the one I was afraid of, and because her sheet was the longest.

Head of risk. The silent woman by the window. Her record wasn't a ticket or a phone call; it was thirty quarterly approvals of a line that said continuity reconciliation (recall index), per flagged person, with her initials against each, going back eleven years to the day she'd got the job. Her sheet had the whole spreadsheet on it. The six steps. The red cell. And her seat, which was on the list, with a dependants number of one, which I'd checked against the intranet and which was correct: a daughter, at university, in Utrecht.

I didn't go to her office. I asked for a meeting, through her assistant, under the programme's name, and I got twenty minutes on a Friday, and I walked in and put the sheet on her desk and sat down, and she read it, and she did not say a word for eleven minutes. I counted. She read the invoice page, the one with her initials on it thirty times, and she turned it over and read the back, which was blank, and turned it back and read it again, and I understood that she was doing what I do: she was reading the middle. She was looking for the place where her own signature stopped being a formality and started being a thing.
When she spoke, it was the first time I'd heard her voice.
"Thirty," she said.
"Thirty."
"I approved this thirty times." She looked at the red cell. "This is you."
"That's me."
"The week you opened a ticket." She was very still. "And the other steps. Before my time, most of them. Who were they?"

"I don't know all of them. I know one. A physicist in Utrecht, in 1993, whose paper got filed under instrumentation. That's a step. A professor who found forty-one edits and wrote to a post box in March. That's the one before mine."

She looked at me for a long moment with the face I'd seen by the window in the reading room: not hostile, not frightened, assessing, the face of a woman whose job is to look at a thing and say what it will cost.
"You were in that room," she said. "In December. You put these on the table and he laughed."
"I didn't."
"No. You turned your head."

"I turned my head because I recognised my own initials, Mr Klippe, on a sheet of paper, in a room I'd been told was about an archive." She put her hand flat on the sheet. "I've been on the foundation's board for four years. I was asked to join because the bank funds it and someone from the bank should sit there. I've sat there. I've approved the minutes. I've never once been told what the reconciliation line reconciles." She stopped. "That's not an excuse. I'm head of risk. It's the opposite of an excuse."
"I'm not here for an excuse."
"What are you here for?"

"For you to read the rest," I said. "There's a schedule. There are four other companies. There's a list of three hundred people in this region who were each told one small thing and a word, and the word was continuity, and not one of them is on the list you're on. I've given them their sheets. I've got eleven left, and they're the board. Your board. The bank's. Twelve people who vote on the foundation's trustees once a year and have never seen an annex." I looked at her. "I'd like you to read the rest before Monday, because Monday is when you sign next quarter's schedule, and I'd like you to know what you're signing."
She was quiet. Then she said: "Give me the rest."
"All of it?"
"All of it. Tonight. Here." She looked at the red cell one more time. "I've approved thirty of these without reading. I'm going to read one."
<hr />
And Aylin.

I'd put her last on the list, and then I'd nearly taken her off it, because she was the one I liked and because her sheet was the thinnest: a woman who sat at a desk in a reading room and kept a card index and booked appointments for dead men. Her record was the diary. Her line on the schedule was the word conservation against a transfer of records from an archive in Apeldoorn, and her seat wasn't on any list, and her word was heritage, and I couldn't make the sheet say anything that would hurt her.
I gave it to her anyway, on the Thursday, at the desk, when I came up the stairs for the appointment she'd booked me into without my asking.
She read it. She read it the way she did everything, calmly, like a woman who's seen a lot of paper. And when she got to the end she looked up and said, "What do you think I'm conserving, Mr Klippe?"
I said I didn't know.

"No. You don't." She got up. She went to the card index, the wooden one, and she didn't open a drawer. She reached behind it and took out a book. A big one, bound, the kind with a ribbon, and she brought it to the desk and opened it and turned it round to face me.

It was the visitor book. Every person who had ever sat at the long table, in her handwriting and the handwriting of whoever had kept it before her, going back, when I turned to the front, to 1931. Name. Date. Shelfmark requested. And in a final column, headed Outcome, a word.

I read down the page she'd opened it at. The professor was there, in March, with a date and the shelfmark that was on the last page of his thin book, and the word in the last column was Deceased. Above him, a name I didn't know and the word Seated. Above that, Quiet. Quiet. Seated. Deceased. Declined. Quiet.
And at the bottom, in December, in Aylin's hand: my name. The date. No shelfmark; I hadn't asked for one. And in the outcome column, in fresh ink, one word.
Pending.

"I keep the book," said Aylin. "That's what I conserve. I've kept it for nine years and I've never been told what the last column means and I've never asked, because I was told it was heritage, and because it's very old, and because somebody has to." She looked at the sheet I'd given her, still on the desk. "You've just told me what it means."
"I didn't tell you anything. I gave you a list."

"You gave me a list I'm not on." She closed the visitor book. "I've had that book under my hand every working day for nine years, Mr Klippe. I know every name in it. I know which ones came back." She put the book down in front of me. "Copy it. Not now. He's upstairs. Come at midnight; the door's on my badge. Copy it and give it to whoever you're giving things to."
She looked at me as if the question were in bad taste.
"Because it's the last column," she said. "Because I wrote pending next to your name in December and I'd like, for once, to know what the word turns into before it does."

chapters.title: The leak
chapters.what: The brewer's report reaches them. The review comes forward to Monday. Handlers are sent to three addresses. Pieter rings from his car: there's a man at my door. Let him in, make tea, say nothing.
blocks: The brewer rang them on a Tuesday afternoon, and by Thursday night the schedule had changed, and I know that because of the one thing I'd done that nobody, not even Ana, knew about.
I'd set a watch.

Not on them. I'm not a hacker; I keep saying it because people keep forgetting. On a date. The new schedule, the one from the phone, had a date at the top: the day it came into force, the day Anneke was due to sign it, a Monday three weeks out. I'd photographed it. And in our own systems, in the continuity programme's own calendar, which I had every right to read, that Monday had an entry, blandly named, a recurring quarterly meeting that had been in the calendar for eleven years and that I'd been invited to because I was on the programme now.
On Thursday night at eleven the meeting moved.

Not far. From three weeks out to four days out. To Monday. This Monday. The entry changed, in the calendar, the way entries do, with a little note that said rescheduled by organiser, and the organiser was a name I'd never heard of at an address that was the foundation's, and I was sitting at the kitchen table with a hundred and ninety sheets still to deliver when my phone made the small sound that means a calendar has changed, and I looked, and I knew.

The review had come forward. The brewer had rung, and somebody had listened, and somebody had looked at the number of helpers who'd suddenly stopped closing tickets in the east of the country that fortnight, which I imagine looked, on their dashboard, like a dial being turned the wrong way, and somebody had done what I'd have done, which is pull the date in before the thing spreads.
She came down. She looked at my face.
"Monday," I said.
<hr />
I'm going to tell you what I thought in the next ten minutes, because it was the clearest I've ever thought and I don't expect to think that clearly again.

Monday was the schedule. Anneke signs, the quarter starts, the visits begin. I'd given Anneke everything on Friday and I didn't know yet what she'd do with it; she'd said I'm going to read one, and she'd taken the folder, and that was all. If she signed, the eleven addresses on the new schedule, plus whatever had been added since the brewer, got their visits, and I had a very good idea now what a visit was.

The board met on Monday too. Not about this. About the foundation's trustees, once a year, a formality, twelve people in a room approving a list of names they'd never met. That was the quarterly meeting in the calendar; that was what had moved. They'd pulled the foundation's annual confirmation forward to the same morning as the schedule, so that whatever the board voted, the schedule would already be signed.
Twelve board members. I had eleven sheets left and they were theirs, and I'd been going to deliver them next week, calmly, one at a time, the way I'd done the others.

I had four days. And they knew about me, properly now, not as a man with papers in a reading room but as a man with three hundred sheets in the east of the country, because the brewer had rung and I'd been in his yard.
"They'll come here," Ana said.
"Tonight?"

"I don't think so." I looked at the window, where the dog had been standing every evening for two months and where he was standing now. "They don't like fingerprints. A visit to the house of the man who's been handing out sheets, the week he hands them out, is a fingerprint. They'll go round me."
"Round you how?"
My phone rang.
<hr />
It was Pieter. It was twenty past eleven at night and it was Pieter, who in eleven years had never once rung me outside working hours, and I could hear, before he spoke, that he was in his car.
"James."
"Pieter."
"There's a man at my door."
I put the phone on the table and put it on speaker and Ana sat down across from me and we both looked at it.
"Tell me."

"I'm in the car. I was coming home. I'm at the end of my street and there's a car outside my house that isn't ours and there's a man on my step talking to Marieke." His voice was very steady, the steadiness of someone who's decided to be steady for the length of a phone call and will pay for it after. "He's got a folder. He's got a—he's got the same kind of coat, James. As the one at the drill. In the car park."
"Can you see his face?"

"No. He's turned away. Marieke's got the door on the chain. She does that. I told her to do that, years ago, I don't know why, she thought I was mad." A pause. "He's just standing there. He's not pushing. He's waiting."
Ana's hand had found mine on the table.
"Pieter, listen to me. I'm going to tell you what to do and I need you to do exactly this, and I'll explain afterwards, and you can be as angry as you want."
"Okay."

"Drive up to the house. Park where you always park. Get out. Walk up to him like it's nothing, because to him it is nothing; he doesn't know you've seen a sheet, and if he did he'd be surprised you were calm, so be calm. Say good evening. Say, can I help you."
"And then?"
"And then let him in."
Silence on the line.
"James—"

"Let him in. Make him tea. Sit down with him in your kitchen with Marieke and the kids upstairs and listen to whatever he says. He'll have a reason. It'll be about the bank, or the programme, or your security clearance, or something about the migration. It'll be plausible. It'll be kind. He'll ask you things. He'll ask whether anyone's been in touch with you about your work, and whether anyone's given you anything."
"And I say—"
"You say nothing."
"I can't say nothing, he's—"

"You can. That's the one thing you can do. You answer every question with something true that isn't the answer. You've been busy. The programme's a lot of lists. You don't really follow the politics. You're very happy to help. You let him talk, and you nod, and you make a second cup of tea, and you say nothing, and in forty minutes he'll leave, because he's not there to hurt you, Pieter. He's there to find out what you know. And if you give him nothing, then nothing is what he's got."
I could hear him breathing. I could hear the indicator ticking in his car.
"Why would he hurt me? I'm on the list. You showed me. I'm on it."
"You're on it because you said leave it. You stopped saying it four days ago. That's why he's on your step."
A long pause.
"Marieke's not on it," Pieter said. "Not separately. She's a number. She's one of my three."
"I know."
"And if I'd—" He stopped. "If I'd closed your ticket. On Monday. Like always. He wouldn't be here."
"So this is you. This is because of your sheet."

"Yes," I said. "It is. And I'm sorry. And I'd do it again. And I need you to go and let him in and make him tea, because the alternative is that he waits on your step until he's been seen waiting, and then it's not a visit any more, it's a thing with a fingerprint on it, and I don't know what they do about those and I don't want to find out at your house."
The indicator stopped. I heard the car move.
"He's turned round," Pieter said. "He's seen the headlights. He's—" A breath. "He's smiling. Jesus. He's waving."
"Wave back."
"James."
"Wave back, Pieter. Park the car. Say good evening. And ring me when he's gone, from the kitchen, with the kettle on, and I'll be here."

The line went quiet for a second, and then I heard a car door, and footsteps on gravel, and Pieter's voice, from a distance, saying "Evening. Can I help you?" in a tone I'd heard him use in a glass box for eleven years, the tone of a man who's never once lost his temper at work and has saved it all for somewhere, and then the call ended.
<hr />
He rang back at ten past midnight.
"He's gone."
"Tell me."

"He was from the foundation. Compliance. Routine, he said. A review of access on the programme, everyone who'd been added since the summer, nothing to worry about. He asked if anyone had approached me about the programme's data. I said the programme was mostly lists. He asked if I'd received any documents from colleagues outside normal channels. I said I got a lot of email. He asked—" Pieter stopped. "He asked about you. By name. Whether you were settling in. Whether I'd noticed anything. I said you liked lists." He laughed, once, not a good laugh. "He wrote that down. He had a little book. He wrote likes lists."
"Good."
"He asked after the kids. Their names. He knew their names, James. He asked if Lotte was still doing the hockey."
I didn't say anything.

"Then he thanked Marieke for the tea and he went. He shook my hand. He said if I thought of anything I should ring, and he gave me a card, and the card's got the foundation's name on it and a number, and the number's—" A pause. "It's the general number. The one with the music."
"I know the one."
"James, what the fuck is this."
"I'll tell you. Properly. Not tonight." I looked at Ana. "Tonight I need to know one thing. The man. Did you see his face in the kitchen?"
"Was it the man from the car park? At the drill? Julian?"
"No." Pieter sounded surprised at the question. "No, nothing like. Older. Grey. Nice voice. The kind of man you'd buy a pension from."
I closed my eyes.
"Okay," I said. "Thank you. Go to bed. Lock the door. You did it exactly right."

"I made him tea," said Pieter, in a voice of wonder. "He was in my kitchen asking about my daughter's hockey and I made him tea and said nothing and he left." And then, differently: "That's what you do. Isn't it. That's what you've been doing for a year. Sitting there saying nothing while they make themselves at home."
"Something like that."
"How do you stand it?"
"I've got a dog," I said, and meant it, and Pieter didn't understand, and said goodnight.
<hr />
Ana took her hand off mine.
"Three addresses," she said. She'd been counting on her fingers; I'd seen her. "You said they'd go round you. Pieter's one."

"Pieter's one. There'll be two more tonight. People who got sheets and stopped. They're checking the ones nearest the top." I pulled the laptop over and opened the list, the three hundred and eleven, with the ticks beside the ones I'd done and the eleven at the bottom with no ticks that were the board. "And on Monday Anneke signs the schedule, and the board confirms the trustees, and all of this goes back to being nothing."
"Unless."

"Unless the board doesn't confirm them. Unless twelve people walk into a room on Monday morning each holding a sheet of paper that says what the foundation they're about to approve has been charging their bank for, per flagged person, for thirty-one years. And who's kept. And who isn't."
"Eleven sheets."
"Eleven. Anneke's got hers."
"In four days."
"In three. Monday morning's too late; they need to have read it. Sunday night."

Ana looked at the list. She looked at the dog at the window. She looked at the clock on the oven, which said twenty to one on a Friday morning, and she did the thing she does, which is put the kettle on, and while it boiled she stood at the counter with her back to me and said, "Where are they? The eleven."
"All over. Two in the city. Three in The Hague. One in Zeeland. One in Groningen. One in Maastricht, God help us. The rest in between."
"That's a thousand kilometres."
"About that."
The kettle clicked. She didn't move.

"Mum can have Buddy till Monday," she said. "Mora comes with us; she's good in a car and she's a Doberman and I'd like a Doberman in the car. We leave tomorrow after dark, because if they're watching the house they're watching it in daylight like normal people. We do the far ones first and work back. You read, I drive, and nobody reads me any signs about pumping stations."

"And on Sunday night, when it's done, we go to Mum's and we sleep, and on Monday morning you're not anywhere near that building, you're somewhere with a scorecard, because if this works I don't want you in the room when it does, and if it doesn't I want to know where you are."

I looked at my wife, in her dressing gown, at one in the morning, with a kettle behind her and a list of eleven strangers in front of her, planning a thousand-kilometre drive to deliver the only thing that could stop a machine she'd told a man to his face she didn't believe in.
"You don't believe any of this," I said.
"Not a word." She poured the tea. "Drink that. Then print the eleven. Then sleep. I'll pack."

Buddy got down from the window at last and came and lay across my feet, and I sat at the table and printed eleven sheets, one at a time, while my wife packed a bag upstairs and the Doberman watched the door, and somewhere in the east of the country two more people were making tea for a nice man with a folder and saying nothing, because I'd told them to, and I hoped to God that nothing was enough.

chapters.title: The night before
chapters.what: Twelve envelopes to the twelve board members before Monday; Ana drives, Mora in the back, Frank has Buddy; a van for a while; midnight at the depot with Aylin; six in the morning, Anneke's doorstep. Source: v7/51. `[Santi: in or out]` — the handler's house by mistake (v8.2 PLACEHOLDER) is OUT: v7 doesn't have it. There's a wrong-house scene with a nobody instead, which you can swap for it.
blocks: We left on Sunday after dark, with a Doberman in the back and twelve envelopes in a supermarket bag on my lap, and I'd like to say we had a plan. We had a list and a full tank. Ana had a thermos. I had a stomach that had stopped working on Friday and hadn't sent anyone to explain.

Ana drove. She's a better driver than me in every way you can measure — and in a few you can't, like how she doesn't take it personally when a Volkswagen cuts in. I only drive when she lets me, which is mostly when she wants to sleep. She drove the way she does anything she's decided on, both hands, radio off, and Mora's head between the seats breathing on the gearstick like a second engine.

Buddy was at Frank's. That had been its own negotiation. Ana's mother's house was on the schedule — "Companion," in a font — so her mother was at her sister's in Gouda, and that left Frank, who lives alone in a flat with a bike in the hallway and a fridge full of oat milk and had never once been responsible for anything that breathes.
"What does he eat?"
"His food. It's in the bag. Not your food."
"What if he wants my food?"
"He'll want your food. He's a dog. Say no."

"I can't say no to that face, mate. Look at it." Buddy was looking at him from the bottom of the stairs to the flat — Frank's on the first floor — with the expression of an old man who has been told about the stairs and is filing a complaint. "Do I carry him?"
"You carry him."

He carried him. Twenty-eight kilos of grey dog up a narrow Rotterdam staircase, Frank going red and saying fuck on every third step, Buddy calm in his arms like a bishop being moved to a new diocese. At the top Frank put him down and said, "I still don't believe any of it, you know," and I said I knew, and he said, "Go on. Go. I've got the dog," and did the skull at me with his actual face, which I'd never seen him do without a phone.
<hr />

The list was twelve names. Twelve people who would sit in a room at nine on Monday morning and, at item four, confirm the trustees of a foundation that had been invoicing their bank per flagged person since 1994. Eleven of them had never heard my name. The twelfth was Anneke, who'd had her sheet for a week and read it twice, which I'm told is a thing she does not do.

Each envelope had a sheet. For the board the last box said something different from the others. Their names weren't missing from the list — they were the list, practically. So it said: On Monday you will be asked to confirm these trustees. This is what the foundation charges, and for what. These are the people it keeps. These are your staff who are not kept. Please check before you vote.
Please check. I'd rewritten that line eleven times. Every version that sounded clever sounded crazy.
"Read me the first one," Ana said.
"Leiderdorp. A woman. Treasury, twenty years. Two kids, one horse."
"How do you know about the horse?"
"She's got a horse in her profile picture."
"That's not knowing about a horse, James. That's a picture."
She was right. I wrote horse? next to it, like a man doing something.
<hr />

Leiderdorp was a letterbox. A neat brick house with a light on downstairs and the blue flicker of a television, and I'd decided — we'd decided, at the kitchen table, with the kettle — not to knock. A man at your door at nine on a Sunday night with a document is a man you call the police about. A letter is a letter.

So I walked up the path with the envelope like it was a parcel of something alive, and I put it through the slot, and the slot had one of those brush things inside, and the envelope stuck. Half in, half out. I pushed. It folded. I pulled it back to straighten it and the brush took the corner off.
Inside, a dog started barking. A small one — the kind that barks with its whole body.
I stood there with half a sheet of evidence in my hand and the other half somewhere in a stranger's hallway, and the television went quiet.

I ran. I'm not proud of it. I ran back down the path and got in the car and said "Go, go, go," and Ana didn't go, because Ana doesn't go for anybody who says it three times. She looked at me, and at the torn corner in my hand, and said, "Did you just post half of it?"
"Most of it. Eighty percent. The important part."
"Which part's in your hand?"
I looked. The bottom right corner. The word check.
"Fuck," I said.

She laughed so hard she had to put her forehead on the wheel, and Mora barked once at nothing, in solidarity, and the hall light came on in the house and we drove away with our lights off for the first twenty meters like idiots in a film, and then turned them on because it's illegal.
"Good start," Ana said. "Very professional."
<hr />

After that I had a system. I'm good at systems. I folded each envelope once more, and I held the flap of the letterbox up with two fingers, and I fed the envelope in slowly, like you'd feed a pill to a dog — and I want it understood that this was the most competent I was all night.

The Hague, two, ten minutes apart. Both letterboxes, both fine, both in streets so quiet I could hear the canal. At the second one a cat watched me from a windowsill with the face of a cat who had seen men post things before and thought less of all of them.
Delft. Leidschendam. Wassenaar. At Wassenaar the house had a gate, and the gate had an intercom, and the letterbox was on the far side of the gate. We sat in the car for four minutes looking at it.
"Throw it over," Ana said.
"It's a bank document."
"It's an envelope. Throw it."

I threw it over. It went beautifully, a little spin on it, and landed face down on a wet gravel drive about a meter from the door, and I stood at the gate in the drizzle and thought about everything I'd ever read about the history of the world, the edits, the forty-one books, the hill in Turkey, the professor in his blue chair, and all of it came down to this — a man in a damp coat watching an envelope get rained on in Wassenaar.
A light went on in the porch. The door opened. A man in a sweater came out, looked at the envelope, looked at the gate, looked at me.
"Klippe?" he said.
I didn't say anything. My mouth wouldn't.

He bent and picked the envelope up and shook the water off it. "Anneke rang. Four of us, this afternoon. She said a man might come with an envelope and that I should read it and then ring her." He looked at the car behind me, at the Doberman's head in the back window, ears up, like a hood ornament. "She didn't say you'd throw it."
"There's a gate."
"There's a bell on the gate."
"I didn't want to ring the bell."
He nodded like that was a reasonable thing for a grown man to say. "I'll read it tonight." Then, because he was Dutch and it was raining: "Do you want a coffee?"

I said we had more to do. He said, "Then go," and went in, and I walked back to the car, and Ana said, "Well?" and I said, "Anneke's been ringing people," and Ana started the engine and said, "Good," in a voice that told me how scared she'd been and wasn't going to say.

So that was two already turned. That's the thing nobody tells you about doing something like this — that halfway through, it stops being yours. Anneke had rung four. One of the four, in Voorschoten, met us at the door at half past eleven in a dressing gown with her own copy already printed, because Anneke had scanned hers and sent it, and she held out my envelope back to me and said, "I don't need two. Give it to someone who hasn't got one." It was the first time anyone had given me anything back in the whole year. I sat in the car afterwards and couldn't talk for about a minute, and Ana let me, and Mora put her nose in my ear, which is wet and enormous and didn't help at all, and helped.
<hr />
The wrong house was in Zoetermeer.

Number fourteen. I walked up to number fourteen, I fed the envelope in with my two-finger pill technique, and I was halfway back down the path when the door opened behind me and a very large man in boxer shorts said, "Hey."
I turned around. He had my envelope in his hand.
"This isn't me," he said.
"It's — fourteen?"
"Fourteen B." He pointed. Next door. A second door I hadn't seen, round the side, with a second bell. He looked at the name on the envelope. "That's the guy upstairs. He's never in. He's got a boat."
"Okay."
"What is it?"

I have spent eleven years at a bank explaining things to people who don't want them explained, and in that moment, in Zoetermeer, at a quarter to midnight, with a stranger in boxer shorts holding the end of the world, the best I had was: "It's about his pension."
"At midnight?"
"It's urgent. For a pension."

He looked at me for a long time. Then he said, "Okay, man," and posted it through the B door himself, carefully, with two fingers, and went back inside. I'd like to think he went to bed and never thought about it again. I'd like to think a lot of things.
"Wrong house?" Ana said.
"Wrong house."
"Was it a handler?"
"It was a guy with a boat. Next door. His neighbor's got a boat."
"So it was nobody."
"It was a very large nobody in his underwear."
She nodded. "This is how they're going to make the film," she said. "The underwear guy. They'll cut everything else."
<hr />
The van picked us up after Zoetermeer, on the A12.

White, no windows in the back, the kind every plumber in the country drives. It came onto the motorway at a junction behind us and stayed there. Three cars back. Then two. Then three again. Ana saw it first. She said, "There's a van," in exactly the voice she'd use for there's a sign, and I turned round, and Mora, who'd been asleep across the back seat with her legs in the air like a dead insect, turned over and sat up and looked out the back window and went completely still. She never goes still. She's a Doberman. She was built still and then someone forgot to turn it on.
"What do we do?"
"Nothing." My voice came out about a third higher than normal. "We drive. If they're following us they're following us to a letterbox. That's a fingerprint. They don't do fingerprints."
"You don't know that."
"I've read their paperwork."
"You've read their paperwork," Ana said, and changed lanes, and the van didn't, and then it did.

Forty kilometers. I counted. I counted the way I count everything when I'm scared, which is out loud in my head — exits, kilometer markers, the number of times Mora's ears moved. I held the supermarket bag of envelopes on my lap with both arms like it was a child that might jump out. I thought about Henk Boersma in his canal. I thought about Noor's message, there's a van on my street, and then nothing. I thought, very clearly, if this is it, I'd like it to be after the next envelope, at least, so I've done eight.
At the junction for Gouda, the van indicated — politely, in plenty of time — and came off, and was gone.
Mora watched the empty road behind us for another minute. Then she lay back down with a groan and put her chin on my seat.
"That was a van," Ana said.
"That was a van."
"I've decided it was a van."
"Good decision."

We never talked about it again. I've thought about it plenty. I think it was a van, and I think those were the longest forty kilometers of my life, and I think both of those things are true, and that's what they do to you, in the end — you can never again just see a van.
<hr />
At midnight I was at the depot.
"I'm not coming in," Ana said, in the car park, with the engine running. "I'm sitting here with the dog. If you're not out by one, I'm coming in with the dog, and I'm not asking anyone's badge."
"That's —"
"That's not a negotiation."

The building looked the way it always looked, low and long and grey behind its car park, the foundation's name on the sign and a smaller name under it, and no lights on the desk floor where I'd eaten a sandwich at desk forty during the drill. One light upstairs, behind the glass door.

Aylin had propped the outer door open with a fire extinguisher. That's the detail I can't get over. In a year of watching her — the pencil, the cards squared to the edge of the desk, the visitor book in its own grey box — I'd never seen her let a single thing lean on anything. A fire extinguisher, against a door, at midnight. It was the loudest thing she ever said to me.

She walked me up without a word. The reading room was lit by the one lamp on the long table. The visitor book was on it, open at 1931, and beside it a flat scanner, the kind libraries use, already warm.
"Forty minutes," she said. "He reads on Sunday nights. He comes at one."
"Okay."
She sat down at her desk with her back to me and picked up a card, and I understood the deal. She wouldn't watch. She wouldn't help. She wouldn't stop me.

My hands were shaking so badly I put the first page in upside down. Then the second. Somewhere around page ten I got a rhythm — lift, flatten, lid, button, the little light crawling across — and I stopped reading the words, on purpose, because I had forty minutes and because I was afraid of whose names I'd see. You can't not see some. Seated. Quiet. Deceased. Quiet. The same few words for ninety-five years in a dozen different hands, and I turned the pages like a man stacking plates.
And under my feet, the whole time, the floor hummed.

I'd heard it at the drill and filed it under air conditioning. It wasn't. It was lower, steadier — a big thing kept running in a room under a room — and somewhere around page sixty I stopped scanning for a second and just stood there with my hand flat on the table, feeling it come up through the wood. The seats weren't a list. They were a place. Right there. Under the carpet tiles.
Mora would have hated it. She hates the dishwasher.
I finished at twenty to one. I put the book back exactly how it had been, open at the front, and slid the memory card into the last envelope, the twelfth — Anneke's — and stood up.
"The last column," Aylin said, without turning around. "Next to you. What does it say now?"
I looked. December. My name, in her hand. One word.
"Pending."
"Good." She turned a card over. "When it changes, I'd like to be the one who writes it. I think I've earned that much."
I went down through the dark floor and out past the fire extinguisher and Ana had the car moving before my door was closed.
"Well?"
"I've got it. All of it."
"The floor hums."
She didn't ask what that meant. She knew me well enough to know I didn't know either.
<hr />

Three more after that. Utrecht, a letterbox, no lights. Bunnik, a man who opened the door himself at two in the morning because he couldn't sleep, read the first paragraph standing in his socks under the hall light, said "Fuck" very quietly, then "Thank you," and closed the door. And one we couldn't do — a farmhouse past Woerden at the end of a dyke road, no car, no lights, nobody. I put the envelope through the door anyway.
"He's away," Ana said. "That's one who votes without reading it."
"I know."
"Ring Anneke."
"It's three in the morning."
"Ring Anneke."
I rang Anneke. She answered on the second ring in a voice that had not been asleep, listened, said, "I'll try him. Thank you. Go to the next one," and hung up.
"I like her," Ana said.
"She approved the invoice thirty times."
"And then she read it."
<hr />
There was no next one. There was only Anneke's.

She lives in a terraced house in Rotterdam-Kralingen with a bike chained to the railing and a pot of something dead on the step. We got there at ten to six, in the first grey, and I sat in the car with the twelfth envelope for a while because I'd suddenly forgotten how to stand up. A year. Twelve envelopes. A torn corner in my coat pocket that said check.
I walked up the three steps. I lifted my hand to knock.
The door opened before I did.
She was dressed. Not in a dressing gown — properly dressed, for work, at ten to six on a Monday morning, shoes on, glasses on her head. She looked like she'd been standing in her hall for some time.
I held out the envelope. "The visitor book. All of it. Nineteen thirty-one to now."
She took it. She didn't open it.
"I've read it," she said. "The sheet. All of it. Twice." She looked past me at the car, at Ana with her head back against the headrest, at the dog's ears in the back window. "Go home, Mr Klippe."
"The farmhouse — Woerden —"
"I got him at four. He's driving back. He's not happy." She almost smiled. "Go home."
She closed the door. I stood on her step and looked at the dead plant for a while.
When I got back in the car, Ana didn't ask. She looked at me and I said, "Twelve," and she put her forehead down on the steering wheel — just for a second — and then lifted it and started the engine.
"Frank's," she said. "Buddy. Then bed. And then you're going to go and hit a ball with a stick and not be anywhere near any of this."
"It's Monday."
"Monday you hit a ball with a stick and keep your phone face down." She pulled out. "You've done your bit, Mulder. Now you just have to not be in the room."

I was asleep before Kralingen. The last thing I remember is Mora's chin landing on my shoulder, heavy and warm and smelling, I'm sorry to say, very strongly of whatever she'd found in Anneke's front garden.

chapters.title: Monday
chapters.what: James on the sixth green at seven with Buddy in the cart and the phone face down; the board votes at item four, eleven to one; Anneke takes the chair; her call; why they don't kill him, said once. Source: v7/52. Decision: Anneke's call gives only the result and the summons to the reading room; the terms and the "one last thing" move to The final conversation so they aren't said twice.
blocks: The sixth green at seven in the morning in December is the loneliest place I know, and I went there on purpose.

Nobody plays in December. The course is open because the course is always open, and the greenkeeper waves at you from the shed with the face of a man who's seen your type before — the ones who come out in the frost because something at home is worse. I'd slept forty minutes in the car — Ana says thirty — and none at all in the forty hours before that. My eyes felt like someone had sanded them.

I'd rung ahead from Frank's to ask if I could take the dog in the cart, which is not allowed. The woman in the shop said, "Buddy? The old one? Go on," because they'd known him for years and because nobody was going to see.
Frank, handing him back at the door of the flat, had looked about as tired as me.
"He snores," he said.
"I know."

"Like a man. Like a fat man on a train." He crouched down and put his forehead against Buddy's forehead for a second, which I'd never seen him do with anything. "He ate a croissant. I didn't give it to him. He took it. Off the table. With his face."
"Did you say no?"
"I said no. He looked at me." Frank stood up. "Go. Text me. Don't text me. I don't know. Text me."
<hr />

Buddy rode beside me with a blanket over his back and his chin on the edge of the cart, watching the fairways go by like an old man revisiting a town he used to live in. He can't walk a hole anymore — hasn't since the vet. But he can ride, and he likes the air, and I think he likes being somewhere that smells of nothing but grass and cold and, faintly, the greenkeeper's diesel, which to him is probably perfume.

I put the phone face down on the bench by the sixth green. I'd promised Ana — face down, on silent, and I'd look at it when I'd finished the hole and not before. I'm a man who checks dashboards for a living. I check the weather app when I can see out of the window. Face down was a big ask, and she knew it, and she'd asked anyway.
Then I took the putter and three balls out onto the frost and started knocking them around, badly, while twenty kilometers away twelve people walked into a room with coffee.
<hr />

I wasn't in the room, and I'm glad. What I know about it I got later — from Anneke, on the phone, and from Pieter, who heard it from someone who heard it from someone, which is how the bank hears everything. The two versions agree, which at a bank almost never happens, so I'll trust it.

The foundation's annual confirmation was item four. After the quarterly numbers and a thing about the Antwerp office. It had been item four for as long as anyone could remember, and it usually took about ninety seconds: the chair reads the trustees' names, someone proposes, someone seconds, hands go up, next.
This year, when the chair finished the names, the man from Wassenaar said, "Before we vote," and put a sheet of paper on the table. Slightly wavy, Pieter's source said. Like it had been wet.
The woman from Voorschoten put hers next to it.

And then — this is Anneke's version, and she's not a woman who decorates — there was a silence of the kind she'd only heard in a boardroom twice, both times in 2008, and in it nine more sheets came out of nine more folders and went down on the table. Not slammed. Just put down, the way you put down a card when everybody's already seen the hand. Leiderdorp's had a corner missing.
The chair looked at them. He looked at Anneke, who had never in four years spoken before a vote.

She said she'd approved the foundation's invoice thirty times and would like to read the line into the minutes. She read it. Continuity reconciliation, per flagged person. She read the number of persons on the last invoice, and on the first one, in 1994. She said she'd asked the foundation's director, on Saturday, by phone, what the line reconciled, and he'd said heritage, and she'd asked him to define heritage, and he hadn't.
Then — and this is the part Pieter's source loved — she asked for a vote to withhold confirmation of the trustees pending an audit. Bunnik seconded before she'd finished the sentence.
Eleven to one.

The one was the farmer from Woerden, who'd driven back from his boat at four in the morning and walked in at five to nine with my envelope still sealed in his coat. He voted no, Anneke said, not because he disagreed, but because he hadn't read it, and he was the kind of man who wouldn't vote for anything he hadn't read. She said she respected that enormously. She said she'd given him her own copy at the coffee break and watched him read it, and that he'd gone a color she hadn't seen on him before, and asked if he could change his vote, and been told no, that's not how minutes work.
Then she proposed that, pending the audit, the bank use its right under the funding agreement to put in interim trustees. She had names. One of them was hers.
That carried too.

By half past nine the foundation that had been counting a four-hundred-year-old bank's questions for thirty-one years had new trustees and a new chair. The old ones had been thanked for their service. The old man had been, in the language of these things, invited to step back. The quarter's schedule, the one with eleven addresses on it and Ana's mother's house and the word Companion in that font, was sitting on Anneke's desk unsigned, and would stay unsigned, she said, until somebody could explain to her satisfaction what a visit was.
Nobody shouted. Nobody was arrested. The minutes ran to a page and a half, and you could read them start to finish and not know anything had happened at all.
<hr />

I'd holed out on the sixth by nine, in eleven strokes — a record, not a good one — and I'd sat down on the bench next to the phone and not turned it over. Buddy had gone to sleep in the cart. The sun had come round enough to start melting the frost in a line across the green, and I watched the line move, the way I used to watch progress bars when I was a junior and didn't know yet that they lie.

I did not pray. I'd like that known. I thought about it, though. I thought: if there is anybody, now would be a good time, and then I thought that if there was anybody they'd been watching this whole year and probably had opinions about the torn corner.

The phone buzzed against the bench at twenty to ten. It buzzed twice. I let it buzz a third time — I don't know why, some superstition about seeming calm in front of a phone — and then I turned it over.
"Mr Klippe."
"Mrs de Wit."

"It's done." Her voice was exactly the same as at six in the morning on her step. "Eleven to one. I'm the chair. The trustees are out. The schedule isn't signed and won't be." A pause. "I'm not going to give you the details. You weren't there, and I'd like that to stay true."
"Okay."
I couldn't say anything else. I was looking at the dog.

"He's asked to see you," she said. "The old one. Thursday, in the reading room. I'll be there. He'd like to talk, he says, because it no longer matters." Another pause. "Bring nothing. I'll tell you the terms there. I don't like telephones."
"Can I ask you something?"
"Once."
"Why am I still here?" It came out smaller than I meant. "They've done it before. The canal. The blue chair. It worked. Why not me?"
She didn't answer straight away. I heard her close a door on her end.

"Because it was cheap," she said. "Before. One man, one address, a plausible ending, nobody to connect it. That's the whole method — nobody ever sees a hand." A breath. "You've given two hundred people a page with their own name on it. Eleven of them sat in a room this morning holding one. If anything happens to you now, two hundred people know who did it, and they're the two hundred who do the work. A body would confirm every envelope." The faintest dryness. "You made yourself too expensive. I don't think you planned it."
"I didn't."
"No. I didn't think so." Then: "Go home. Sleep. There's frost."
She hung up.
<hr />

I said "fuck" — quietly, to the green, not angry, just to have said something out loud to somebody. Then I sat there a while longer. The greenkeeper came past on the mower and lifted a hand and I lifted one back. I texted Ana one word, which was eleven, and then I texted Frank the same word, and Frank sent back the skull and then, about a minute later, wait is that good, and then, ok it's good, I googled the board, which I still don't understand.

Then I rang my dad, which I hadn't planned and don't do on Mondays, and he asked if something was wrong, and I said no, and we talked about his gutters for six minutes. It was the best conversation we've had in years. He doesn't know why.
The line of melted frost reached the far edge of the green, and the whole thing went from grey to that green that looks freshly painted.

Buddy woke up. He looked at me. He looked at the course. He made the small grunt that means he'd like to get down, which he hadn't made on a golf course since the summer, and I lifted him down — carefully, all twenty-eight kilos, my back registering a formal complaint — and set him on the grass.

He stood there with his legs not quite trusting him and his nose up in the cold. Then he walked out onto the sixth green. Four steps. Slow. He stopped about a meter from the hole, right in the sun, and lay down on it, on the actual putting surface, which you are absolutely not allowed to do, and put his chin on his paws.
The greenkeeper, at the far end of the fairway, saw. He looked for a second. Then he turned the mower round and went to cut something else.

chapters.title: The final conversation
chapters.what: The old man, removed, in the reading room one last time, Anneke beside him, James with nothing in his hands; the nine beats in order, as a conversation that keeps getting interrupted; the terms; the one last thing, never written down. Source: v7/53, rewritten. The film/people claims are only the old man's boasts; James confirms none of them. The book James may publish is one of Anneke's terms, separate from the unspoken last thing.
blocks: Aylin booked it. That's the part I keep coming back to. The Thursday after the vote I came up the stairs with nothing in my hands — Anneke had said nothing, and I'm a literal man — and Aylin looked up from her cards and said, "He's in. He's got the room till four. I've put you down," in exactly the voice she'd used on the second of December. Then she wrote something in the visitor book. I didn't look.

He was at the long table. Anneke was next to him, not by the window this time — next to him, with a notebook, like a lawyer sitting with a client who's agreed to talk. No tray. The lamp on. He looked, I'm sorry to say, extremely well. Better than me. I'd slept about nine hours since Sunday.
There was no dog under the table. First table in a year. I noticed it the way you notice a tooth is gone.
"Mr Klippe. Sit. You've brought nothing."
"I was told."

"Good. People have been bringing things to this table for forty years. I never needed any of it." He folded his hands. "I've been retired. I'm to have an office and no keys. I find I don't mind. I'd like to talk — because I enjoy it, and because it no longer matters. So. Ask."
I'd made a list all week and thrown it away that morning in the car park.
"Why does it never come out?"

He laughed, the small pleased sound from December. "Oh, that's the right one. Everybody asks what is it. Nobody asks why it never comes out." He tapped the table near Anneke's notebook. "Write that down."
"I'm not your secretary," Anneke said, and didn't write it down.
<hr />

"It comes out all the time," he said. "That's what you've got wrong. It comes out every few years, and every time, we're there first, telling it bigger. You know the phrase — soft disclosure. Films easing people toward the truth." He shook his head. "It was never disclosure. It's inoculation. Show people the truth as a film and they can never again hear it as a fact."
"That's a nice line. Did you practice it?"

"For about thirty years. Men in Black — every man who finds the agency is now the man in the film. I Origins — a good theory, you can track a person by the eye across lives, so we made it a love story with a twist and nobody ever said it again with a straight face. The moon as a collector of souls — that one was just for fun. Sometimes we have fun. Inception, so the writers we nudge would think their best ideas were their own dreams. Dracula, so we don't die belongs to a man in a cape."
"Right."
"And Walt."
"Walt Disney."
"Walt was our best customer. He never knew."
I laughed. I didn't mean to. It came out of me like a sneeze — a real laugh, in that room, with the lamp — and once it started I couldn't stop it, and I had to put my hand over my face.
"Something funny?"
"Walt fucking Disney," I said. "Sorry. You've got a building full of — and you're telling me Walt Disney. Is he frozen? Is that next? Is he downstairs?"
"Freezing," he said, quite seriously, "is meaningless. I'll come to that."
"Course you will."
Anneke was looking at her notebook. I think — I'm not sure — the corner of her mouth moved.
<hr />

"The second thing is the mirror," he said. "Sometimes a person is handed a true thing. Not finds it. Is handed it. A writer in California, 1974 — pink light, he said. It told him his son was sick, and he took the boy to a doctor and the boy was." He spread his hands. "And then he spent eight years and a million words trying to prove to himself it hadn't happened. We didn't touch him. The true thing, in a mind trained to doubt, eats itself. Now anyone who has what he had thinks of him and thinks madman."
"You've got a shelf," I said. "The professor had a shelf. VALIS was on it."
"Of course it was. He was a careful man."
"So which is it — you made him or you just read him?"
"We read everybody, Mr Klippe."
<hr />

"The internet frightened us," he said. "I was in this room when it arrived. For five years I thought it was the end — people telling each other things faster than we could tell the other version. Then the social part came. Then the machines that write." He smiled. "We'd misunderstood our own job for four hundred years. We thought it was to make people believe the wrong thing. It's not. It's to make them doubt everything. Doubt is cheaper than belief. A machine that makes everything sound equally possible is the best employee we've ever had, and it doesn't want a seat."
"You're saying AI is yours."
"I'm saying it doesn't need to be."

I thought about Frank and his skull and his tools that were going to replace all of us. I thought about page 212. I didn't say any of it. I was scared he'd say yes and I'd believe him, which is exactly the problem he'd just described, and I was sitting in the middle of it, believing.
<hr />
"The seats," I said. "Under us. I can hear them."

"You found the seats and thought they were the point. They all do. A few hundred people kept alive through something, coming out, inheriting." He made a face like he'd smelled milk. "That's what they're told. The seats are fuel. Promise a middle manager a seat and he'll keep the machine running for thirty years. Give him one and he'll do anything to deserve it. Nobody's being saved. Freezing —"
"Is meaningless. Yeah. Walt."
"— is meaningless," he said, slightly louder.
"And the boy in Tibet?" I don't know why I asked that one. It was on the list I'd thrown away.

"Real." He said it like he was confirming a train time. "The search finds something, often enough. We left it as public as possible. Robes. Cameras. Once it's done in a palace, it can't be done in a kitchen. A boy who points at his dead grandfather's pen and says mine — his mother thinks of the palace, and laughs."
I thought about a hand cracked at the knuckles. I didn't say that either.
<hr />
"And now," he said, and leaned in — not for secrecy, for pleasure — "the one you came for."
"I didn't come for anything. I was told to come."

"You came for the forty-one." He waited. I let him. "You think we took a fact out of those books. Given to arose. We didn't take a fact. We took the passing. How a thing goes from a person to a person. And the thing that was passed —" he lowered his voice — "is how to keep what you are across the gap. Nobody here is frozen, Mr Klippe. Some of us simply remember. Life to life. That's what we took out of every book in the world. And kept."
The floor hummed.
"So you come back," I said. "Same people. Same building. Same names, more or less."
"More or less."
"With the manual."
"With the manual."
And then I said it, and I hadn't planned to, and it came up from a kitchen floor in November, the fourth night, and I said it the way you'd say it to a dog.
"It's not for staying."
He looked at me.

"The remembering," I said. "What you kept. I had it — not from a book. On a floor. And the thing you're shown, when you're shown it, isn't how to come back. It's how to leave. Remembering is so you don't have to do this again. You've got the instructions for the door, and you've been using them to go round and round the same room."
It was very quiet. Even the floor seemed to go quiet, which it didn't, I know it didn't, but that's how I remember it.
"Yes," he said.

That was all, for a second. Then: "We chose to stay. What would you have done? On one side of the door, everything you've ever been afraid of. On the other, this room, these people, the work, a chair you know. We chose the room. Every time it costs us more. Every time there's less of us to bring." He looked at his hands. "We don't know where the door goes. We stopped wanting to know a long time ago."
I wanted to feel sorry for him. I checked, the way you check a pocket. I didn't.
<hr />
"So tell it," I said. "If you're done. If it doesn't matter. Let it out."
"It can't come out," Anneke said.
We both looked at her. She hadn't spoken since I'm not your secretary.

"I've spent a week on this," she said. "Not his version. Mine. Suppose everybody knew, tomorrow, as a fact — that it goes on, that fear's what scatters you. What happens on Thursday? Nobody goes to work. The hospitals, the water, the grid — all of it runs on people who are more afraid of dying than of their jobs." She closed the notebook. "They made sure of that. It's been built that way on purpose for a very long time. Take the fear out fast and you don't get enlightenment. You get collapse. And after a collapse with no continuity, the people who run what's left are killers and savages. That's not his theory. I've read the recovery plans. That's what they're for."
"So the deal's the same as it always was," I said.

"No. The deal's mine now." She opened the notebook again, to a page she'd already written. "The nightly job goes. Frank closes it, through a ticket, like a normal person. The line on the invoice steps down — not to nothing, there's a contract, but down. The annex gets rewritten by HR, not by a foundation. We'll help where we see fit. We won't help it collapse. Continuity stays. And you keep quiet." She looked up. "The bank, the names, the foundation. Nothing."
"And him?" I didn't say the name. I didn't have to.
"Julian Kalder's contract is under review. He didn't come in Monday. He's not answering." She paused. "He's not the bank's problem anymore. He may be somebody's. I've chosen not to ask whose."
The old man smiled at the table. It was the only time I wanted to hit him.

"And you can write a book," Anneke said. "You asked me the day you gave me my sheet whether you would ever be allowed to. Under your own name. It claims nothing and names nobody. If anyone asks, it's a novel."
"We've been publishing those for four hundred years," the old man said. "Nobody reads the middle."
"I read the middle," I said.
"Yes. Well. There's one of you."
"Agreed," I said. To her, not to him. "All of it."
"Good." She capped her pen. "Is there anything else?"
"One thing. It's small."
"Say it."

I didn't say it out loud. I leaned over and said it to her, low, close to her ear, like a man telling a secret at a wedding, and the old man watched us and didn't hear it, and I've never written it down and I'm not going to now. It wasn't about the bank. It was mine.
She sat back. She looked at me for a long moment.
"Yes," she said. "That I can do." And she wrote one line in the notebook, and turned the page so it was face down.
<hr />
He stood up. He was old and it took him a moment. Anneke didn't help and he didn't ask.
"Leave it," he said to me.
Two words. The ones Pieter had used. The ones the whole building was built on.

"Not as a threat. As advice from a man who's had the keys. You've bought time — a generation, perhaps, in this part of the world. Then it starts again somewhere else, under a different word. You'll be dead by then. So will I." He looked at the door. "When it's your turn, do what you did on the floor. And go. Don't come back. I'd like one of us to get it right."
He went out. Anneke stayed sitting with her hand flat on her notebook.
"Is he right?" I said. "Eighteen months and you're him?"

"I don't know." She stood. "I approved an invoice thirty times without reading it. I'm reading things now." She picked up her coat. "He's got the room till four. Stay, if you like. It's the only room in the building that doesn't hum."
